Painting - Wikipedia — Ink paintings are done with a liquid that contains pigments or dyes and is used to color a
Painting - Wikipedia — surface to produce an image, text, or design. Ink is used for drawing with a pen, brush, or
Painting - Wikipedia — quill. Ink can be a complex medium, composed of solvents, pigments, dyes, resins,
Painting - Wikipedia — lubricants, solubilizers, surfactants, particulate maer, ﬂuorescers, and other materials. e
Painting - Wikipedia — components of inks serve many purposes; the ink's carrier, colorants, and other
Painting - Wikipedia — additives control ﬂow and thickness of the ink and its appearance when dry.
Painting - Wikipedia — Enamels are made by painting a substrate, typically metal, with powdered glass;
Painting - Wikipedia — minerals called color oxides provide coloration. Aer ﬁring at a temperature of 750–850 degrees Celsius (1380–1560 degrees
Painting - Wikipedia — Fahrenheit), the result is a fused lamination of glass and metal. Unlike most painted techniques, the surface can be handled
Painting - Wikipedia — and weed. Enamels have traditionally been used for decoration of precious objects,[42] but have also been used for other
Painting - Wikipedia — purposes. Limoges enamel was the leading centre of Renaissance enamel painting, with small religious and mythological
Painting - Wikipedia — scenes in decorated surrounds, on plaques or objects such as salts or caskets. In the 18th century, enamel painting enjoyed a
Painting - Wikipedia — vogue in Europe, especially as a medium for portrait miniatures.[43] In the late 20th century, the technique of porcelain
Painting - Wikipedia — enamel on metal has been used as a durable medium for outdoor murals.[44]

Painting - Wikipedia — ceilings. e word fresco comes from the Italian word aﬀresco [afˈfresːko], which
Painting - Wikipedia — derives from the Latin word for fresh. Frescoes were oen made during the Renaissance and
Painting - Wikipedia — other early time periods. Buon fresco technique consists of painting in pigment mixed with

Painting - Wikipedia — plaster, intonaco, is used. A secco painting, in contrast, is done on dry plaster (secco is "dry" in Italian). e pigments require a binding
Painting - Wikipedia — medium, such as egg (tempera), glue or oil to aach the pigment to the wall.
Painting - Wikipedia — Oil painting is the process of painting with pigments that are bound with a medium of
Painting - Wikipedia — drying oil, such as linseed oil, poppyseed oil which was widely used in early modern
Painting - Wikipedia — Europe. Oen the oil was boiled with a resin such as pine resin or even frankincense; these
Painting - Wikipedia — were called 'varnishes' and were prized for their body and gloss. Oil paint eventually
Painting - Wikipedia — became the principal medium used for creating artworks as its advantages became widely
Painting - Wikipedia — known. e transition began with Early Netherlandish painting in northern Europe, and by
Painting - Wikipedia — the height of the Renaissance oil painting techniques had almost completely replaced
Painting - Wikipedia — tempera paints in the majority of Europe.
Painting - Wikipedia — Pastel is a painting medium in the form of a stick, consisting of pure powdered pigment and a binder.[45] e pigments used
Painting - Wikipedia — in pastels are the same as those used to produce all colored art media, including oil paints; the binder is of a neutral hue and
Painting - Wikipedia — low saturation. e color eﬀect of pastels is closer to the natural dry pigments than that of any other process.[46] Because the
Painting - Wikipedia — surface of a pastel painting is fragile and easily smudged, its preservation requires protective measures such as framing under glass; it may also be sprayed with a
Painting - Wikipedia — ﬁxative. Nonetheless, when made with permanent pigments and properly cared for, a pastel painting may endure unchanged for centuries. Pastels are not susceptible, as
Painting - Wikipedia — are paintings made with a ﬂuid medium, to the cracking and discoloration that result from changes in the color, opacity, or dimensions of the medium as it dries.

Painting - Wikipedia — Acrylic paint is fast drying paint containing pigment suspension in acrylic polymer
Painting - Wikipedia — emulsion. Acrylic paints can be diluted with water but become water-resistant when dry.
Painting - Wikipedia — Depending on how much the paint is diluted (with water) or modiﬁed with acrylic gels,
Painting - Wikipedia — media, or pastes, the ﬁnished acrylic painting can resemble a watercolor or an oil painting,
Painting - Wikipedia — or have its own unique characteristics not aainable with other media. e main practical
Painting - Wikipedia — diﬀerence between most acrylics and oil paints is the inherent drying time.[47] Oils allow
Painting - Wikipedia — for more time to blend colors and apply even glazes over under-paintings. is slow drying
Painting - Wikipedia — aspect of oil can be seen as an advantage for certain techniques but may also impede the
Painting - Wikipedia — artist's ability to work quickly. Another diﬀerence is that watercolors must be painted onto
Painting - Wikipedia — a porous surface, primarily watercolor paper. Acrylic paints can be used on many diﬀerent
Painting - Wikipedia — surfaces.[47][48] Both acrylic and watercolor are easy to clean up with water. Acrylic paint
Painting - Wikipedia — should be cleaned with soap and water immediately following use. Watercolor paint can be
Painting - Wikipedia — cleaned with just water.[49][50][51]

Painting - Wikipedia — Aerosol paint (also called spray paint)[55] is a type of paint that comes in a sealed pressurized container and is released in a ﬁne spray mist when depressing a valve
Painting - Wikipedia — buon. A form of spray painting, aerosol paint leaves a smooth, evenly coated surface. Standard sized cans are portable, inexpensive and easy to store. Aerosol primer
Painting - Wikipedia — can be applied directly to bare metal and many plastics.

Painting - Wikipedia — Miniature paintings were the primary form of painting in pre-colonial India. ese were done on a special paper (known as wasli) using mineral and natural colours.
Painting - Wikipedia — Miniature painting is not one style but a group of several styles of schools of painting such as Mughal, Pahari, Rajasthani, Company style etc.
Painting - Wikipedia — Mughal miniature painting is a particular style of South Asian, particularly North Indian (more speciﬁcally, modern day India and Pakistan), painting conﬁned to
Painting - Wikipedia — miniatures either as book illustrations or as single works to be kept in albums (muraqqa). It emerged[73] from Persian miniature painting (itself partly of Chinese origin)
Painting - Wikipedia — and developed in the court of the Mughal Empire of the 16th to 18th centuries. Mughal painting immediately took a much greater interest in realistic portraiture than
Painting - Wikipedia — was typical of Persian miniatures. Animals and plants were the main subject of many miniatures for albums, and were more realistically depicted.[74][75][76]

Painting - Wikipedia — Rajasthani painting evolved and ﬂourished in the royal courts of Rajputana[77] in northern India, mainly during the
Painting - Wikipedia — 17th century. Artists trained in the tradition of the Mughal miniature were dispersed from the imperial Mughal court, and
Painting - Wikipedia — developed styles also drawing from local traditions of painting, especially those illustrating the Sanskrit Epics, the
Painting - Wikipedia — Mahabharata and Ramayana. Subjects varied, but portraits of the ruling family, oen engaged in hunting or their daily
Painting - Wikipedia — activities, were generally popular, as were narrative scenes from the epics or Hindu mythology, as well as some genre
Painting - Wikipedia — scenes of landscapes, and humans.[78][79]
Painting - Wikipedia — Punjab Hills or Pahari painting of which Kangra, Guller, Basholi were major sub-styles. Kangra painting is the
Painting - Wikipedia — pictorial art of Kangra, named aer Kangra, Himachal Pradesh, a former princely state, which patronized the art. It
Painting - Wikipedia — became prevalent with the fading of Basohli school of painting in mid-18th century.[80][81] e focal theme of Kangra
Painting - Wikipedia — painting is Shringar (the erotic sentiment). e subjects are seen in Kangra painting exhibit the taste and the traits of the
Painting - Wikipedia — lifestyle of the society of that period.[82] e artists adopted themes from the love poetry of Jayadeva and Keshav Das
Painting - Wikipedia — who wrote ecstatically of the love of Radha and Krishna with Bhakti being the driving force.[83][84]
Painting - Wikipedia — Company style is a term for a hybrid Indo-European style of paintings made
Painting - Wikipedia — in India by Indian artists, many of whom worked for European patrons in the
Painting - Wikipedia — British East India Company or other foreign Companies in the 18th and 19th
Painting - Wikipedia — centuries.[85] ree distinct styles of Company Painting emerged in three British
Painting - Wikipedia — Power Centres – Delhi, Calcua and Madras. e subject maer of company
Painting - Wikipedia — paintings made for western patrons was oen documentary rather than
Painting - Wikipedia — imaginative, and as a consequence, the Indian artists were required to adopt a
Painting - Wikipedia — more naturalistic approach to painting than had traditionally been usual.[86][87]

Painting - Wikipedia — Pichwai paintings are paintings on textile and usually depicting stories from the

Painting - Wikipedia — Pichwai paintings were made and are still made mainly in Rajasthan, India. However very few were made in the Deccan
Painting - Wikipedia — region, but these are extremely rare. e purpose of pichhwais, other than artistic appeal, is to narrate tales of Krishna to the
Painting - Wikipedia — illiterate. Temples have sets with diﬀerent images, which are changed according to the calendar of festivals celebrating the
Painting - Wikipedia — deity.[89]

Painting - Wikipedia — e Bengal School[96] was an art movement and a style of Indian painting that originated in Bengal, primarily Kolkata and Shantiniketan, and ﬂourished throughout the
Painting - Wikipedia — Indian subcontinent, during the British Raj in the early 20th century.[97] e Bengal school arose as an avant garde and nationalist movement reacting against the
Painting - Wikipedia — academic art styles previously promoted in India, both by Indian artists such as Raja Ravi Varma and in British art schools. e school wanted to establish a distinct
Painting - Wikipedia — Indian style which celebrated the indigenous cultural heritage. In an aempt to reject colonial aesthetics, Abanindranath Tagore also turned to China and Japan with the
Painting - Wikipedia — intent of promoting a pan-Asian aesthetic and incorporated elements from Far Eastern art, such as the Japanese wash technique.[98][99][100]

Painting - Wikipedia — Allegory is a ﬁgurative mode of representation conveying meaning other than the literal. Allegory communicates its message
Painting - Wikipedia — by means of symbolic ﬁgures, actions, or symbolic representation. Allegory is generally treated as a ﬁgure of rhetoric, but an
Painting - Wikipedia — allegory does not have to be expressed in language: it may be addressed to the eye and is oen found in realistic painting. An
Painting - Wikipedia — example of a simple visual allegory is the image of the grim reaper. Viewers understand that the image of the grim reaper is a
Painting - Wikipedia — symbolic representation of death.
Painting - Wikipedia — In Spanish art, a bodegón is a still life painting depicting pantry items, such as victuals, game, and drink, oen arranged on a
Painting - Wikipedia — simple stone slab, and also a painting with one or more ﬁgures, but signiﬁcant still life elements, typically set in a kitchen or
Painting - Wikipedia — tavern. Starting in the Baroque period, such paintings became popular in Spain in the second quarter of the 17th century. e tradition
Painting - Wikipedia — of still life painting appears to have started and was far more popular in the contemporary Low Countries, today Belgium and
Painting - Wikipedia — Netherlands (then Flemish and Dutch artists), than it ever was in southern Europe. Northern still lifes had many subgenres: the
Painting - Wikipedia — breakfast piece was augmented by the trompe-l'œil, the ﬂower bouquet, and the vanitas. In Spain, there were much fewer patrons for
Painting - Wikipedia — this sort of thing, but a type of breakfast piece did become popular, featuring a few objects of food and tableware laid on a table.
Painting - Wikipedia — A ﬁgure painting is a work of art in any of the painting media with the primary subject being the human ﬁgure, whether clothed or
Painting - Wikipedia — nude. Figure painting may also refer to the activity of creating such a work. e human ﬁgure has been one of the contrast subjects of
Painting - Wikipedia — art since the ﬁrst Stone Age cave paintings and has been reinterpreted in various styles throughout history.[102] Some artists well
Painting - Wikipedia — known for ﬁgure painting are Peter Paul Rubens, Edgar Degas, and Édouard Manet.
Painting - Wikipedia — Illustration paintings are those used as illustrations in books, magazines, and theater or movie posters and comic books. Today, there is
Painting - Wikipedia — a growing interest in collecting and admiring the original artwork. Various museum exhibitions, magazines, and art galleries have
Painting - Wikipedia — devoted space to the illustrators of the past. In the visual art world, illustrators have sometimes been considered less important in comparison with ﬁne artists and
Painting - Wikipedia — graphic designers. But as the result of computer game and comic industry growth, illustrations are becoming valued as popular and proﬁtable artworks that can acquire
Painting - Wikipedia — a wider market than the other two, especially in Korea, Japan, Hong Kong and the United States.

Painting - Wikipedia — Landscape painting is a term that covers the depiction of natural scenery such as mountains, valleys, trees, rivers, lakes, and
Painting - Wikipedia — forests, and especially art where the main subject is a wide view, with its elements arranged into a coherent composition. In
Painting - Wikipedia — other works, landscape backgrounds for ﬁgures can still form an important part of the work. e sky is almost always
Painting - Wikipedia — included in the view, and weather is oen an element of the composition. Detailed landscapes as a distinct subject are not
Painting - Wikipedia — found in all artistic traditions and develop when there is already a sophisticated tradition of representing other subjects. e
Painting - Wikipedia — two main traditions spring from Western painting and Chinese art, going back well over a thousand years in both cases.
Painting - Wikipedia — Portrait paintings are representations of a person, in which the face and its expression is
Painting - Wikipedia — predominant. e intent is to display the likeness, personality, and even the mood of the
Painting - Wikipedia — person. e art of the portrait ﬂourished in Ancient Greek and especially Roman sculpture,
Painting - Wikipedia — where siers demanded individualized and realistic portraits, even unﬂaering ones. One
Painting - Wikipedia — of the best-known portraits in the Western world is Leonardo da Vinci's painting titled Mona Lisa, which is thought to be a portrait of
Painting - Wikipedia — Lisa Gherardini, the wife of Francesco del Giocondo.[109]
Painting - Wikipedia — Warhol was one of the most proliﬁc portrait painters of the 20th century. Warhol's painting Orange Shot Marilyn of Marilyn Monroe is
Painting - Wikipedia — an iconic early example of his work from the 1960s, and Orange Prince (1984) of the pop singer Prince is later example, both exhibiting
Painting - Wikipedia — Warhol's unique graphic style of portraiture.[110][111][112]
Painting - Wikipedia — A still life is a work of art depicting mostly inanimate subject maer, typically commonplace objects—which may be either natural
Painting - Wikipedia — (food, ﬂowers, plants, rocks, or shells) or human-made (drinking glasses, books, vases, jewelry, coins, pipes, and so on). With origins in
Painting - Wikipedia — the Middle Ages and Ancient Greek/Roman art, still life paintings give the artist more leeway in the arrangement of design elements
Painting - Wikipedia — within a composition than do paintings of other types of subjects such as landscape or portraiture. Still life paintings, particularly
Painting - Wikipedia — before 1700, oen contained religious and allegorical symbolism relating to the objects depicted. Some modern still life breaks the two-dimensional barrier and employs

Painting - Wikipedia — A veduta is a highly detailed, usually large-scale painting of a cityscape or some other vista. is genre of landscape
Painting - Wikipedia — originated in Flanders, where artists such as Paul Bril painted vedute as early as the 16th century. As the itinerary of the
Painting - Wikipedia — Grand Tour became somewhat standardized, vedute of familiar scenes like the Roman Forum or the Grand Canal recalled
Painting - Wikipedia — early ventures to the Continent for aristocratic Englishmen. In the later 19th century, more personal impressions of
Painting - Wikipedia — cityscapes replaced the desire for topographical accuracy, which was satisﬁed instead by painted panoramas.

Drawing - Wikipedia — Drawing
Drawing - Wikipedia — Drawing is a visual art that uses an instrument to mark paper or another two-dimensional surface. e instruments used to
Drawing - Wikipedia — make a drawing are pencils, crayons, pens with inks, brushes with paints, or combinations of these, and in more modern
Drawing - Wikipedia — times, computer styluses with graphics tablets or gamepads in VR drawing soware.
Drawing - Wikipedia — A drawing instrument releases a small amount of material onto a surface, leaving a visible mark. e most common support
Drawing - Wikipedia — for drawing is paper, although other materials, such as cardboard, vellum, wood, plastic, leather, canvas, and board, have
Drawing - Wikipedia — been used. Temporary drawings may be made on a blackboard or whiteboard. Drawing has been a popular and fundamental
Drawing - Wikipedia — means of public expression throughout human history. It is one of the simplest and most eﬃcient means of communicating
Drawing - Wikipedia — ideas.[1] e wide availability of drawing instruments makes drawing one of the most common artistic activities.
Drawing - Wikipedia — In addition to its more artistic forms, drawing is frequently used in commercial illustration, animation, architecture,
Drawing - Wikipedia — engineering, and technical drawing. A quick, freehand drawing, usually not intended as a ﬁnished work, is sometimes called
Drawing - Wikipedia — a sketch. An artist who practices or works in technical drawing may be called a draer, drasman, or draughtsman.[2]
Drawing - Wikipedia — Drawing is one of the oldest forms of human expression within the visual arts. It is generally concerned with the marking of
Drawing - Wikipedia — lines and areas of tone onto paper/other material, where the accurate representation of the visual world is expressed upon a
Drawing - Wikipedia — plane surface.[3] Traditional drawings were monochrome, or at least had lile colour,[4] while modern colored-pencil
Drawing - Wikipedia — drawings may approach or cross a boundary between drawing and painting. In Western terminology, drawing is distinct
Drawing - Wikipedia — from painting, even though similar media oen are employed in both tasks. Dry media, normally associated with drawing, such as chalk, may be used in pastel
Drawing - Wikipedia — paintings. Drawing may be done with a liquid medium, applied with brushes or pens. Using a brush for drawing is very widespread and here it is more the process of
Drawing - Wikipedia — using lines and hatching, that characterises something as a drawing. Similar supports likewise can serve both: painting generally involves the application of liquid paint
Drawing - Wikipedia — onto prepared canvas or panels, but sometimes an underdrawing is drawn ﬁrst on that same support.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Drawing is oen exploratory, with considerable emphasis on observation, problem-solving and composition. Drawing is also regularly used in preparation for a
Drawing - Wikipedia — painting, further obfuscating their distinction. Drawings created for these purposes are called sketches.

Drawing - Wikipedia — when they have been transferred to another medium by printing.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Drawing is one of the oldest forms of human expression, with evidence for its existence preceding that of wrien communication.[5] It is believed that drawing was
Drawing - Wikipedia — used as a specialised form of communication before the invention of the wrien language,[5][6] demonstrated by the production of cave and rock paintings around
Drawing - Wikipedia — 30,000 years ago (Art of the Upper Paleolithic).[7] ese drawings, known as pictograms, depicted objects and abstract concepts.[8] e sketches and paintings produced
Drawing - Wikipedia — by Neolithic times were eventually stylised and simpliﬁed in to symbol systems (proto-writing) and eventually into early writing systems.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Before the widespread availability of paper in Europe, monks in European monasteries used drawings, either as underdrawings for illuminated manuscripts on vellum
Drawing - Wikipedia — or parchment, or as the ﬁnal image. Drawing has also been used extensively in the ﬁeld of science, as a method of discovery, understanding and explanation.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Drawing diagrams of observations is an important part of scientiﬁc study.

Drawing - Wikipedia — In 1609, astronomer Galileo Galilei explained the changing phases of Venus and also the sunspots through his observational telescopic
Drawing - Wikipedia — drawings.[9] In 1924, geophysicist Alfred Wegener used illustrations to visually demonstrate the origin of the continents.[9]
Drawing - Wikipedia — Drawing is one of the easiest ways to visualise ideas and to express one's creativity; therefore it has been prominent in the world of art.
Drawing - Wikipedia — roughout much of history, drawing was regarded as the foundation for artistic practice.[10] Initially, artists used and reused wooden
Drawing - Wikipedia — tablets for the production of their drawings.[11] Following the widespread availability of paper in the 14th century, the use of drawing in
Drawing - Wikipedia — the arts increased. At this point, drawing was commonly used as a tool for thought and investigation, acting as a study medium whilst
Drawing - Wikipedia — artists were preparing for their ﬁnal pieces of work.[12][13] e Renaissance brought about a great sophistication in drawing techniques,
Drawing - Wikipedia — enabling artists to represent things more realistically than before,[14] and revealing an interest in geometry and philosophy.[15]
Drawing - Wikipedia — e invention of the ﬁrst widely available form of photography led to a shi in the hierarchy of the arts.[16] Photography oﬀered an
Drawing - Wikipedia — alternative to drawing as a method for accurately representing visual phenomena, and traditional drawing practice was given less
Drawing - Wikipedia — emphasis as an essential skill for artists, particularly so in Western society.[9]
Drawing - Wikipedia — Drawing became signiﬁcant as an art form around the late 15th century, with artists and master engravers such as Albrecht Dürer and
Drawing - Wikipedia — Martin Schongauer (c. 1448–1491), the ﬁrst Northern engraver known by name. Schongauer came from Alsace, and was born into a family of goldsmiths. Albrecht
Drawing - Wikipedia — Dürer, a master of the next generation, was also the son of a goldsmith.[17][18]
Drawing - Wikipedia — Old Master Drawings oen reﬂect the history of the country in which they were produced, and the fundamental characteristics of a nation at that time. In 17th-century
Drawing - Wikipedia — Holland, a Protestant country, there were almost no religious artworks, and, with no King or court, most art was bought privately. Drawings of landscapes or genre
Drawing - Wikipedia — scenes were oen viewed not as sketches but as highly ﬁnished works of art. Italian drawings, however, show the inﬂuence of Catholicism and the Church, which
Drawing - Wikipedia — played a major role in artistic patronage. e same is oen true of French drawings, although in the 17th century the disciplines of French Classicism[19] meant
Drawing - Wikipedia — drawings were less Baroque than the more free Italian counterparts, which conveyed a greater sense of movement.[20]
Drawing - Wikipedia — In the 20th century Modernism encouraged "imaginative originality"[21] and some artists' approach to drawing became less literal, more abstract. World-renowned
Drawing - Wikipedia — artists such as Pablo Picasso, Andy Warhol and Jean-Michel Basquiat helped challenge the status quo, with drawing being very much at the centre of their practice, and
Drawing - Wikipedia — oen re-interpreting traditional technique.[22]
Drawing - Wikipedia — Basquiat's drawings were produced in many diﬀerent mediums, most commonly ink, pencil, felt-tip or marker, and oil-stick, and he drew on any surface that came to
Drawing - Wikipedia — hand, such as doors, clothing, refrigerators, walls and baseball helmets.[23]

Drawing - Wikipedia — e medium is the means by which ink, pigment, or color are delivered onto the drawing surface. Most drawing media either are dry (e.g. graphite, charcoal, pastels,
Drawing - Wikipedia — Conté, silverpoint), or use a ﬂuid solvent or carrier (marker, pen and ink). Watercolor pencils can be used dry like ordinary pencils, then moistened with a wet brush to
Drawing - Wikipedia — get various painterly eﬀects. Very rarely, artists have drawn with (usually decoded) invisible ink. Metalpoint drawing usually employs either silver or lead.[25] More
Drawing - Wikipedia — rarely used are gold, platinum, copper, brass, bronze, and tinpoint.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Paper comes in a variety of diﬀerent sizes and qualities, ranging from newspaper grade up to high quality and relatively expensive paper sold as individual sheets.[26]
Drawing - Wikipedia — Papers vary in texture, hue, acidity, and strength when wet. Smooth paper is good for rendering ﬁne detail, but a more "toothy" paper holds the drawing material beer.
Drawing - Wikipedia — us a coarser material is useful for producing deeper contrast.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Newsprint and typing paper may be useful for practice and rough sketches. Tracing paper is used to experiment over a half-ﬁnished drawing, and to transfer a design
Drawing - Wikipedia — from one sheet to another. Cartridge paper is the basic type of drawing paper sold in pads. Bristol board and even heavier acid-free boards, frequently with smooth
Drawing - Wikipedia — ﬁnishes, are used for drawing ﬁne detail and do not distort when wet media (ink, washes) are applied. Vellum is extremely smooth and suitable for very ﬁne detail.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Coldpressed watercolor paper may be favored for ink drawing due to its texture.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Acid-free, archival quality paper keeps its color and texture far longer than wood pulp based paper such as newsprint, which turns yellow and becomes brile much
Drawing - Wikipedia — sooner.
Drawing - Wikipedia — e basic tools are a drawing board or table, pencil sharpener and eraser, and for ink drawing, bloing paper. Other tools used are circle compass, ruler, and set square.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Fixative is used to prevent pencil and crayon marks from smudging. Draing tape is used to secure paper to drawing surface, and also to mask an area to keep it free of
Drawing - Wikipedia — accidental marks, such as sprayed or spaered materials and washes. An easel or slanted table is used to keep the drawing surface in a suitable position, which is
Drawing - Wikipedia — generally more horizontal than the position used in painting.

Drawing - Wikipedia — Almost all drasmen use their hands and ngers to apply the media, with the exception of some disabled individuals who

Drawing - Wikipedia — Prior to working on an image, the artist typically explores how various media work. ey may try diﬀerent drawing
Drawing - Wikipedia — implements on practice sheets to determine value and texture, and how to apply the implement to produce various eﬀects.
Drawing - Wikipedia — e artist's choice of drawing strokes aﬀects the appearance of the image. Pen and ink
Drawing - Wikipedia — drawings oen use hatching – groups of parallel lines.[28] Cross-hatching uses hatching in
Drawing - Wikipedia — two or more diﬀerent directions to create a darker tone. Broken hatching, or lines with
Drawing - Wikipedia — intermient breaks, form lighter tones – and controlling the density of the breaks achieves
Drawing - Wikipedia — a gradation of tone. Stippling uses dots to produce tone, texture and shade. Diﬀerent
Drawing - Wikipedia — textures can be achieved depending on the method used to build tone.[29]
Drawing - Wikipedia — Drawings in dry media oen use similar techniques, though pencils and drawing sticks can
Drawing - Wikipedia — achieve continuous variations in tone. Typically a drawing is ﬁlled in based on which hand the artist favors. A right-handed artist
Drawing - Wikipedia — draws from le to right to avoid smearing the image. Erasers can remove unwanted lines, lighten tones, and clean up stray marks. In a
Drawing - Wikipedia — sketch or outline drawing, lines drawn oen follow the contour of the subject, creating depth by looking like shadows cast from a
Drawing - Wikipedia — light in the artist's position.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Sometimes the artist leaves a section of the image untouched while ﬁlling in the remainder. e shape of the area to preserve can be
Drawing - Wikipedia — painted with masking ﬂuid or cut out of a frisket and applied to the drawing surface, protecting the surface from stray marks until the
Drawing - Wikipedia — mask is removed.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Another method to preserve a section of the image is to apply a spray-on ﬁxative to the surface. is holds loose material more ﬁrmly
Drawing - Wikipedia — to the sheet and prevents it from smearing. However the ﬁxative spray typically uses chemicals that can harm the respiratory system,
Drawing - Wikipedia — so it should be employed in a well-ventilated area such as outdoors.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Another technique is subtractive drawing in which the drawing surface is covered with graphite or charcoal and then erased to make the image.[30]
Drawing - Wikipedia — Shading is the technique of varying the tonal values on the paper to represent the shade of the material as well as the placement of the shadows. Careful aention to
Drawing - Wikipedia — reﬂected light, shadows and highlights can result in a very realistic rendition of the image.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Blending uses an implement to soen or spread the original drawing strokes. Blending is most easily done with a medium that does not immediately ﬁx itself, such as
Drawing - Wikipedia — graphite, chalk, or charcoal, although freshly applied ink can be smudged, wet or dry, for some eﬀects. For shading and blending, the artist can use a blending stump,
Drawing - Wikipedia — tissue, a kneaded eraser, a ﬁngertip, or any combination of them. A piece of chamois is useful for creating smooth textures, and for removing material to lighten the
Drawing - Wikipedia — tone. Continuous tone can be achieved with graphite on a smooth surface without blending, but the technique is laborious, involving small circular or oval strokes with
Drawing - Wikipedia — Tone
Drawing - Wikipedia — A pencil portrait by Henry
Drawing - Wikipedia — Macbeth-Raeburn, with
Drawing - Wikipedia — hatching and shading (1909)
Drawing - Wikipedia — Proportions of the human body
Drawing - Wikipedia — a somewhat blunt point.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Shading techniques that also introduce texture to the drawing include hatching and stippling. A number of other methods produce
Drawing - Wikipedia — texture. In addition to the choice of paper, drawing material and technique aﬀect texture. Texture can be made to appear more
Drawing - Wikipedia — realistic when it is drawn next to a contrasting texture; a coarse texture is more obvious when placed next to a smoothly blended
Drawing - Wikipedia — area. A similar eﬀect can be achieved by drawing diﬀerent tones close together. A light edge next to a dark background stands out to
Drawing - Wikipedia — the eye, and almost appears to ﬂoat above the surface.
Drawing - Wikipedia — e direction and quality of light play a crucial role in shading, inﬂuencing the depth and dimension of a drawing. Understanding
Drawing - Wikipedia — how light interacts with diﬀerent surfaces helps artists create a sense of realism, whether rendering smooth, reﬂective materials or
Drawing - Wikipedia — rough, mae textures. Observing real-world lighting conditions and practicing from life can enhance an artist’s ability to depict
Drawing - Wikipedia — convincing shadows and highlights.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Additionally, advanced shading techniques, such as cross-hatching and scumbling, allow for greater control over tonal transitions
Drawing - Wikipedia — and surface detail. Cross-hatching involves layering intersecting lines to build depth and tone, while scumbling uses circular or
Drawing - Wikipedia — scribbled strokes to create so, organic shading. ese methods, when combined with careful blending and texture application,
Drawing - Wikipedia — provide artists with a versatile toolkit for achieving a range of eﬀects, from so gradients to bold, high-contrast compositions.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Measuring the dimensions of a subject while blocking in the drawing is an important step in producing a realistic rendition
Drawing - Wikipedia — of the subject. Tools such as a compass can be used to measure the angles of diﬀerent sides. ese angles can be reproduced
Drawing - Wikipedia — on the drawing surface and then rechecked to make sure they are accurate. Another form of measurement is to compare the
Drawing - Wikipedia — relative sizes of diﬀerent parts of the subject with each other. A ﬁnger placed at a point along the drawing implement can be
Drawing - Wikipedia — used to compare that dimension with other parts of the image. A ruler can be used both as a straightedge and a device to
Drawing - Wikipedia — compute proportions.
Drawing - Wikipedia — When aempting to draw a complicated shape such as a human ﬁgure, it is helpful at ﬁrst to represent the form with a set of
Drawing - Wikipedia — primitive volumes. Almost any form can be represented by some combination of the cube, sphere, cylinder, and cone. Once
Drawing - Wikipedia — these basic volumes have been assembled into a likeness, then the drawing can be reﬁned into a more accurate and polished
Drawing - Wikipedia — form. e lines of the primitive volumes are removed and replaced by the ﬁnal likeness. Drawing the underlying construction
Drawing - Wikipedia — is a fundamental skill for representational art, and is taught in many books and schools. Its correct application resolves most
Drawing - Wikipedia — uncertainties about smaller details, and makes the ﬁnal image look consistent.[31]
Drawing - Wikipedia — A more reﬁned art of ﬁgure drawing relies upon the artist possessing a deep understanding of anatomy and the human proportions. A trained artist is familiar with the
Drawing - Wikipedia — skeleton structure, joint location, muscle placement, tendon movement, and how the diﬀerent parts work together during movement. is allows the artist to render
Drawing - Wikipedia — more natural poses that do not appear artiﬁcially stiﬀ. e artist is also familiar with how the proportions vary depending on the age of the subject, particularly when

Drawing - Wikipedia — Linear perspective is a method of portraying objects on a ﬂat surface so that the dimensions shrink with
Drawing - Wikipedia — distance. Each set of parallel, straight edges of any object, whether a building or a table, follows lines that
Drawing - Wikipedia — eventually converge at a vanishing point. Typically this convergence point is somewhere along the
Drawing - Wikipedia — horizon, as buildings are built level with the ﬂat surface. When multiple structures are aligned with each
Drawing - Wikipedia — other, such as buildings along a street, the horizontal tops and booms of the structures typically
Drawing - Wikipedia — converge at a vanishing point.
Drawing - Wikipedia — When both the fronts and sides of a building are drawn, then the parallel lines forming a side converge at
Drawing - Wikipedia — a second point along the horizon (which may be oﬀ the drawing paper.) is is a two-point perspective.
Drawing - Wikipedia — [32] Converging the vertical lines to a third point above or below the horizon then produces a three-point
Drawing - Wikipedia — perspective.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Depth can also be portrayed by several techniques in addition to the perspective approach above. Objects of similar size should appear ever smaller
Drawing - Wikipedia — the further they are from the viewer. us the back wheel of a cart appears slightly smaller than the front wheel. Depth can be portrayed through
Drawing - Wikipedia — the use of texture. As the texture of an object gets further away it becomes more compressed and busy, taking on an entirely diﬀerent character
Drawing - Wikipedia — than if it was close. Depth can also be portrayed by reducing the contrast in more distant objects, and by making their colors less
Drawing - Wikipedia — saturated. is reproduces the eﬀect of atmospheric haze, and cause the eye to focus primarily on objects drawn in the foreground.
Drawing - Wikipedia — e composition of the image is an important element in producing an interesting work of artistic merit. e artist plans element
Drawing - Wikipedia — placement in the art to communicate ideas and feelings with the viewer. e composition can determine the focus of the art, and result
Drawing - Wikipedia — in a harmonious whole that is aesthetically appealing and stimulating.
Drawing - Wikipedia — e illumination of the subject is also a key element in creating an artistic piece, and the interplay of light and shadow is a valuable
Drawing - Wikipedia — method in the artist's toolbox. e placement of the light sources can make a considerable diﬀerence in the type of message that is
Drawing - Wikipedia — being presented. Multiple light sources can wash out any wrinkles in a person's face, for instance, and give a more youthful
Drawing - Wikipedia — appearance. In contrast, a single light source, such as harsh daylight, can serve to highlight any texture or interesting features.
Drawing - Wikipedia — When drawing an object or ﬁgure, the skilled artist pays aention to both the area within the silhouee and what lies outside. e
Drawing - Wikipedia — exterior is termed the negative space, and can be as important in the representation as the ﬁgure. Objects placed in the background of
Drawing - Wikipedia — the ﬁgure should appear properly placed wherever they can be viewed.

Drawing - Wikipedia — A study is a dra drawing that is made in preparation for a planned nal image. Studies can be used to determine the appearances of
Drawing - Wikipedia — speciﬁc parts of the completed image, or for experimenting with the best approach for accomplishing the end goal. However a well-
Drawing - Wikipedia — craed study can be a piece of art in its own right, and many hours of careful work can go into completing a study.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Individuals display diﬀerences in their ability to produce visually accurate drawings,[33]
Drawing - Wikipedia — when a visually accurate drawing is "recognized as a particular object at a particular time
Drawing - Wikipedia — and in a particular space, rendered with lile addition of visual detail that can not be seen
Drawing - Wikipedia — in the object represented or with lile deletion of visual detail."[34]
Drawing - Wikipedia — Investigative studies have aimed to explain the reasons why some individuals draw beer
Drawing - Wikipedia — than others. One study posited four key abilities in the drawing process: motor skills
Drawing - Wikipedia — required for mark-making, the drawer's own perception of their drawing, perception of
Drawing - Wikipedia — objects being drawn, and the ability to make good representational decisions.[34] Following
Drawing - Wikipedia — this hypothesis, several studies have sought to conclude which of these processes are most
Drawing - Wikipedia — signiﬁcant in aﬀecting the accuracy of drawings.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Motor control
Drawing - Wikipedia — Motor control is an important physical component in the 'Production Phase' of the drawing process.[35] It has been suggested that
Drawing - Wikipedia — motor control plays a role in drawing ability, though its eﬀects are not signiﬁcant.[34]
Drawing - Wikipedia — Perception
Drawing - Wikipedia — It has been suggested that an individual's ability to perceive an object they are drawing is the most important stage in the drawing
Drawing - Wikipedia — process.[34] is suggestion is supported by the discovery of a robust relationship between perception and drawing ability.[36]
Drawing - Wikipedia — is evidence acted as the basis of Bey Edwards' how-to-draw book, Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain.[37] Edwards aimed to
Drawing - Wikipedia — teach her readers how to draw, based on the development of the reader's perceptual abilities.
Drawing - Wikipedia — Furthermore, the inﬂuential artist and art critic John Ruskin emphasised the importance of perception in the drawing process in his
Drawing - Wikipedia — book e Elements of Drawing.[38] He stated, "For I am nearly convinced, that once we see keenly enough, there is very lile diﬃcult in
Drawing - Wikipedia — drawing what we see."
Drawing - Wikipedia — Visual memory
Drawing - Wikipedia — is has also been shown to inﬂuence one's ability to create visually accurate drawings. Short-term memory plays an important part in drawing as one's gaze shis
Drawing - Wikipedia — Process
Drawing - Wikipedia — between the object they are drawing and the drawing itself.[39]
Drawing - Wikipedia — Decision-making
Drawing - Wikipedia — Some studies comparing artists to non-artists have found that artists spend more time thinking strategically while drawing. In particular, artists spend more time on
Drawing - Wikipedia — 'metacognitive' activities such as considering diﬀerent hypothetical plans for how they might progress with a drawing.[40]

Performance art - Wikipedia — Performance art is an artwork or art exhibition created through actions executed by the artist or other participants. It may
Performance art - Wikipedia — be witnessed live or through documentation, spontaneously developed or wrien, and is traditionally presented to a public in
Performance art - Wikipedia — a ﬁne art context in an interdisciplinary mode.[1] Also known as artistic action, it has been developed through the years as a
Performance art - Wikipedia — genre of its own in which art is presented live. It had an important and fundamental role in 20th century avant-garde art.[2][3]
Performance art - Wikipedia — It involves ﬁve basic elements: time, space, body, presence of the artist, and the relation between the artist and the public. e
Performance art - Wikipedia — actions, generally developed in art galleries and museums, can take place in any kind of seing or space, and during any time
Performance art - Wikipedia — period.[4] Its goal is to generate a reaction, sometimes with the support of improvisation and a sense of aesthetics. e themes
Performance art - Wikipedia — are commonly linked to life experiences of the artist themselves, the need for denunciation or social criticism and with a
Performance art - Wikipedia — spirit of transformation.[5]
Performance art - Wikipedia — e term "performance art" and "performance" became widely used in the 1970s, even though the history of performance in
Performance art - Wikipedia — visual arts dates back to futurist productions and cabarets from the 1910s.[6][1] Art critic and performance artist John

Performance art - Wikipedia — Abel Azcona,[14] Regina José Galindo,[15] Marta Minujín,[16] Melati Suryodarmo and Petr Pavlensky. e discipline is linked
Performance art - Wikipedia — to the happenings and "events" of the Fluxus movement, Viennese Actionism, body art and conceptual art.[17]

Performance art - Wikipedia — "Performance art" is a term usually reserved to refer to a conceptual art that conveys a content-based meaning in a more
Performance art - Wikipedia — drama-related sense, rather than being simple performance for its own sake for entertainment purposes. It largely refers to a
Performance art - Wikipedia — performance presented to an audience, but which does not seek to present a conventional theatrical play or a formal linear
Performance art - Wikipedia — narrative, or which alternately does not seek to depict a set of ﬁctitious characters in formal scripted interactions. It therefore
Performance art - Wikipedia — can include action or spoken word as a communication between the artist and audience, or even ignore expectations of an
Performance art - Wikipedia — audience, rather than following a script wrien beforehand.
Performance art - Wikipedia — Some types of performance art nevertheless can be close to performing arts. Such performance may use a script or create a
Performance art - Wikipedia — ﬁctitious dramatic seing, but still constitute performance art in that it does not seek to follow the usual dramatic norm of
Performance art - Wikipedia — creating a ﬁctitious seing with a linear script which follows conventional real-world dynamics; rather, it would intentionally
Performance art - Wikipedia — seek to satirize or to transcend the usual real-world dynamics which are used in conventional theatrical plays.
Performance art - Wikipedia — Performance artists oen challenge the audience to think in new and unconventional ways, break conventions of traditional
Performance art - Wikipedia — arts, and break down conventional ideas about "what art is". As long as the performer does not become a player who repeats
Performance art - Wikipedia — a role, performance art can include satirical elements; use robots and machines as performers, as in pieces of the Survival
Performance art - Wikipedia — Research Laboratories; involve ritualised elements (e.g. Shaun Caton); or borrow elements of any performing arts such as
Performance art - Wikipedia — dance, music, and circus. Performance art can also involve intersection with architecture, and may intertwine with religious
Performance art - Wikipedia — practice[24][25] and with theology.[26]

Performance art - Wikipedia — declared themselves a sociological art movement. Fluxus was informally organized in 1962 by George Maciunas (1931–1978).
Performance art - Wikipedia — is movement had representation in Europe, the United States and Japan.[72] e Fluxus movement, mostly developed in
Performance art - Wikipedia — North America and Europe under the stimulus of John Cage, did not see the avant-garde as a linguistic renovation, but it
Performance art - Wikipedia — sought to make a diﬀerent use of the main art channels that separate themselves from speciﬁc language; it tries to be
Performance art - Wikipedia — interdisciplinary and to adopt mediums and materials from diﬀerent ﬁelds. Language is not the goal, but the mean for a renovation of art, seen as a global art.[73] As well
Performance art - Wikipedia — as Dada, Fluxus escaped any aempt for a deﬁnition or categorization. As one of the movement's founders, Dick Higgins, stated:

Performance art - Wikipedia — critical and political discourse were in this discipline. Until the decline of the European Eastern bloc during the late 1980s, performance art had actively been rejected by
Performance art - Wikipedia — most communist governments. With the exception of Poland and Yugoslavia, performance art was more or less banned in countries where any independent public event
Performance art - Wikipedia — was feared. In the GDR, Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Latvia it happened in apartments, at seemingly spontaneous gatherings in artist studios, in church-controlled
Performance art - Wikipedia — seings, or was covered as another activity, like a photo-shoot. Isolated from the western conceptual context, in diﬀerent seings it could be like a playful protest or a
Performance art - Wikipedia — bier comment, using subversive metaphors to express dissent with the political situation.[170] Amongst the most remarkable performance art works of political content
Performance art - Wikipedia — in this time were those of Tehching Hsieh between July 1983 and July 1984, Art/Life: One Year Performance (Rope Piece).[171]

Dance - Wikipedia — Dance
Dance - Wikipedia — Dance is an art form, consisting of sequences of body movements with aesthetic and oen symbolic value, either improvised
Dance - Wikipedia — or purposefully selected. Dance can be categorized and described by its choreography, by its repertoire of movements or by
Dance - Wikipedia — its historical period or place of origin. Dance is typically performed with musical accompaniment, and sometimes with the
Dance - Wikipedia — dancer simultaneously using a musical instrument themselves.
Dance - Wikipedia — Two common types of group dance are theatrical and participatory dance. Both types of dance may have special functions,
Dance - Wikipedia — whether social, ceremonial, competitive, erotic, martial, sacred or liturgical. Dance is not solely restricted to performance, as
Dance - Wikipedia — dance is used as a form of exercise and occasionally training for other sports and activities. Dance performances and dancing
Dance - Wikipedia — competitions are found across the world exhibiting various diﬀerent styles and standards.
Dance - Wikipedia — Dance may also be participated in alone as a form of exercise or self expression. Dancing is common human behaviour, and
Dance - Wikipedia — does not necessarily require speciﬁc choreography.
Dance - Wikipedia — eatrical dance, also called performance or concert dance, is intended primarily as a spectacle, usually a performance upon a
Dance - Wikipedia — stage by virtuoso dancers. It oen tells a story, potentially using mime, costume and scenery, or it may interpret the musical
Dance - Wikipedia — accompaniment, which is oen specially composed and performed in a theatre seing but it is not a requirement. Examples
Dance - Wikipedia — are Western ballet and modern dance, Classical Indian dance such as Bharatanatyam, and Chinese and Japanese song and dance dramas, such as the dragon dance. Most
Dance - Wikipedia — classical forms are centred upon dance alone, but performance dance may also appear in opera and other forms of musical theatre.
Dance - Wikipedia — Participatory dance, whether it be a folk dance, a social dance, a group dance such as a line, circle, chain or square dance, or a partner dance, such as in Western
Dance - Wikipedia — ballroom dancing, is undertaken primarily for a common purpose, such as social interaction or exercise, or building ﬂexibility of participants rather than to serve any
Dance - Wikipedia — beneﬁt to onlookers. Such dance seldom has any narrative. A group dance and a corps de ballet, a social partner dance and a pas de deux, diﬀer profoundly. Even a solo
Dance - Wikipedia — dance or interpretive dance may be undertaken solely for the satisfaction of the dancer. Participatory dancers oen all employ the same movements and steps but, for
Dance - Wikipedia — example, in the rave culture of electronic dance music, vast crowds may engage in free dance, uncoordinated with those around them. On the other hand, some cultures
Dance - Wikipedia — lay down strict rules as to the particular dances people may or must participate.[1]

Dance - Wikipedia — invention of wrien languages, dance was an important part of the
Dance - Wikipedia — oral and performance methods of passing stories down from one

Dance - Wikipedia — References to dance can be found in very early recorded history; Greek dance (choros) is referred to by Plato,
Dance - Wikipedia — Aristotle, Plutarch and Lucian.[5] e Bible and Talmud refer to many events related to dance, and contain over
Dance - Wikipedia — 30 diﬀerent dance terms.[6] In Chinese poery as early as the Neolithic period, groups of people are depicted
Dance - Wikipedia — dancing in a line holding hands,[7] and the earliest Chinese word for "dance" is found wrien in the oracle
Dance - Wikipedia — bones.[8] Dance is described in the Lüshi Chunqiu.[9][10] Primitive dance in ancient China was associated with
Dance - Wikipedia — sorcery and shamanic rituals.[11]
Dance - Wikipedia — During the ﬁrst millennium BCE in India, many texts were composed which aempted to
Dance - Wikipedia — codify aspects of daily life. Bharata Muni's Natya Shastra (literally "the text of
Dance - Wikipedia — dramaturgy") is one early text. It mainly deals with drama, in which dance plays an
Dance - Wikipedia — important part in Indian culture. A strong continuous tradition of dance has since
Dance - Wikipedia — continued in India, through to modern times, where it continues to play a role in culture,
Dance - Wikipedia — ritual, and the Bollywood entertainment industry. Many other contemporary dance forms
Dance - Wikipedia — can likewise be traced back to historical, traditional, ceremonial, and ethnic dance.[12]
Dance - Wikipedia — Dance is generally, but not exclusively, performed with the accompaniment of music and may or may not be performed in time to
Dance - Wikipedia — such music. Some dance (such as tap dance or gumboot dance) may provide its own audible accompaniment in place of (or in
Dance - Wikipedia — addition to) music. Many early forms of music and dance were created for each other and are frequently performed together. Notable
Dance - Wikipedia — examples of traditional dance-music couplings include the jig, waltz, tango, disco, and salsa. Some musical genres have a parallel
Dance - Wikipedia — dance form such as baroque music and baroque dance; other varieties of dance and music may share nomenclature but developed
Dance - Wikipedia — separately, such as classical music and classical ballet. e choreography and music are meant to complement each other, to express a
Dance - Wikipedia — story told by the choreographer and dancers.[13]

Dance - Wikipedia — Rhythm and dance are deeply linked in history and practice. e American dancer Ted Shawn wrote; "e conception of
Dance - Wikipedia — rhythm which underlies all studies of the dance is something about which we could talk forever, and still not ﬁnish."[14] A
Dance - Wikipedia — musical rhythm requires two main elements; a regularly-repeating pulse (also called the "beat" or "tactus") that establishes
Dance - Wikipedia — the tempo, and a paern of accents and rests that establishes the character of the metre or basic rhythmic paern. e basic
Dance - Wikipedia — pulse is roughly equal in duration to a simple step or gesture.
Dance - Wikipedia — Dances generally have a characteristic tempo and rhythmic paern. e tango, for example, is usually danced in 2
Dance - Wikipedia — 4 time at
Dance - Wikipedia — approximately 66 beats per minute. e basic slow step, called a "slow", lasts for one beat, so that a full "right–le" step is
Dance - Wikipedia — equal to one 2
Dance - Wikipedia — 4 measure. e basic forward and backward walk of the dance is so counted – "slow-slow" – while many
Dance - Wikipedia — additional ﬁgures are counted "slow – quick-quick".[15]
Dance - Wikipedia — Repetitive body movements oen depend on alternating "strong" and "weak" muscular movements.[16] Given this alternation
Dance - Wikipedia — of le-right, of forward-backward and rise-fall, along with the bilateral symmetry of the human body, many dances and
Dance - Wikipedia — much music are in duple and quadruple meter. Since some such movements require more time in one phase than the other – such as the longer time required to li a
Dance - Wikipedia — hammer than to strike – some dance rhythms fall into triple metre.[17] Occasionally, as in the folk dances of the Balkans, dance traditions depend heavily on more
Dance - Wikipedia — complex rhythms. Complex dances composed of a ﬁxed sequence of steps require phrases and melodies of a certain ﬁxed length to accompany that sequence.
Dance - Wikipedia — Musical accompaniment arose in the earliest dance, so that ancient Egyptians aributed the origin of the dance to the divine Athotus, who was said to have observed
Dance - Wikipedia — that music accompanying religious rituals caused participants to move rhythmically and to have brought these movements into proportional measure. e idea that
Dance - Wikipedia — dance arises from musical rhythm, was found in renaissance Europe, in the works of the dancer Guglielmo Ebreo da Pesaro. Pesaro speaks of dance as a physical
Dance - Wikipedia — movement that arises from and expresses inward, spiritual motion agreeing with the "measures and perfect concords of harmony" that fall upon the human ear,[16]
Dance - Wikipedia — while earlier, Mechthild of Magdeburg, seizing upon dance as a symbol of the holy life foreshadowed in Jesus' saying "I have piped and ye have not danced",[18] writes;
Dance - Wikipedia — I can not dance unless thou leadest. If thou wouldst have me spring alo, sing thou and I will spring, into love and from love to knowledge and from
Dance - Wikipedia — knowledge to ecstasy above all human sense[19]
Dance - Wikipedia — oinot Arbeau's celebrated 16th-century dance-treatise Orchésographie, indeed, begins with deﬁnitions of over eighty distinct drum-rhythms.[20]
Dance - Wikipedia — Dance has been represented through the ages as having emerged as a response to music yet, as Lincoln Kirstein implied, it is at least as likely that primitive music arose
Dance - Wikipedia — from dance. Shawn concurs, stating that dance "was the ﬁrst art of the human race, and the matrix out of which all other arts grew" and that even the "metre in our
Dance - Wikipedia — poetry today is a result of the accents necessitated by body movement, as the dancing and reciting was performed simultaneously"[14] – an assertion somewhat
Dance - Wikipedia — supported by the common use of the term "foot" to describe the fundamental rhythmic units of poetry.
Dance - Wikipedia — Scholes, a musician, oﬀers support for this view, stating that the steady measures of music, of two, three or four beats to the bar, its equal and balanced phrases, regular

Dance - Wikipedia — e ballet developed out of courtly dramatic productions of 16th- and 17th-century France and Italy and for some time
Dance - Wikipedia — dancers performed dances developed from those familiar from the musical suite,[31] all of which were deﬁned by deﬁnite
Dance - Wikipedia — rhythms closely identiﬁed with each dance. ese appeared as character dances in the era of romantic nationalism.
Dance - Wikipedia — Ballet reached widespread vogue in the romantic era, accompanied by a larger orchestra and grander musical conceptions
Dance - Wikipedia — that did not lend themselves easily to rhythmic clarity and by dance that emphasised dramatic mime. A broader concept of
Dance - Wikipedia — rhythm was needed, that which Rudolf Laban terms the "rhythm and shape" of movement that communicates character,
Dance - Wikipedia — emotion and intention,[32] while only certain scenes required the exact synchronisation of step and music essential to other
Dance - Wikipedia — dance styles, so that, to Laban, modern Europeans seemed totally unable to grasp the meaning of "primitive rhythmic movements",[33] a situation that began to change
Dance - Wikipedia — in the 20th century with such productions as Igor Stravinsky's e Rite of Spring with its new rhythmic language evoking primal feelings of a primitive past.[34]
Dance - Wikipedia — Indian classical dance styles, like ballet, are oen in dramatic form, so that there is a similar complementarity between narrative expression and "pure" dance. In this
Dance - Wikipedia — case, the two are separately deﬁned, though not always separately performed. e rhythmic elements, which are abstract and technical, are known as nria. Both this
Dance - Wikipedia — and expressive dance (nritya), though, are closely tied to the rhythmic system (tala). Teachers have adapted the spoken rhythmic mnemonic system called bol to the
Dance - Wikipedia — needs of dancers.
Dance - Wikipedia — Japanese classical dance-theatre styles such as Kabuki and Noh, like Indian dance-drama, distinguish between narrative and abstract dance productions. e three main
Dance - Wikipedia — categories of kabuki are jidaimono (historical), sewamono (domestic) and shosagoto (dance pieces).[35] Somewhat similarly, Noh distinguishes between Geki Noh, based
Dance - Wikipedia — around the advancement of plot and the narration of action, and Furyū Noh, dance pieces involving acrobatics, stage properties, multiple characters and elaborate stage
Dance - Wikipedia — action.[36]
Dance - Wikipedia — Social dances, those intended for participation rather than for an audience, may include various forms of mime and narrative,
Dance - Wikipedia — but are typically set much more closely to the rhythmic paern of music, so that terms like waltz and polka refer as much to
Dance - Wikipedia — musical pieces as to the dance itself. e rhythm of the dancers' feet may even form an essential part of the music, as in tap
Dance - Wikipedia — dance. African dance, for example, is rooted in ﬁxed basic steps, but may also allow a high degree of rhythmic interpretation:
Dance - Wikipedia — the feet or the trunk mark the basic pulse while cross-rhythms are picked up by shoulders, knees, or head, with the best
Dance - Wikipedia — dancers simultaneously giving plastic expression to all the elements of the polyrhythmic paern.[37]

Dance - Wikipedia — Dance in Africa is deeply integrated into society and major events in a community are frequently reected in dances: dances
Dance - Wikipedia — are performed for births and funerals, weddings and wars.[38]: 13 Traditional dances impart cultural morals, including religious
Dance - Wikipedia — traditions and sexual standards; give vent to repressed emotions, such as grief; motivate community members to cooperate,
Dance - Wikipedia — whether ﬁghting wars or grinding grain; enact spiritual rituals; and contribute to social cohesiveness.[39]

Dance - Wikipedia — Diﬀerent dance styles
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Ballet originated during the Italian Renaissance and developed further in France and Russia. It is known for its graceful, precise movements,
Dance - Wikipedia — pointe work, and storytelling through choreography. Classical ballet follows strict techniques, while contemporary ballet incorporates modern
Dance - Wikipedia — inﬂuences.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Contemporary dance emerged in the mid-20th century. It blends elements of ballet, modern, and jazz dance. It emphasizes ﬂuidity, emotion,
Dance - Wikipedia — and expression over rigid technique. Pioneers like Martha Graham and Merce Cunningham contributed to its development.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Jazz dance is evolved from African American vernacular dance and became popular in the early 20th century. It features energetic movements,
Dance - Wikipedia — syncopated rhythms, and inﬂuences from ballet and contemporary styles. It is commonly seen in musical theatre and commercial
Dance - Wikipedia — performances.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Hip-hop dance emerged in the 1970s in the Bronx, New York, as a part of hip-hop culture. Styles such as breaking, popping, locking, and
Dance - Wikipedia — krumping fall under this genre. It emphasizes freestyle movements, rhythm, and personal expression.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Tap dance is characterized by rhythmic footwork using metal-soled shoes to create percussive sounds. It has roots in African and Irish dance
Dance - Wikipedia — traditions and became prominent in Vaudeville and Broadway productions.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Ballroom dance is a social and competitive dance style that includes forms such as the waltz, tango, foxtrot, and cha-cha. These dances are
Dance - Wikipedia — typically performed with a partner and emphasize posture, elegance, and synchronization.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Latin dance encompasses styles such as salsa, bachata, merengue, and samba. These dances are known for their vibrant, energetic movements
Dance - Wikipedia — and rhythmic footwork, often performed socially and competitively.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Traditional and folk dance is deeply rooted in history and tradition. Examples include Irish step dancing, Indian Bharatanatyam, Spanish
Dance - Wikipedia — ﬂamenco, and African tribal dances.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Modern dance developed in the early 20th century as a rebellion against classical ballet, modern dance focuses on self-expression, gravity, and
Dance - Wikipedia — unconventional movement. Inﬂuential ﬁgures include Isadora Duncan and Martha Graham.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Lyrical dance is a fusion of ballet and jazz that emphasizes emotional storytelling and ﬂuid movement. It is often performed to contemporary
Dance - Wikipedia — music and focuses on grace and expression.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Belly dance originates in the Middle East and is characterized by intricate hip movements, shimmies, and undulations. It is often performed
Dance - Wikipedia — solo and has variations across diﬀerent regions, including Egyptian and Turkish styles.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Street dance refers to urban dance styles that developed outside of traditional dance studios. These include hip-hop, house, and breakdancing,
Dance - Wikipedia — often performed in freestyle battles and social settings.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Bollywood dance is a vibrant fusion of classical Indian dance, folk dance, and modern styles. It is widely seen in Indian cinema and incorporates
Dance - Wikipedia — expressive gestures, energetic movements, and dramatic storytelling.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Aerial dance combines dance and acrobatics performed on apparatuses such as silks, hoops, and trapezes. It requires strength, ﬂexibility, and
Dance - Wikipedia — coordination to create breath-taking performances.

Dance - Wikipedia — opportunity for students to take beginner level dance classes, as well as participate in dance teams that perform at school

Dance - Wikipedia — Professional dancers are usually employed on contract or for particular performances or productions. e professional life of a dancer is generally one of constantly
Dance - Wikipedia — changing work situations, strong competitive pressure and low pay. Consequently, professional dancers oen must supplement their incomes to achieve ﬁnancial
Dance - Wikipedia — stability. In the U.S. many professional dancers belong to unions (such as the American Guild of Musical Artists, Screen Actors Guild and Actors' Equity Association)
Dance - Wikipedia — that establish working conditions and minimum salaries for their members. Professional dancers must possess large amounts of athleticism. To lead a successful career,
Dance - Wikipedia — it is advantageous to be versatile in many styles of dance, have a strong technical background and to use other forms of physical training to remain ﬁt and healthy.[55]
Dance - Wikipedia — Dance teachers typically focus on teaching dance performance, or coaching competitive dancers, or both. ey typically have performance experience in the types of
Dance - Wikipedia — dance they teach or coach. For example, dancesport teachers and coaches are oen tournament dancers or former dancesport performers. Dance teachers may be self-
Dance - Wikipedia — employed, or employed by dance schools or general education institutions with dance programs. Some work for university programs or other schools that are associated
Dance - Wikipedia — with professional classical dance (e.g., ballet) or modern dance companies. Others are employed by smaller, privately owned dance schools that oﬀer dance training and
Dance - Wikipedia — performance coaching for various types of dance.[56]

Dance - Wikipedia — anywhere between two and four days, depending whether it is a regional or national competition.

Dance - Wikipedia — competitions will take place in a professional seing or may vary to non-performance spaces, such as a high

Dance - Wikipedia — their performance than given a score. As far as competitive categories go, most competitions base their
Dance - Wikipedia — categories according to the dance style, age, experience level and the number of dancers competing in the
Dance - Wikipedia — routine.[59] Major types of dance competitions include:
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Dancesport, which is focused exclusively on ballroom and latin dance.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Competitive dance, in which a variety of theater dance styles, such as acrobatics, ballet, jazz, hip-hop, lyrical, stepping, and tap, are permitted.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Commercial Dance, consisting of as hip hop, jazz, locking, popping, breakdancing, contemporary etc.[59]
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Single-style competitions, such as; highland dance, dance team, and Irish dance, that only permit a single dance style.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Open competitions, that permit a wide variety of dance styles. An example of this is the TV program So You Think You Can Dance.
Dance - Wikipedia — ▪ Olympic, Dance has been trying to be part of the Olympic sport since 1930s.

Dance - Wikipedia — People's Republic of China, for example, developed a formula for dance diplomacy that sought to learn from and express respect for the aesthetic traditions of recently
Dance - Wikipedia — independent states that were former European colonies, such as Indonesia, India, and Burma, as a show of anti-colonial solidarity.[60]
