Writing - Wikipedia — Writing
Writing - Wikipedia — Writing is the act of creating a persistent representation of language. A writing system includes a particular set
Writing - Wikipedia — of symbols called a script, as well as the rules by which they encode a particular spoken language. Every wrien
Writing - Wikipedia — language arises from a corresponding spoken language; while the use of language is universal across human
Writing - Wikipedia — societies, most spoken languages are not wrien.[1]
Writing - Wikipedia — Writing is a cognitive and social activity involving neuropsychological and physical processes. e outcome of
Writing - Wikipedia — this activity, also called writing, and sometimes a text, is a series of physically inscribed, mechanically
Writing - Wikipedia — transferred, or digitally represented symbols. e interpreter or activator of a text is called a reader.[2]
Writing - Wikipedia — In general, writing systems do not constitute languages in and of themselves, but rather a means of encoding
Writing - Wikipedia — language such that it can be read by others across time and space.[3][4] While not all languages use a writing
Writing - Wikipedia — system, those that do can complement and extend the capacities of spoken language by creating durable forms of
Writing - Wikipedia — language that can be transmied across space (e.g. wrien correspondence) and stored over time (e.g. libraries).
Writing - Wikipedia — [5] Writing can also impact what knowledge people acquire, since it allows humans to externalize their thinking
Writing - Wikipedia — in forms that are easier to reﬂect on, elaborate on, reconsider, and revise.[6][7][8]
Writing - Wikipedia — Any instance of writing involves a complex interaction among available tools, intentions, cultural customs,
Writing - Wikipedia — cognitive routines, genres, tacit and explicit knowledge, and the constraints and limitations of the systems used.
Writing - Wikipedia — [9] Inscriptions have been made with ﬁngers, styluses, quills, ink brushes, pencils, pens, and many styles of
Writing - Wikipedia — lithography; surfaces used for these inscriptions include stone tablets, clay tablets, bamboo slats, papyrus, wax
Writing - Wikipedia — tablets, vellum, parchment, paper, copperplate, slate, porcelain, and other enameled surfaces.
Writing - Wikipedia — e typewriter and subsequently various digital word processors have recently become widespread writing tools,
Writing - Wikipedia — and studies have compared the ways in which writers have framed the experience of writing with such tools as
Writing - Wikipedia — compared with the pen or pencil.[10]
Writing - Wikipedia — Advancements in natural language processing and natural language generation have resulted in soware capable of producing certain forms of formulaic writing (e.g.,
Writing - Wikipedia — weather forecasts and brief sports reporting) without the direct involvement of humans[11] aer initial conﬁguration or, more commonly, to be used to support writing
Writing - Wikipedia — processes such as generating initial dras, producing feedback with the help of a rubric, copy-editing, and helping translation.[12]
Writing - Wikipedia — Tools, materials, and motivations to write
Writing - Wikipedia — A bronze tympanum representing writing,
Writing - Wikipedia — above the main entrance to the Thomas
Writing - Wikipedia — Jeﬀerson Building in Washington, D.C., sculpted
Writing - Wikipedia — by Olin Levi Warner in 1896
Writing - Wikipedia — Writing technologies from dierent eras coexist easily in many homes and workplaces. During the course of a day or
Writing - Wikipedia — even a single episode of writing, for example, a writer might instinctively switch among a pencil, a touchscreen, a
Writing - Wikipedia — text-editor, a whiteboard, a legal pad, and adhesive notes as diﬀerent purposes arise.[13]
Writing - Wikipedia — As human societies emerged, collective motivations for the development of writing were driven by pragmatic
Writing - Wikipedia — exigencies like keeping track of produce and other wealth, recording history, maintaining culture, codifying
Writing - Wikipedia — knowledge through curricula and lists of texts deemed to contain foundational knowledge (e.g. e Canon of
Writing - Wikipedia — Medicine) or artistic value (e.g. the literary canon), organizing and governing societies through texts including legal
Writing - Wikipedia — codes, census records, contracts, deeds of ownership, taxation, trade agreements, and treaties.[14] As Charles
Writing - Wikipedia — Bazerman explains, the "marking of signs on stones, clay, paper, and now digital memories—each more portable and
Writing - Wikipedia — rapidly traveling than the previous—provided means for increasingly coordinated and extended action as well as
Writing - Wikipedia — memory across larger groups of people over time and space."[15] For example, around the 4th millennium BC, the
Writing - Wikipedia — complexity of trade and administration in Mesopotamia outgrew human memory, and writing became a more dependable method for creating permanent records of
Writing - Wikipedia — transactions.[16] On the other hand, writing in both ancient Egypt and Mesoamerica may have evolved through the political necessity to manage the calendar for
Writing - Wikipedia — recording historical and environmental events.[17][18] Further innovations included more uniform, predictable, and widely dispersed legal systems, the distribution of
Writing - Wikipedia — accessible versions of sacred texts, and furthering practices of scientiﬁc inquiry and knowledge management, all of which were largely reliant on portable and easily
Writing - Wikipedia — reproducible forms of inscribed language. e history of writing is co-extensive with uses of writing and the elaboration of activity systems that give rise to and
Writing - Wikipedia — circulate writing.
Writing - Wikipedia — Individual motivations for writing include improvised additional capacity for the limitations of human memory[19] (e.g. to-do lists, recipes, reminders, logbooks, maps,
Writing - Wikipedia — the proper sequence for a complicated task or important ritual), dissemination of ideas and coordination (e.g. essays, monographs, broadsides, plans, petitions, or
Writing - Wikipedia — manifestos), creativity and storytelling, maintaining kinship and other social networks,[20] business correspondence regarding goods and services, and life writing (e.g. a
Writing - Wikipedia — diary or journal).[21]
Writing - Wikipedia — e global spread of digital communication systems such as e-mail and social media has made writing an increasingly important feature of daily life, where these
Writing - Wikipedia — systems mix with older technologies like paper, pencils, whiteboards, printers, and copiers.[22] Substantial amounts of everyday writing characterize most workplaces in
Writing - Wikipedia — developed countries.[23] In many occupations (e.g. law, accounting, soware design, human resources), wrien documentation is not only the main deliverable but also
Writing - Wikipedia — the mode of work itself.[24] Even in occupations not typically associated with writing, routine records management has most employees writing at least some of the
Writing - Wikipedia — time.[25]
Writing - Wikipedia — Some professions are typically associated with writing, such as literary authors, journalists, and technical writers, but writing is pervasive in most modern forms of
Writing - Wikipedia — work, civic participation, household management, and leisure activities.[26]
Writing - Wikipedia — Motivations and purposes
Writing - Wikipedia — Contemporary uses
Writing - Wikipedia — Writing permeates everyday commerce. For example, in the course of an aernoon, a wholesaler might receive a wrien inquiry about the availability of a product line,
Writing - Wikipedia — then communicate with suppliers and fabricators through work orders and purchase agreements, correspond via email to aﬃrm shipping availability with a drayage
Writing - Wikipedia — company, write an invoice, and request proof of receipt in the form of a wrien signature. At a much larger scale, modern systems of ﬁnances, banking, and business
Writing - Wikipedia — rest on many forms of wrien documents – including wrien regulations, policies, and procedures; the creation of reports and other monitoring documents to make,
Writing - Wikipedia — evaluate, and provide accountability for decisions and operations; the creation and maintenance of records; internal wrien communications within departments to
Writing - Wikipedia — coordinate work; wrien communications that comprise work products presented to other departments and to clients; and external communications to clients and the
Writing - Wikipedia — public.[27][28] Business and ﬁnancial organizations also rely on many wrien legal documents, such as contracts, reports to government agencies, tax records, and
Writing - Wikipedia — accounting reports.[29] Financial institutions and markets that hold, transmit, trade, insure, or regulate holdings for clients or other institutions are particularly
Writing - Wikipedia — dependent on wrien records (though now oen in digital form) to maintain the integrity of their roles.[30]
Writing - Wikipedia — Many modern systems of government are organized and sanctiﬁed through wrien constitutions at the national and sometimes state or other organizational levels.
Writing - Wikipedia — Wrien rules and procedures typically guide the operations of the various branches, departments, and other bodies of government, which regularly produce reports and
Writing - Wikipedia — other documents as work products and to account for their actions. In addition to legislatures that dra and pass laws, these laws are administered by an executive
Writing - Wikipedia — branch, which can present further wrien regulations specifying the laws and how they are carried out.[31] Governments at diﬀerent levels also typically maintain
Writing - Wikipedia — wrien records on citizens concerning identities, life events such as births, deaths, marriages, and divorces, the granting of licenses for controlled activities, criminal
Writing - Wikipedia — charges, traﬃc oﬀences, and other penalties small and large, and tax liability and payments.
Writing - Wikipedia — Research undertaken in academic disciplines is typically published as articles in journals or within book-length monographs. Arguments, experiments, observational
Writing - Wikipedia — data, and other evidence collated in the course of research is represented in writing, and serves as the basis for later work. Data collection and draing of manuscripts
Writing - Wikipedia — may be supported by grants, which usually require proposals establishing the value of such work and the need for funding.[32] e data and procedures are also
Writing - Wikipedia — typically collected in lab notebooks or other preliminary ﬁles.[33] Preprints of potential publications may also be presented at academic or disciplinary conferences or on
Writing - Wikipedia — publicly accessible web servers to gain peer feedback and build interest in the work. Prior to oﬃcial publication, these documents are typically read and evaluated by
Writing - Wikipedia — peer review from appropriate experts, who determine whether the work is of suﬃcient value and quality to be published.[34]
Writing - Wikipedia — Publication does not establish the claims or ﬁndings of work as being authoritatively true, only that they are worth the aention of other specialists. As the work
Writing - Wikipedia — appears in review articles, handbooks, textbooks, or other aggregations, and others cite it in the advancement of their own research, does it become codiﬁed as
Writing - Wikipedia — contingently reliable knowledge.[35]
Writing - Wikipedia — News and news reporting are central to citizen engagement and knowledge of many spheres of activity people may be interested in about the state of their community,
Writing - Wikipedia — including the actions and integrity of their governments and government oﬃcials, economic trends, natural disasters and responses to them, international geopolitical
Writing - Wikipedia — Business and ﬁnance

Writing - Wikipedia — Journalism
Writing - Wikipedia — events, including conicts, but also sports, entertainment, books, and other leisure activities. While news and newspapers have grown rapidly from the eighteenth to the
Writing - Wikipedia — twentieth centuries, the changing economics and ability to produce and distribute news have brought about radical and rapid challenges to journalism and the
Writing - Wikipedia — consequent organization of citizen knowledge and engagement.[36][37]</ref> ese changes have also created challenges for journalism ethics that have been developed
Writing - Wikipedia — over the past century.[38]
Writing - Wikipedia — Formal education is the social context most strongly associated with the learning of writing, and students may carry these particular associations long aer leaving
Writing - Wikipedia — school.[39] Alongside the writing that students read (in the forms of textbooks, assigned books, and other instructional materials as well as self-selected books) students
Writing - Wikipedia — do much writing within schools at all levels, on subject exams, in essays, in taking notes, in doing homework, and in formative and summative assessments. Some of
Writing - Wikipedia — this is explicitly directed toward the learning of writing, but much is focused more on subject learning.[40][41]
Writing - Wikipedia — Writing systems may be broadly classiﬁed according to what units of language are generally represented by its symbols:[42][43]
Writing - Wikipedia — ▪ Phonographies represent sounds of speech – with alphabets and syllabaries using symbols for phonemes and syllables respectively.
Writing - Wikipedia — ▪ Logographies represent a language's units of meaning (words or morphemes), though still associated by readers with their given
Writing - Wikipedia — pronunciations in the corresponding spoken language.
Writing - Wikipedia — A logography is wrien using logograms – wrien characters which represent individual words or morphemes.[42] For example, in Mayan, the glyph for "ﬁn",
Writing - Wikipedia — pronounced ka, was also used to represent the syllable ka whenever the pronunciation of a logogram needed to be indicated. Many logograms have an ideographic
Writing - Wikipedia — component (Chinese "radicals", hieroglyphic "determiners"). In Chinese, about 90% of characters are compounds of a semantic (meaning) element called a radical with an
Writing - Wikipedia — existing character to indicate the pronunciation, called a phonetic. However, such phonetic elements complement the logographic elements, rather than vice versa.
Writing - Wikipedia — e main logographic system in use today is Chinese characters, used with some modiﬁcation for the various languages or dialects of China, Japan, and sometimes in
Writing - Wikipedia — Korean, although in South and North Korea, the phonetic hangul system is mainly used. Other logographic systems include cuneiform and Maya.
Writing - Wikipedia — A syllabary is a set of wrien symbols that represent syllables,[42] typically a consonant followed by a vowel, or just a vowel alone. In some scripts more complex
Writing - Wikipedia — syllables (e.g. consonant-vowel-consonant, or consonant-consonant-vowel) may have dedicated glyphs. Phonetically similar syllables are not wrien similarly.[42] For
Writing - Wikipedia — instance, the syllable ka may look nothing like the syllable ki, nor will syllables with the same vowels be similar.

Writing - Wikipedia — Syllabaries are best suited to languages with a relatively simple syllable structure, such as Japanese. Other languages that use
Writing - Wikipedia — syllabic writing include Mycenaean Greek (Linear B), Cherokee,[44] the Ndjuka creole language of Suriname, and the Vai
Writing - Wikipedia — language of Liberia.
Writing - Wikipedia — An alphabet is a set of wrien symbols that represent consonants and vowels.[42] In a perfectly phonological alphabet, the
Writing - Wikipedia — leers would correspond perfectly to the language's phonemes. us, a writer could predict the spelling of a word given its
Writing - Wikipedia — pronunciation, and a speaker could predict the pronunciation of a word given its spelling. However, as languages oen
Writing - Wikipedia — evolve independently of their writing systems, and writing systems have been borrowed for languages they were not
Writing - Wikipedia — designed for, the degree to which leers of an alphabet correspond to phonemes of a language varies greatly from one
Writing - Wikipedia — language to another and even within a single language.
Writing - Wikipedia — In most of the alphabets of the Middle East, it is usually only the consonants of a word that are wrien, although vowels may
Writing - Wikipedia — be indicated by the addition of various diacritical marks. Writing systems based primarily on writing just consonants
Writing - Wikipedia — phonemes date back to the hieroglyphs of ancient Egypt. Such systems are called abjads or consonantaries.[42]
Writing - Wikipedia — In most of the alphabets of India and Southeast Asia, vowels are indicated through diacritics or modiﬁcation of the shape of
Writing - Wikipedia — the consonant. ese are called abugidas.[42] Some abugidas, such as Geʽez and the Canadian Aboriginal syllabics, are learned
Writing - Wikipedia — by children as syllabaries, and so are oen called "syllabics". However, unlike true syllabaries, there is not an independent
Writing - Wikipedia — glyph for each syllable.
Writing - Wikipedia — While research into the development of writing during the Neolithic is ongoing, the current consensus is that it ﬁrst evolved from economic necessity in the ancient
Writing - Wikipedia — Near East. Writing most likely began as a consequence of political expansion in ancient cultures, which needed reliable means for transmiing information, maintaining
Writing - Wikipedia — ﬁnancial accounts, keeping historical records, and similar activities. Around the 4th millennium BC, the complexity of trade and administration outgrew the power of
Writing - Wikipedia — memory, and writing became a more dependable method of recording and presenting transactions in a permanent form.[45]
Writing - Wikipedia — e invention of the ﬁrst writing systems is roughly contemporary with the emergence of civilizations and the beginning of the Bronze Age during the late 4th

Writing - Wikipedia — millenniumBC. Cuneiform used to write the Sumerian language and Egyptian hieroglyphs are generally considered the earliest writing systems, both emerging out of
Writing - Wikipedia — ancestral proto-writing systems between 3500 and 2900 BC,[46] with earliest coherent texts from c. 2600 BC. It is generally agreed that Sumerian writing was an
Writing - Wikipedia — independent invention; however, it is debated whether Egyptian writing was developed completely independently of Sumerian, or was a case of cultural diﬀusion.
Writing - Wikipedia — Archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat determined the link between previously uncategorized clay "tokens", the oldest of which
Writing - Wikipedia — have been found in the Zagros region of Iran, and cuneiform, the ﬁrst known writing. Around 8000 BC, Mesopotamians began using
Writing - Wikipedia — clay tokens to count their agricultural and manufactured goods. Later they began placing these tokens inside large, hollow clay
Writing - Wikipedia — containers (bulla, or globular envelopes) which were then sealed. e quantity of tokens in each container came to be expressed by
Writing - Wikipedia — impressing, on the container's surface, one picture for each instance of the token inside. ey next dispensed with the tokens, relying
Writing - Wikipedia — solely on symbols for the tokens, drawn on clay surfaces. To avoid making a picture for each instance of the same object (for
Writing - Wikipedia — example: 100 pictures of a hat to represent 100 hats), they counted the objects by using various small marks.[47]
Writing - Wikipedia — e original Mesopotamian writing system emerged c. 3200 BC from this method of keeping accounts. By the end of the 4th
Writing - Wikipedia — millennium BC,[48] the Mesopotamians were using a triangular-shaped stylus pressed into so clay to record numbers. is system
Writing - Wikipedia — was gradually augmented with using a sharp stylus to indicate what was being counted by means of pictographs. Round and sharp
Writing - Wikipedia — styluses were gradually replaced for writing by wedge-shaped styluses (hence the term cuneiform), at ﬁrst only for logograms, but by
Writing - Wikipedia — the 29th century BC also for phonetic elements. Around 2700 BC, cuneiform began to represent syllables of spoken Sumerian. About
Writing - Wikipedia — that time, Mesopotamian cuneiform became a general purpose writing system for logograms, syllables, and numbers. is script was
Writing - Wikipedia — adapted to another Mesopotamian language, the East Semitic Akkadian (Assyrian and Babylonian) c. 2600 BC, and then to others
Writing - Wikipedia — such as Elamite, Haian, Hurrian and Hiite. Scripts similar in appearance to this writing system include those for Ugaritic and Old
Writing - Wikipedia — Persian. With the adoption of Aramaic as the lingua franca of the Neo-Assyrian Empire (911–609 BC), Old Aramaic was also adapted
Writing - Wikipedia — to Mesopotamian cuneiform. e latest cuneiform texts in Akkadian discovered thus far date from the 1st century AD.[49]
Writing - Wikipedia — e earliest known hieroglyphs date back around 5,200 years, such as the clay labels of a Predynastic ruler called "Scorpion I"
Writing - Wikipedia — (Naqada IIIA period, c. 33nd century BC) recovered at Abydos (modern Umm el-Qa'ab) in 1998 or the Narmer Palee, dating to
Writing - Wikipedia — around c. 3100 BC.[50] e hieroglyphic script was logographic with phonetic adjuncts that included an eﬀective alphabet. e world's oldest deciphered sentence was
Writing - Wikipedia — found on a seal impression in the tomb of Seth-Peribsen at Abydos, dating to the Second Dynasty (28th or 27th century BC). ere are around 800 hieroglyphs dating
Writing - Wikipedia — back to the Old Kingdom, Middle Kingdom and New Kingdom Eras. By the Greco-Roman period, there are more than 5,000.[51]
Writing - Wikipedia — Writing was very important in maintaining the Egyptian empire, and literacy was concentrated among an educated elite of scribes.[52] Only people from certain
Writing - Wikipedia — backgrounds were allowed to train to become scribes, in the service of temple, pharaonic, and military authorities. e hieroglyph system was complex and diﬃcult to
Writing - Wikipedia — master.

Writing - Wikipedia — Serabit el-Khadem, with symbols that stood for single consonant sounds rather than whole words or concepts – the basis of an alphabetic system. It was not until the

Writing - Wikipedia — Of several pre-Columbian scripts in Mesoamerica, the one that appears to have been best developed, and the only one to be
Writing - Wikipedia — deciphered, is the Maya script. e earliest inscription identiﬁed as Maya dates to the 3rd century BC.[54] Maya writing used
Writing - Wikipedia — logograms complemented by a set of syllabic glyphs, somewhat similar in function to modern Japanese writing.
Writing - Wikipedia — e earliest surviving examples of writing in China – inscriptions on oracle bones, usually tortoise plastrons and ox scapulae which
Writing - Wikipedia — were used for divination – date from around 1200 BC, during the Late Shang period. A small number of bronze inscriptions from the
Writing - Wikipedia — same period have also survived.[55]
Writing - Wikipedia — Over the centuries, three distinct Elamite scripts developed. Proto-Elamite is the oldest known writing system from Iran. In use
Writing - Wikipedia — (c. 3200 – c. 2900 BC), clay tablets with Proto-Elamite writing have been found at diﬀerent sites across Iran, with the majority having
Writing - Wikipedia — been excavated at Susa, an ancient city located east of the Tigris and between the Karkheh and Dez rivers.[56] e Proto-Elamite
Writing - Wikipedia — script is thought to have developed from early cuneiform (proto-cuneiform). e Proto-Elamite script consists of more than 1,000
Writing - Wikipedia — signs and is thought to be partly logographic. e Elamite cuneiform script was used from about 2500 to 331 BC, and was adapted from the Akkadian cuneiform. At any
Writing - Wikipedia — given point within this period, the Elamite cuneiform script consisted of about 130 symbols, and over this entire period only 206 total signs were used. is is far fewer
Writing - Wikipedia — than most other cuneiform scripts.[42]
Writing - Wikipedia — Cretan hieroglyphs are found on artefacts of Crete (early-to-mid-2nd millennium BC, MM I to MM III, overlapping with Linear A from MM IIA at the earliest). Linear B,
Writing - Wikipedia — the writing system of the Mycenaean Greeks,[57] has been deciphered while Linear A has yet to be deciphered. e sequence and the geographical spread of the three
Writing - Wikipedia — overlapping, but distinct writing systems can be summarized as follows (beginning date refers to ﬁrst aestations, the assumed origins of all scripts lie further back in
Writing - Wikipedia — the past): Cretan hieroglyphs were used in Crete c. 1625–1500 BC; Linear A was used in the Aegean Islands, and the Greek mainland c. 1700–1450 BC; Linear B was used
Writing - Wikipedia — in Crete (Knossos), and the mainland c. 1375–1200 BC.

Writing - Wikipedia — was adapted from the Proto-Canaanite script sometime before the 14th centuryBC, which in turn borrowed principles of representing phonetic information from

Literature - Wikipedia — Literature
Literature - Wikipedia — Literature is any collection of wrien work, but it is also used more narrowly for writings speciﬁcally considered to
Literature - Wikipedia — be an art form, especially novels, plays, and poems.[1] It includes both print and digital writing.[2] In recent centuries,
Literature - Wikipedia — the deﬁnition has expanded to include oral literature, much of which has been transcribed.[3][4] Literature is a method
Literature - Wikipedia — of recording, preserving, and transmiing knowledge and entertainment. It can also have a social, psychological,
Literature - Wikipedia — spiritual, or political role.
Literature - Wikipedia — Literary criticism is one of the oldest academic disciplines, and is concerned with the literary merit or intellectual
Literature - Wikipedia — signiﬁcance of speciﬁc texts. e study of books and other texts as artifacts or traditions is instead encompassed by
Literature - Wikipedia — textual criticism or the history of the book. "Literature", as an art form, is sometimes used synonymously with literary
Literature - Wikipedia — ﬁction, ﬁction wrien with the goal of artistic merit,[5][6] but can also include works in various non-ﬁction genres,
Literature - Wikipedia — such as biography, diaries, memoirs, leers, and essays. Within this broader deﬁnition, literature includes non-
Literature - Wikipedia — ﬁctional books, articles, or other wrien information on a particular subject.[7][8]
Literature - Wikipedia — Developments in print technology have allowed an ever-growing distribution and proliferation of wrien works, while the digital era had blurred the lines between
Literature - Wikipedia — online electronic literature and other forms of modern media.
Literature - Wikipedia — Deﬁnitions of literature have varied over time.[9] In Western Europe, prior to the 18th century, literature denoted all books and writing. It can be seen as returning to
Literature - Wikipedia — older, more inclusive notions, so that cultural studies, for instance, include, in addition to canonical works, popular and minority genres. e word is also used in
Literature - Wikipedia — reference to non-wrien works: to "oral literature" and "the literature of preliterate culture".
Literature - Wikipedia — Etymologically, the term derives from Latin literatura/lieratura, "learning, writing, grammar," originally "writing formed with leers," from litera/liera, "leer."[10] In
Literature - Wikipedia — spite of this, the term has also been applied to spoken or sung texts.[11][12] Literature is oen referred to synecdochically as "writing," especially creative writing, and
Literature - Wikipedia — poetically as "the cra of writing" (or simply "the cra"). Syd Field described his discipline, screenwriting, as "a cra that occasionally rises to the level of art."[13]
Literature - Wikipedia — A value judgment deﬁnition of literature considers it as consisting solely of high quality writing that forms part of the belles-leres ("ﬁne writing") tradition.[14] An
Literature - Wikipedia — example of this is in the 1910–1911 Encyclopædia Britannica, which classiﬁed literature as "the best expression of the best thought reduced to writing".[15]
Literature - Wikipedia — Deﬁnitions
Literature - Wikipedia — A traditional Kyrgyz manaschi
Literature - Wikipedia — performing part of the Epic of Manas

Literature - Wikipedia — creative work may be in a literary, artistic, educational, or musical form. Copyright is intended to protect the original expression of an idea in the form of a creative
Literature - Wikipedia — work, but not the idea itself.[146][147][148]
Literature - Wikipedia — Literary works have been protected by copyright law from unauthorized reproduction since at least 1710.[149] Literary works are deﬁned by copyright law to mean "any

Literature - Wikipedia — Literary works are all works of literature; that is all works expressed in print or writing (other than dramatic or musical works).[151]
Literature - Wikipedia — e copyright law of the United States has a long and complicated history, dating back to colonial times. It was established as federal
Literature - Wikipedia — law with the Copyright Act of 1790. is act was updated many times, including a major revision in 1976.
Literature - Wikipedia — e copyright law of the European Union is the copyright law applicable within the European Union. Copyright law is largely
Literature - Wikipedia — harmonized in the Union, although country to country diﬀerences exist. e body of law was implemented in the EU through a
Literature - Wikipedia — number of directives, which the member states need to enact into their national law. e main copyright directives are the Copyright
Literature - Wikipedia — Term Directive, the Information Society Directive and the Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market. Copyright in the
Literature - Wikipedia — Union is furthermore dependent on international conventions to which the European Union is a member (such as the TRIPS
Literature - Wikipedia — Agreement and conventions to which all Member States are parties (such as the Berne Convention)).
Literature - Wikipedia — Japan was a party to the original Berne convention in 1899, so its copyright law is in sync with most international regulations. e convention protected copyrighted
Literature - Wikipedia — works for 50 years aer the author's death (or 50 years aer publication for unknown authors and corporations). However, in 2004 Japan extended the copyright term to
Literature - Wikipedia — 70 years for cinematographic works. At the end of 2018, as a result of the Trans-Paciﬁc Partnership negotiations, the 70-year term was applied to all works.[152] is
Literature - Wikipedia — new term is not applied retroactively; works that had entered the public domain between 1999 and 2018 by expiration would remain in the public domain.
Literature - Wikipedia — Censorship of literature is employed by states, religious organizations, educational institutions, etc., to control what can be portrayed, spoken, performed, or wrien.
Literature - Wikipedia — [153] Generally such bodies aempt to ban works for political reasons, or because they deal with other controversial maers such as race, or sex.[154]
Literature - Wikipedia — A notable example of censorship is James Joyce's novel Ulysses, which has been described by Russian-American novelist Vladimir Nabokov as a "divine work of art" and
Literature - Wikipedia — the greatest masterpiece of 20th century prose.[155] It was banned in the United States from 1921 until 1933 on the grounds of obscenity. Nowadays it is a central literary
Literature - Wikipedia — text in English literature courses, throughout the world.[156]

Literature - Wikipedia — ere are numerous awards recognizing achievements and contributions in literature. Given the diversity of the ﬁeld, awards
Literature - Wikipedia — are typically limited in scope, usually on: form, genre, language, nationality and output (e.g. for ﬁrst-time writers or debut
Literature - Wikipedia — novels).[157]
Literature - Wikipedia — e Nobel Prize in Literature was one of the six Nobel Prizes established by the will of Alfred Nobel in 1895,[158] and is
Literature - Wikipedia — awarded to an author on the basis of their body of work, rather than to, or for, a particular work itself.[note 2] Other literary
Literature - Wikipedia — prizes for which all nationalities are eligible include: the Neustadt International Prize for Literature, the Man Booker
Literature - Wikipedia — International Prize, Pulitzer Prize, Hugo Award, Guardian First Book Award and the Franz Kaa Prize.

Creative coding - Wikipedia — Creative coding
Creative coding - Wikipedia — Creative coding is a type of computer programming in which the goal is to create something expressive instead of something
Creative coding - Wikipedia — functional. It is used to create live visuals and for VJing, as well as creating visual art and design, entertainment (e.g. video games), art
Creative coding - Wikipedia — installations, projections and projection mapping, sound art, advertising, product prototypes, and much more.
Creative coding - Wikipedia — Using programming to create art is a practice that started in the 1960s. In later decades groups such as Compos 68[1] successfully
Creative coding - Wikipedia — explored programming for artistic purposes, having their work exhibited in international exhibitions. From the 80s onward expert
Creative coding - Wikipedia — programmers joined the demoscene, and tested their skills against each other by creating "demos": highly technically competent visual
Creative coding - Wikipedia — creations.
Creative coding - Wikipedia — Recent exhibitions and books, including Dominic Lopes' A Philosophy of Computer Art (2009) have sought to examine the integral role
Creative coding - Wikipedia — of coding in contemporary art beyond that of Human Computer Interface (HCI).[2] Criticising Lopes however, Juliﬀ and Cox argue
Creative coding - Wikipedia — that Lopes continues to privilege interface and user at the expense of the integral condition of code in much computer art. Arguing for
Creative coding - Wikipedia — a more nuanced appreciation of coding, Juliﬀ and Cox set out contemporary creative coding as the examination of code and
Creative coding - Wikipedia — intentionality as integral to the users understanding of the work.[3]
Creative coding - Wikipedia — Currently there is a renewed interest in the question of why programming as a method of producing art hasn't ﬂourished. Google has
Creative coding - Wikipedia — renewed interest in their Dev Art initiative,[4] but this in turn has elicited strong reactions from a number of creative coders who claim that coining a new term to
Creative coding - Wikipedia — describe their practice is counterproductive.[5]
Creative coding - Wikipedia — Some contemporary artists who use creative coding in their work are Daniel Shiﬀman, Zachary Lieberman, Golan Levin, Ben Fry, and Giles Whitaker (artist).
Creative coding - Wikipedia — Although any technology or programming language can potentially be used for creative purposes, certain libraries and frameworks have been speciﬁcally craed to aid
Creative coding - Wikipedia — in the rapid prototyping and development of creative works. Soware toolkits frequently used in this context include:

ASCII art - Wikipedia — ASCII art of a ﬁsh
ASCII art - Wikipedia — ASCII art
ASCII art - Wikipedia — ASCII art is a graphic design technique that uses computers for presentation and consists of pictures pieced together from
ASCII art - Wikipedia — the 95 printable (from a total of 128) characters deﬁned by the ASCII Standard from 1963 and ASCII compliant character sets
ASCII art - Wikipedia — with proprietary extended characters (beyond the 128 characters of standard 7-bit ASCII). e term is also loosely used to
ASCII art - Wikipedia — refer to text-based visual art in general. ASCII art can be created with any text editor, and is oen used with free-form
ASCII art - Wikipedia — languages. Most examples of ASCII art require a ﬁxed-width font (non-proportional fonts, as on a traditional typewriter) such
ASCII art - Wikipedia — as Courier or Consolas for presentation.
ASCII art - Wikipedia — Among the oldest known examples of ASCII art are the creations by computer-art pioneer Kenneth Knowlton from around
ASCII art - Wikipedia — 1966, who was working for Bell Labs at the time.[1] "Studies in Perception I" by Knowlton and Leon Harmon from 1966 shows
ASCII art - Wikipedia — some examples of their early ASCII art.[2]
ASCII art - Wikipedia — ASCII art was invented, in large part, because early printers oen lacked graphics ability and thus, characters were used in
ASCII art - Wikipedia — place of graphic marks. Also, to mark divisions between diﬀerent print jobs from diﬀerent users, bulk printers oen used
ASCII art - Wikipedia — ASCII art to print large banner pages, making the division easier to spot so that the results could be more easily separated by a computer operator or clerk.[3] ASCII art
ASCII art - Wikipedia — was also used in early e-mail when images could not be embedded.
ASCII art - Wikipedia — Since 1867, typewriters have been used for creating visual art.[4][5] Typists could ﬁnd guides in books or magazines with instructions on how to type portraits or other
ASCII art - Wikipedia — depictions.[6]
ASCII art - Wikipedia — TTY stands for "TeleTYpe" or "TeleTYpewriter", and is also known as Teleprinter or Teletype. RTTY stands for Radioteletype; character sets such as Baudot code, which
ASCII art - Wikipedia — predated ASCII, were used. According to a chapter in the "RTTY Handbook", text images have been sent via teletypewriter as early as 1923.[7] However, none of the
ASCII art - Wikipedia — "old" RTTY art has been discovered yet. What is known is that text images appeared frequently on radioteletype in the 1960s and the 1970s.[4][8]

ASCII art - Wikipedia — e Atari 400/800, which were released in 1979, did not follow the ASCII standard and had their own character set, called ATASCII.[36][37] e emergence of ATASCII art
ASCII art - Wikipedia — coincided with the growing popularity of BBS Systems caused by availability of the acoustic couplers that were compatible with the 8-bit home computers. ATASCII text
ASCII art - Wikipedia — animations are also referred to as "break animations" by the Atari sceners.
ASCII art - Wikipedia — e Commodore 64, which was released in 1982, also did not follow the ASCII standard. e C-64 character set is called PETSCII, an extended form of ASCII-1963. As
ASCII art - Wikipedia — with the Atari's ATASCII art, C-64 fans developed a similar scene that used PETSCII for their creations.
ASCII art - Wikipedia — So-called "block ASCII" or "high ASCII" uses the extended characters of the 8-bit code page 437, which is a proprietary standard
ASCII art - Wikipedia — introduced by IBM in 1979 (ANSI Standard x3.16) for the IBM PC DOS and MS-DOS operating systems. "Block ASCIIs" were widely
ASCII art - Wikipedia — used on the PC during the 1990s until the Internet replaced BBSes as the main communication platform. Until then, "block ASCIIs"
ASCII art - Wikipedia — dominated the PC Text Art Scene.[38][39]
ASCII art - Wikipedia — e ﬁrst art scene group that focused on the extended character set of the PC in their artwork was called "Aces of ANSI Art", or
ASCII art - Wikipedia — <A.A.A>. Some members le in 1990 and formed a group called "ANSI Creators in Demand", or ACiD. In that same year the second
ASCII art - Wikipedia — major underground art scene group "Insane Creators Enterprise", or ICE, was founded.[40]
ASCII art - Wikipedia — ere is some debate between ASCII and block ASCII artists, with "Hardcore" ASCII artists maintaining that block ASCII art is in fact
ASCII art - Wikipedia — not ASCII art, because it does not use the 128 characters of the original ASCII standard. On the other hand, block ASCII artists argue
ASCII art - Wikipedia — that if their art uses only characters of the computer's character set, then it is to be called ASCII, regardless if the character set is proprietary or not.
ASCII art - Wikipedia — Microso Windows does not support the ANSI Standard x3.16. One can view block ASCIIs with a text editor using the font "Terminal", but it will not look exactly as it
ASCII art - Wikipedia — was intended by the artist. With a special ASCII/ANSI viewer, such as ACiDView for Windows , one can see block ASCII and ANSI ﬁles properly. An example that
ASCII art - Wikipedia — illustrates the diﬀerence in appearance is part of this article. Alternatively, one could look at the ﬁle using the TYPE command in the command prompt.

ASCII art - Wikipedia — "Newskool" upon its comeback and renewed popularity at the end of the 1990s.[38]

ASCII art - Wikipedia — further aer the introduction and adaptation of Unicode.

ASCII art - Wikipedia — keyboard, one needs to know the Alt code for each character. For example, Alt + 1 7 8 will produce ▓, Alt + 1 7 7 will produce ▒, and Alt + 8 will produce ◘.
ASCII art - Wikipedia — e special text editors have sets of special characters assigned to existing keys on the keyboard. Popular DOS-based editors, such as eDraw and ACiDDraw had
ASCII art - Wikipedia — multiple sets of diﬀerent special characters mapped to the function keys to make the use of those characters easier for the artist who can switch between individual sets

ASCII art - Wikipedia — Other programs allow one to automatically convert an image to text characters, which is a special case of vector quantization. A method is to sample the image down to
ASCII art - Wikipedia — grayscale with less than 8-bit precision, and then assign a character for each value. Such ASCII art generators oen allow users to choose the intensity and contrast of
ASCII art - Wikipedia — the generated image.[41]
ASCII art - Wikipedia — ree factors limit the ﬁdelity of the conversion, especially of photographs:
ASCII art - Wikipedia — ▪ depth (solutions: reduced line spacing; bold style; block elements; colored background; good shading);
ASCII art - Wikipedia — ▪ sharpness (solutions: a longer text, with a smaller font; a greater set of characters; variable width fonts);
ASCII art - Wikipedia — ▪ ratio (solutions with compatibility issues: font with a square grid; stylized without extra line spacing).

ASCII art - Wikipedia — Most ASCII art is created using a monospaced font, such as Courier, where all characters are identical in width. Early computers in use when ASCII art came into vogue
ASCII art - Wikipedia — had monospaced fonts for screen and printer displays. Today, most of the more commonly used fonts in word processors, web browsers and other programs are
ASCII art - Wikipedia — proportional fonts, such as Helvetica or Times Roman, where diﬀerent widths are used for diﬀerent characters. ASCII art drawn for a ﬁxed width font will usually
ASCII art - Wikipedia — appear distorted, or even unrecognizable when displayed in a proportional font.
ASCII art - Wikipedia — Some ASCII artists have produced art for display in proportional fonts. ese ASCIIs, rather than using a purely shade-based correspondence, use characters for slopes
ASCII art - Wikipedia — and borders and use block shading. ese ASCIIs generally oﬀer greater precision and aention to detail than ﬁxed-width ASCIIs for a lower character count, although
ASCII art - Wikipedia — they are not as universally accessible since they are usually relatively font-speciﬁc.
ASCII art - Wikipedia — Animated ASCII art started in 1970 from so-called VT100 animations produced on VT100 terminals. ese animations were simply text with cursor movement
ASCII art - Wikipedia — instructions, deleting and erasing the characters necessary to appear animated. Usually, they represented a long hand-craed process undertaken by a single person to
ASCII art - Wikipedia — tell a story.
ASCII art - Wikipedia — Contemporary web browser revitalized animated ASCII art again. It became possible to display animated ASCII art via JavaScript or Java applets. Static ASCII art
ASCII art - Wikipedia — pictures are loaded and displayed one aer another, creating the animation, very similar to how movie projectors unreel ﬁlm reel and project the individual pictures on
ASCII art - Wikipedia — the big screen at movie theaters. A new term was born: "ASCIImation" – another name of animated ASCII art. A seminal work in this arena is the Star Wars
ASCII art - Wikipedia — ASCIImation.[43] More complicated routines in JavaScript generate more elaborate ASCIImations showing eﬀects like Morphing eﬀects, star ﬁeld emulations, fading
ASCII art - Wikipedia — eﬀects and calculated images, such as mandelbrot fractal animations.[44][45]

ASCII art - Wikipedia — In the 1970s and early 1980s it was popular to produce a kind of text art that relied on overprinting. is could be produced either on a screen or on a printer by typing a
ASCII art - Wikipedia — character, backing up, and then typing another character, just as on a typewriter. is developed into sophisticated graphics in some cases, such as the PLATO system
ASCII art - Wikipedia — (circa 1973), where superscript and subscript allowed a wide variety of graphic eﬀects. A common use was for emoticons, with WOBTAX and VICTORY both producing
ASCII art - Wikipedia — convincing smiley faces.[55] Overprinting had previously been used on typewriters, but the low-resolution pixelation of characters on video terminals meant that
ASCII art - Wikipedia — overprinting here produced seamless pixel graphics, rather than visibly overstruck combinations of leers on paper.
ASCII art - Wikipedia — Beyond pixel graphics, this was also used for printing photographs, as the overall darkness of a particular character space dependent on how many characters, as well as
ASCII art - Wikipedia — the choice of character, were printed in a particular place. anks to the increased granularity of tone, photographs were oen converted to this type of printout. Even
ASCII art - Wikipedia — manual typewriters or daisy wheel printers could be used. e technique has fallen from popularity since all cheap printers can easily print photographs, and a normal
ASCII art - Wikipedia — text ﬁle (or an e-mail message or Usenet posting) cannot represent overprinted text. However, something similar has emerged to replace it: shaded or colored ASCII art,
ASCII art - Wikipedia — using ANSI video terminal markup or color codes (such as those found in HTML, IRC, and many internet message boards) to add a bit more tone variation. In this way,
ASCII art - Wikipedia — it is possible to create ASCII art where the characters only diﬀer in color.

Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Filmmaking
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Filmmaking or ﬁlm production is the process by which a motion picture is produced. Filmmaking involves a number of complex and discrete stages, beginning with
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — an initial story, idea, or commission. Production then continues through screenwriting, casting, pre-production, shooting, sound recording, post-production, and
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — screening the ﬁnished product before an audience, which may result in a ﬁlm release and exhibition. e process is nonlinear, in that the ﬁlmmaker typically shoots the
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — script out of sequence, repeats shots as needed, and puts them together through editing later. Filmmaking occurs in a variety of economic, social, and political contexts
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — around the world, and uses a variety of technologies and cinematic techniques to make theatrical ﬁlms, episodic ﬁlms for television and streaming platforms, music
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — videos, and promotional and educational ﬁlms.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Although ﬁlmmaking originally involved the use of ﬁlm, most ﬁlm productions are now digital.[1] Today, ﬁlmmaking refers to the process of craing an audio-visual
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — story commercially for distribution or broadcast.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Film production consists of ﬁve major stages:[2]
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Development: Ideas for the ﬁlm are created, rights to existing intellectual properties are purchased, etc., and the screenplay is written.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Financing for the project is sought and obtained.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Pre-production: Arrangements and preparations are made for the shoot, such as hiring cast and ﬁlm crew, selecting locations, and constructing
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — sets.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Production: The raw footage and other elements of the ﬁlm are recorded during the ﬁlm shoot, including principal photography.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Post-production: The images, sound, and visual eﬀects of the recorded ﬁlm are edited and combined into a ﬁnished product.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Distribution: The completed ﬁlm is distributed, marketed, and screened in cinemas and released on home video to be viewed at home.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — e development stage contains both general and speciﬁc components. Each ﬁlm studio has a yearly retreat where their top creative executives meet and interact on a
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — variety of areas and topics they wish to explore through collaborations with producers and screenwriters, and then ultimately, directors, actors, and actresses. ey
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — choose trending topics from the media and real life, as well as many other sources, to determine their yearly agenda. For example, in a year when action is popular, they
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — may wish to explore that topic in one or more movies. Sometimes, they purchase the rights to articles, bestselling novels, plays, the remaking of older ﬁlms, stories with
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — some basis in real life through a person or event, a video game, fairy tale, comic book, graphic novel. Likewise, research through surveys may inform their decisions.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ey may have had blockbusters from their previous year and wish to explore a sequel. ey will additionally acquire a completed and independently ﬁnanced and

Filmmaking - Wikipedia — produced ﬁlm. Such notable examples are Lile Miss Sunshine, e English Patient, and Roma.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Studios hold general meetings with producers and screenwriters about original story ideas. "In my decade working as a writer, I knew of only a few that were sold and
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — fewer that made it to the screen," relays writer Wayne Powers. Alan Wa, writer-director and Founder of e LA Writer's Lab conﬁrmed that completed original
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — screenplays, referred to as "specs", make big news when they sell, but these make up a very small portion of movies that are ultimately given the green light to be
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — produced by the president of a studio.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — e executives return from the retreat with fairly well-established instructions. ey spread these concepts through the industry community, especially to producers
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — they have deals with (traditional studios will have those producers in oﬃces on their lots). Also, agents for screenwriters are made aware. is results in a pairing of
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — producers with writers, where they develop a "take", a basic story idea that utilizes the concept given by studio executives. Oen it is a competition with several pairings
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — meeting with studio executives and "pitching" their "take". Very few writing jobs are from original ideas brought to studios by producers or writers. Perhaps one movie a
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — year will be a "spec" script that was purchased.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Once the producer and writer have sold their approach to the desired subject maer, they begin to work. However, many writers and producers usually pass before a
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — particular concept is realized in a way that is awarded a green light to production. Production of Unforgiven, which earned Oscars for its Director/Star Clint Eastwood,
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — as well as its screenwriter, David Webb Peoples, required ﬁeen years. Powers related that e Italian Job took approximately eight years from concept to screen, which,
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — as Powers added, "is average." And most concepts turned into paid screenplays wind up gathering dust on some executive's shelf, never to see production.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Writers have diﬀerent styles and creative processes; some have stronger track records than others. Because of this, how the development process proceeds from there
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — and how much detail a writer returns to the studio to divulge before beginning writing can vary greatly. Screenwriters are oen protected by the union, the Writers
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Guild of America, or WGA. e WGA allows a screenwriter to contract for One Dra, One Revision, and One Polish. Bob Eisle, Writer and Member of the Guild Board,
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — states, "Additional writing requires an extension of contracts and payment for additional work". ey are paid 80% of their fee aer the First Dra. Preliminary
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — discussions are minimal with studio executives but might be quite detailed with the producer.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Next, a screenwriter writes a screenplay over a period of several months, or however long it takes. Deadlines are in their contracts but there is no pressure to adhere to
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — them. Again, every writer's process and speed vary. e screenwriter may rewrite the script several times to improve dramatization, clarity, structure, characters,
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — dialogue, and overall style.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Script Coverage, a freelance job held by recent university graduates, does not feed scripts into the system that are ready for production nor already produced.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — "Coverage" is a way for young screenwriters to be read and their ideas might make their way up to an executive or famous producer and result in "meet and greets"
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — where relations with up-and-comers can be formed. But it has not historically yielded ideas studios pursue into production.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — e studio is the ﬁlm distributor who at an early stage aempts to choose a slate of concepts that are likely to have market appeal and ﬁnd potential ﬁnancial success.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Hollywood distributors consider factors such as the ﬁlm genre, the target audience and assumed audience, the historical success of similar ﬁlms, the actors who might
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — appear in the ﬁlm, and potential directors. All these factors imply a certain appeal of the ﬁlm to a possible audience. Not all ﬁlms make a proﬁt from the theatrical
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — release alone, however, the studio mainly targets the opening weekend and the second weekend to make most domestic proﬁts. Occasionally, a ﬁlm called a "word of
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — mouth ﬁlm" does not market strongly but its success spreads by word of mouth. It slowly gains its audience. ese are special circumstances and these ﬁlms may remain
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — in theaters for 5 months while a typical ﬁlm run is closer to 5 weekends. Further earnings result from pay television purchases, foreign market purchases and DVD sales
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — to establish worldwide distribution gross of a lm.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Once a screenplay is "green-lit", directors and actors are aached and the ﬁlm proceeds into the pre-production stage, although sometimes development and pre-
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — production stages will overlap. Projects which fail to obtain a green light may have protracted diﬃculties in making the transition to pre-production and enter a phase
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — referred to as development hell for extended period of time or until developmental turnaround.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Analogous to almost any business venture, ﬁnancing of a ﬁlm project deals with the study of ﬁlmmaking as the management and procurement of investments. It
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — includes the dynamics of assets that are required to fund the ﬁlmmaking and liabilities incurred during the ﬁlmmaking over the time period from early development
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — through the management of proﬁts and losses aer distribution under conditions of diﬀerent degrees of uncertainty and risk. e practical aspects of ﬁlmmaking
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ﬁnance can also be deﬁned as the science of the money management of all phases involved in ﬁlmmaking. Film ﬁnance aims to price assets based on their risk level and
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — their expected rate of return based upon anticipated proﬁts and protection against losses.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — In pre-production, every step of actually creating the ﬁlm is carefully designed and planned. is is the phase where one would narrow down all the options of the
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — production. It is where all the planning takes place before the camera rolls and sets the overall vision of the project. e production company is created and a
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — production oﬃce established. e ﬁlm is pre-visualized by the director and may be storyboarded with the help of illustrators and concept artists. A production budget is
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — drawn up to plan expenditures for the ﬁlm. For major productions, insurance is procured to protect against accidents. Pre-production also includes working out the
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — shoot location and casting process. e Producer hires a Line Manager or a Production Manager to create the schedule and budget for the ﬁlm.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — e nature of the ﬁlm, and the budget, determine the size and type of crew used during ﬁlmmaking. Many Hollywood blockbusters employ a cast and crew of hundreds,
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — while a low-budget, independent ﬁlm may be made by a "skeleton crew" of eight or nine (or fewer). ese are typical crew positions:
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Storyboard artist: creates visual images to help the director and production designer communicate their ideas to the production team.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Director: is primarily responsible for the storytelling, creative decisions and acting of the ﬁlm.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Assistant director (AD): manages the shooting schedule and logistics of the production, among other tasks. There are several types of AD,
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — each with diﬀerent responsibilities.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Film producer: hires the ﬁlm's crew.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Unit production manager: manages the production budget and production schedule. They also report, on behalf of the production oﬃce, to
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — the studio executives or ﬁnanciers of the ﬁlm.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Location manager: ﬁnds and manages ﬁlm locations. Nearly all pictures feature segments that are shot in the controllable environment
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — of a studio sound stage, while outdoor sequences call for ﬁlming on location.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Production designer: the one who creates the visual conception of the ﬁlm, working with the art director, who manages the art department
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — which makes production sets.[3]

Filmmaking - Wikipedia — dialogue, presence and sound eﬀects in monaural and ambience in stereo.[4][5] They work with the boom operator, Director, DA, DP, and First
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — AD.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Sound designer: creates the aural conception of the ﬁlm,[3] working with the supervising sound editor. On Bollywood-style Indian
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — productions the sound designer plays the role of a director of audiography.[6]
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — ▪ Composer: creates new music for the ﬁlm. (usually not until post-production)
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — In production, the ﬁlm is created and shot. In this phase, it is key to keep planning ahead of the daily shoot. e primary aim is to
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — stick to the budget and schedule, which requires constant vigilance. More crew will be recruited at this stage, such as the property
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — master, script supervisor, assistant directors, stills photographer, picture editor, and sound editors. ese are the most common roles
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — in ﬁlmmaking; the production oﬃce will be free to create any unique blend of roles to suit the various responsibilities needed during
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — the production of a ﬁlm. Communication is key between the location, set, oﬃce, production company, distributors and all other
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — parties involved.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — A typical day shooting begins with the crew arriving on the set/location by their call time. Actors usually have their own separate call
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — times. Since set construction, dressing and lighting can take many hours or even days, they are oen set up in advance.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — e grip, electric and production design crews are typically a step ahead of the camera and sound departments: for eﬃciency's sake,
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — while a scene is being ﬁlmed, they are already preparing the next one.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — While the crew prepares their equipment, the actors do their costumes and aend the hair and make-up departments. e actors
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — rehearse the script and blocking with the director, and the camera and sound crews rehearse with them and make ﬁnal tweaks.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Finally, the action is shot in as many takes as the director wishes. Most American productions follow a speciﬁc procedure:
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — e assistant director (AD) calls "picture is up!" to inform everyone that a take is about to be recorded, and then "quiet, everyone!"
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Once everyone is ready to shoot, the AD calls "roll sound" (if the take involves sound), and the production sound mixer will start their
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — equipment, record a verbal slate of the take's information, and announce "sound speed", or just "speed", when they are ready. e AD

Filmmaking - Wikipedia — A take is over when the director calls "Cut!" and the camera and sound stop recording. e script supervisor will note any continuity
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — issues, and the sound and camera teams log technical notes for the take on their respective report sheets. If the director decides
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — additional takes are required, the whole process repeats. Once satisﬁed, the crew moves on to the next camera angle or "setup", until
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — the whole scene is "covered." When shooting is ﬁnished for the scene, the assistant director declares a "wrap" or "moving on", and the
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — crew will "strike", or dismantle, the set for that scene.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — At the end of the day, the director approves the next day's shooting schedule and a daily progress report is sent to the production oﬃce.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — is includes the report sheets from continuity, sound, and camera teams. Call sheets are distributed to the cast and crew to tell them
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — when and where to turn up the next shooting day. Later on, the director, producer, other department heads, and, sometimes, the cast,
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — may gather to watch that day or yesterday's footage, called dailies, and review their work.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — With workdays oen lasting fourteen or eighteen hours in remote locations, ﬁlm production tends to create a team spirit.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — When the entire ﬁlm is "in the can", or in the completion of the production phase, it is customary for the production oﬃce to
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — arrange a wrap party, to thank all the cast and crew for their eﬀorts.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — For the production phase on live-action ﬁlms, synchronizing work schedules of key cast and crew members is very
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — important.[7] For many scenes, several cast members and many crew members must be physically present at the same place
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — at the same time (and bankable stars may need to rush from one project to another). Animated ﬁlms have diﬀerent workﬂow
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — at the production phase, in that voice actors can record their takes in the recording studio at diﬀerent times and may not see
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — one another until the ﬁlm's premiere.[8] Animated ﬁlms also have diﬀerent crew, since most physical live-action tasks are
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — either unnecessary or are simulated by various types of animators.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — is stage is usually thought of as starting when principal photography ends, but they may overlap. e bulk of post-production consists of the ﬁlm editor reviewing the
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — footage with the director and assembling the ﬁlm out of selected takes. e production sound (dialogue) is also edited; music tracks and songs are composed and
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — recorded if a ﬁlm is intended to have a score; sound eﬀects are designed and recorded. Any computer-generated visual eﬀects are digitally added by an artist. Finally, all
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — sound elements are mixed down into "stems", which are synchronized to the images on the screen, and the ﬁlm is fully completed ("locked").

Filmmaking - Wikipedia — from a digital media provider. e ﬁlm is duplicated as required (either onto ﬁlm or hard disk drives) and distributed in cinemas for exhibition (screening). Press kits,

Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Since the advent of home video in the late 1970s, most major ﬁlms have followed a paern of having several distinct release windows. A ﬁlm may ﬁrst be released to a
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — few select cinemas, or if it tests well enough, may go directly into wide release. Next, it is released, normally at diﬀerent times several weeks (or months) apart, into
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — diﬀerent market segments like rental, retail, pay-per-view, in-ﬂight entertainment, cable television, satellite television, or free-to-air broadcast television. e
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — distribution rights for the ﬁlm are also usually sold for worldwide distribution. e distributor and the production company share proﬁts and manage losses.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Filmmaking also takes place outside of the mainstream and is commonly called independent ﬁlmmaking. Since the
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — introduction of DV technology, the means of production have become more democratized and economically viable.
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — Filmmakers can conceivably shoot and edit a ﬁlm, create and edit the sound and music, and mix the ﬁnal cut on a home
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — computer. However, while the means of production may be democratized, ﬁnancing, traditional distribution, and marketing
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — remain diﬃcult to accomplish outside the traditional system. In the past, most independent ﬁlmmakers have relied on ﬁlm
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — festivals (such as Sundance Film Festival, Venice Film Festival, Cannes Film Festival, and Toronto International Film Festivals)
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — to get their ﬁlms noticed and sold for distribution and production. However, the internet has allowed for the relatively
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — inexpensive distribution of independent ﬁlms on websites such as YouTube. As a result, several companies have emerged to
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — assist ﬁlmmakers in geing independent movies seen and sold via mainstream internet marketplaces, oen adjacent to
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — popular Hollywood titles. With internet movie distribution, independent ﬁlmmakers who choose to forego a traditional
Filmmaking - Wikipedia — distribution deal now have the ability to reach global audiences.

Music - Wikipedia — Music is the arrangement of sound to create some combination of form, harmony, melody, rhythm, or otherwise
Music - Wikipedia — expressive content.[1][2][3] Music is generally agreed to be a cultural universal that is present in all human societies.[4]
Music - Wikipedia — Deﬁnitions of music vary widely in substance and approach.[5] While scholars agree that music is deﬁned by a small
Music - Wikipedia — number of speciﬁc elements, there is no consensus as to what these necessary elements are.[6] Music is oen
Music - Wikipedia — characterized as a highly versatile medium for expressing human creativity.[7] Diverse activities are involved in the
Music - Wikipedia — creation of music, and are oen divided into categories of composition, improvisation, and performance.[8] Music may
Music - Wikipedia — be performed using a wide variety of musical instruments, including the human voice. It can also be composed,
Music - Wikipedia — sequenced, or otherwise produced to be indirectly played mechanically or electronically, such as via a music box,
Music - Wikipedia — barrel organ, or digital audio workstation soware on a computer.
Music - Wikipedia — Music oen plays a key role in social events and religious ceremonies. e techniques of making music are oen
Music - Wikipedia — transmied as part of a cultural tradition. Music is played in public and private contexts, highlighted at events such as
Music - Wikipedia — festivals and concerts for various diﬀerent types of ensembles. Music is used in the production of other media, such as
Music - Wikipedia — in soundtracks to ﬁlms, TV shows, operas, and video games.
Music - Wikipedia — Listening to music is a common means of entertainment. e culture surrounding music extends into areas of
Music - Wikipedia — academic study, journalism, philosophy, psychology, and therapy. e music industry includes songwriters,
Music - Wikipedia — performers, sound engineers, producers, tour organizers, distributors of instruments, accessories, and publishers of
Music - Wikipedia — sheet music and recordings. Technology facilitating the recording and reproduction of music has historically included
Music - Wikipedia — sheet music, microphones, phonographs, and tape machines, with playback of digital musics being a common use for
Music - Wikipedia — MP3 players, CD players, and smartphones.

Music - Wikipedia — It is oen debated to what extent the origins of music will ever be understood,[23] and there are competing theories that aim to explain it.[24] Many scholars highlight a
Music - Wikipedia — relationship between the origin of music and the origin of language, and there is disagreement surrounding whether music developed before, aer, or simultaneously
Music - Wikipedia — with language.[25] A similar source of contention surrounds whether music was the intentional result of natural selection or was a byproduct spandrel of evolution.[25]
Music - Wikipedia — e earliest inﬂuential theory was proposed by Charles Darwin in 1871, who stated that music arose as a form of sexual selection, perhaps via mating calls.[26] Darwin's
Music - Wikipedia — original perspective has been heavily criticized for its inconsistencies with other sexual selection methods,[27] though many scholars in the 21st century have developed
Music - Wikipedia — and promoted the theory.[28] Other theories include that music arose to assist in organizing labor, improving long-distance communication, beneﬁting communication
Music - Wikipedia — with the divine, assisting in community cohesion or as a defense to scare oﬀ predators.[29]

Music - Wikipedia — Music was an important part of social and cultural life in ancient Greece, in fact it was one of the main subjects taught to children.
Music - Wikipedia — Musical education was considered important for the development of an individual's soul. Musicians and singers played a prominent role
Music - Wikipedia — in Greek theater,[38] and those who received a musical education were seen as nobles and in perfect harmony (as can be read in the
Music - Wikipedia — Republic, Plato). Mixed gender choruses performed for entertainment, celebration, and spiritual ceremonies.[39] Instruments included
Music - Wikipedia — the double-reed aulos and a plucked string instrument, the lyre, principally a special kind called a kithara. Music was an important part
Music - Wikipedia — of education, and boys were taught music starting at age six. Greek musical literacy created signiﬁcant musical development. Greek
Music - Wikipedia — music theory included the Greek musical modes, that eventually became the basis for Western religious and classical music. Later,
Music - Wikipedia — inﬂuences from the Roman Empire, Eastern Europe, and the Byzantine Empire changed Greek music. e Seikilos epitaph is the oldest
Music - Wikipedia — surviving example of a complete musical composition, including musical notation, from anywhere in the world.[40] e oldest surviving
Music - Wikipedia — work wrien about music theory is Harmonika Stoicheia by Aristoxenus.[41]
Music - Wikipedia — Asian music covers a swath of music cultures surveyed in the articles on Arabia, Central Asia, East Asia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia. Several have traditions
Music - Wikipedia — reaching into antiquity.
Music - Wikipedia — Indian classical music is one of the oldest musical traditions in the world.[42] Sculptures from the Indus Valley civilization show dance[43] and old musical instruments,
Music - Wikipedia — like the seven-holed ﬂute. Stringed instruments and drums have been recovered from Harappa and Mohenjo Daro by excavations carried out by Mortimer Wheeler.[44]
Music - Wikipedia — e Rigveda, an ancient Hindu text, has elements of present Indian music, with musical notation to denote the meter and mode of chanting.[45] Indian classical music
Music - Wikipedia — (marga) is monophonic, and based on a single melody line or raga rhythmically organized through talas. e poem Cilappatikaram provides information about how new
Music - Wikipedia — scales can be formed by modal shiing of the tonic from an existing scale.[46] Present day Hindi music was inﬂuenced by Persian traditional music and Afghan Mughals.
Music - Wikipedia — Carnatic music, popular in the southern states, is largely devotional; the majority of the songs are addressed to the Hindu deities. ere are songs emphasizing love and
Music - Wikipedia — other social issues.

Music - Wikipedia — e medieval music era (500 to 1400), which took place during the Middle Ages, started with the introduction of
Music - Wikipedia — monophonic (single melodic line) chanting into Catholic Church services. Musical notation was used since ancient
Music - Wikipedia — times in Greek culture, but in the Middle Ages, notation was ﬁrst introduced by the Catholic Church, so chant
Music - Wikipedia — melodies could be wrien down, to facilitate the use of the same melodies for religious music across the Catholic
Music - Wikipedia — empire. e only European Medieval repertory that has been found, in wrien form, from before 800 is the
Music - Wikipedia — monophonic liturgical plainsong chant of the Catholic Church, the central tradition of which was called Gregorian
Music - Wikipedia — chant. Alongside these traditions of sacred and church music there existed a vibrant tradition of secular song (non-religious songs). Examples of composers from this
Music - Wikipedia — period are Léonin, Pérotin, Guillaume de Machaut, and Walther von der Vogelweide.[50][51][52][53]
Music - Wikipedia — Renaissance music (c. 1400 to 1600) was more focused on secular themes, such as courtly love. Around 1450, the printing press was invented, which made printed sheet
Music - Wikipedia — music much less expensive and easier to mass-produce (prior to the invention of the press, all notated music was hand-copied). e increased availability of sheet music
Music - Wikipedia — spread musical styles quicker and across a larger area. Musicians and singers oen worked for the church, courts and towns. Church choirs grew in size, and the church
Music - Wikipedia — remained an important patron of music. By the middle of the 15th century, composers wrote richly polyphonic sacred music, in which diﬀerent melody lines were
Music - Wikipedia — interwoven simultaneously. Prominent composers from this era include Guillaume Du Fay, Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, omas Morley, Orlando di Lasso and
Music - Wikipedia — Josquin des Prez. As musical activity shied from the church to aristocratic courts, kings, queens and princes competed for the ﬁnest composers. Many leading
Music - Wikipedia — composers came from the Netherlands, Belgium, and France; they are called the Franco-Flemish composers.[54] ey held important positions throughout Europe,
Music - Wikipedia — especially in Italy. Other countries with vibrant musical activity included Germany, England, and Spain.
