Career - Wikipedia — Career
Career - Wikipedia — A career is an individual's metaphorical "journey" through learning, work and other aspects of life. ere
Career - Wikipedia — are a number of ways to deﬁne career and the term is used in a variety of ways.
Career - Wikipedia — e Oxford English Dictionary deﬁnes "career" as a person's "course or progress through life (or a distinct
Career - Wikipedia — portion of life)". is deﬁnition relates "career" to a range of aspects of an individual's life, learning, and
Career - Wikipedia — work. "Career" is also frequently understood to relate to the working aspects of an individual's life - as in
Career - Wikipedia — "career woman", for example. A third way in which the term "career" is used describes an occupation or a
Career - Wikipedia — profession that usually involves speciﬁc training and/or formal education,[1] considered to be a person's
Career - Wikipedia — lifework.[2] In this case "a career" is seen as a sequence of related jobs, usually pursued within a single
Career - Wikipedia — industry or sector: one can speak for example of "a career in education", of "a criminal career" or of "a
Career - Wikipedia — career in the building trade". A career has been deﬁned by organizational behavior researchers as "an
Career - Wikipedia — individual's work-related and other relevant experiences, both inside and outside of organizations, that
Career - Wikipedia — form a unique paern over the individual's life span."[3]
Career - Wikipedia — e word "career" ultimately derives from Latin carrus, referring to a chariot.[4]
Career - Wikipedia — e Online Etymology Dictionary claims the semantic extension whereby "career" came to mean "course of one's public or professional life" appears from 1803.[5] It is
Career - Wikipedia — used in dozens of books published in the year 1800, in reference to Goethe's "literary career,"[6] other biographical ﬁgures' "business career" and "professional career," so
Career - Wikipedia — the phrase likely was in regular use by the year 1800.[7]
Career - Wikipedia — For a pre-modernist notion of "career", compare cursus honorum.
Career - Wikipedia — By the late 20th century, a wide range of variations (especially in the range of potential professions) and more widespread education had allowed it to become possible
Career - Wikipedia — to plan (or design) a career: In this respect the careers of the career counselor and of the career advisor have grown up. It is also not uncommon for adults in the late
Career - Wikipedia — Deﬁnitions
Career - Wikipedia — Etymology
Career - Wikipedia — Historic changes in careers
Career - Wikipedia — 20th/early 21st centuries to have dual or multiple careers, either sequentially or concurrently. us, professional identities have become hyphenated or hybridized to
Career - Wikipedia — reﬂect this shi in work ethic. Economist Richard Florida notes this trend generally and more speciﬁcally among the "creative class".
Career - Wikipedia — Career management or career development describes the active and purposeful management of a career by an individual. Ideas of what comprise "career management
Career - Wikipedia — skills" are described by the Blueprint model (in the United States, Canada, Australia, Scotland, and England[8])[9] and the Seven C's of Digital Career Literacy
Career - Wikipedia — (speciﬁcally relating to the Internet skills).[10]
Career - Wikipedia — Key skills include the ability to reﬂect on one's current career, research the labour market, determine whether education is necessary, ﬁnd openings, and make career
Career - Wikipedia — changes.
Career - Wikipedia — According to Behling and others, an individual's decision to join a ﬁrm may depend on any of the three factors viz. objective factor, subjective factor and critical contact.
Career - Wikipedia — [11]
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Objective factor theory assumes that the applicants are rational. The choice, therefore, is exercised after an objective assessment of the
Career - Wikipedia — tangible beneﬁts of the job. Factors may include the salary, other beneﬁts, location, opportunities for career advancement, etc.
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Subjective factor theory suggests that decision making is dominated by social and psychological factors. The status of the job, reputation of
Career - Wikipedia — the organization, and other similar factors plays an important role.
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Critical contact theory advances the idea that a candidate's observations while interacting with the organization plays a vital role in decision
Career - Wikipedia — making. For example, how the recruiter keeps in touch with the candidate, the promptness of response and similar factors are important. This
Career - Wikipedia — theory is more valid with experienced professionals.
Career - Wikipedia — ese theories assume that candidates have a free choice of employers and careers. In reality, the scarcity of jobs and strong competition for desirable jobs severely
Career - Wikipedia — skews the decision-making process. In many markets, employees work particular careers simply because they were forced to accept whatever work was available to
Career - Wikipedia — them. Additionally, O-Holland and colleagues found that culture can have a major inﬂuence on career choice, depending on the type of culture.[12]
Career - Wikipedia — When choosing a career that's best for you, according to US News, there are multiple things to consider. Some of those include: natural talents, work style, social
Career - Wikipedia — interaction, work–life balance, whether or not you are looking to give back, whether you are comfortable in the public eye, dealing with stress or not, and ﬁnally, how
Career - Wikipedia — much money you want to make. If choosing a career feels like too much pressure, here's another option: pick a path that feels right today by making the best decision
Career - Wikipedia — you can, and know that you can change your mind in the future. In today's workplace, choosing a career doesn't necessarily mean you have to stick with that line of
Career - Wikipedia — work for your entire life. Make a smart decision, and plan to re-evaluate down the line based on your long-term objectives.[13]
Career - Wikipedia — Career management
Career - Wikipedia — Career choice
Career - Wikipedia — Career (occupation) changing
Career - Wikipedia — Changing occupation is an important aspect of career and career management. Over a lifetime, both the individual and the labour market will change; it is to be
Career - Wikipedia — expected that many people will change occupations during their lives. Data collected by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics through the National Longitudinal Survey of
Career - Wikipedia — Youth in 1979 showed that individuals between the ages of 18 and 38 will hold more than 10 jobs.[14]
Career - Wikipedia — ere are various reasons why people might want to change their careers. Sometimes career change can come as the result of a long-anticipated layoﬀ, while other
Career - Wikipedia — times it can occur unexpectedly and without warning.[15]
Career - Wikipedia — A survey conducted by Right Management[16] suggests the following reasons for career changing.
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ The downsizing or the restructuring of an organization (54%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ New challenges or opportunities that arise (30%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Poor or ineﬀective leadership (25%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Having a poor relationship with a manager(s) (22%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ For the improvement of work/life balance (21%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Contributions are not being recognized (21%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ For better compensation and beneﬁts (18%),
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ For better alignment with personal and organizational values (17%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Personal strengths and capabilities are not a good ﬁt with an organization (16%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ The ﬁnancial instability of an organization (13%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ An organization relocated (12%).
Career - Wikipedia — According to an article on Time.com, one out of three people currently employed (as of 2008) spends about an hour per day searching for another position.[16]
Career - Wikipedia — Career success is a term used frequently in academic and popular writing about career. It refers to the extent and ways in which an individual can be described as
Career - Wikipedia — successful in his or her working life so far.[17]
Career - Wikipedia — During the 1950s and 1960s, individuals typically worked for one or two ﬁrms during their career and success was deﬁned by the organization and measured by
Career - Wikipedia — promotions, increases in salary, and/or status.[18] Such traditional careers were exempliﬁed by Donald Super's career stage model.[19] Super's linear career stage model
Career - Wikipedia — suggested that careers take place within the context of stable, organizational structures. Individuals moved up the organization's hierarchy seeking greater extrinsic
Career - Wikipedia — rewards.[20]
Career - Wikipedia — Early career success may breed disappointment later, especially when a person's self-worth is tied up in their career or achievements.[21] Professional success tends to
Career - Wikipedia — come early in some ﬁelds, such as scientiﬁc research, and later in other ﬁelds, such as teaching.[21]
Career - Wikipedia — Career success
Career - Wikipedia — Earnings can be expressed either in absolute terms (e.g. the amount a person earns) or in relative terms (e.g. the amount a person earns compared with their starting
Career - Wikipedia — salary). Earnings and status are examples of objective criteria of success, where "objective" means that they can be factually veriﬁed, and are not purely a maer of
Career - Wikipedia — opinion.
Career - Wikipedia — Many observers argue that careers are less predictable than they once were, due to the fast pace of economic and technological change.[22] is means that career
Career - Wikipedia — management is more obviously the responsibility of the individual rather than his or her employing organisation, because a "job for life" is a thing of the past. is has
Career - Wikipedia — put more emphasis on subjective criteria of career success.[23] ese include job satisfaction, career satisfaction, work-life balance, a sense of personal achievement, and
Career - Wikipedia — aaining work that is consistent with one's personal values. A person's assessment of his or her career success is likely to be inﬂuenced by social comparisons, such as
Career - Wikipedia — how well family members, friends, or contemporaries at school or college have done.[24]
Career - Wikipedia — e amount and type of career success a person achieves is aﬀected by several forms of career capital.[25] ese include social capital (the extent and depth of personal
Career - Wikipedia — contacts a person can draw upon), human capital (demonstrable abilities, experiences and qualiﬁcations), economic capital (money and other material resources which
Career - Wikipedia — permit access to career-related resources), and cultural capital (having skills, aitudes or general know-how to operate eﬀectively in a particular social context).[26]
Career - Wikipedia — ere are a range of diﬀerent educational, counseling, and human resource management interventions that can support individuals to develop and manage their careers.
Career - Wikipedia — Career support is commonly oﬀered while people are in education, when they are transitioning to the labour market, when they are changing career, during periods of
Career - Wikipedia — unemployment, and during transition to retirement. Support may be oﬀered by career professionals, other professionals or by non-professionals such as family and
Career - Wikipedia — friends. Professional career support is sometimes known as "career guidance" as in the OECD deﬁnition of career guidance:
Career - Wikipedia — e activities may take place on an individual or group basis, and may be face-to-face or at a distance (including helplines and web-based services). ey
Career - Wikipedia — include career information provision (in print, ICT-based and other forms), assessment and self-assessment tools, counselling interviews, career education
Career - Wikipedia — programmes (to help individuals develop their self-awareness, opportunity awareness, and career management skills), taster programmes (to sample options
Career - Wikipedia — before choosing them), work search programmes, and transition services."[27]
Career - Wikipedia — However this use of the term "career guidance" can be confusing as the term is also commonly used to describe the activities of career counselors.
Career - Wikipedia — Career support is oﬀered by a range of diﬀerent mechanisms. Much career support is informal and provided through personal networks or existing relationships such as
Career - Wikipedia — management. ere is a market for private career support however the bulk of career support that exists as a professionalised activity is provided by the public sector.
Career - Wikipedia — Key types of career support include:
Career - Wikipedia — Career support
Career - Wikipedia — Provision of career support
Career - Wikipedia — Types of career support
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Career information describes information that supports career and learning choices. An important sub-set of career information is labour
Career - Wikipedia — market information (LMI), such as salaries of various professions, employment rate in various professions, available training programs, and
Career - Wikipedia — current job openings.
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Career assessments are tests that come in a variety of forms and rely on both quantitative and qualitative methodologies. Career assessments
Career - Wikipedia — can help individuals identify and better articulate their unique interests, personality, values, and skills to determine how well they may match
Career - Wikipedia — with a certain career. Some skills that career assessments could help determine are job-speciﬁc skills, transferable skills, and self-management
Career - Wikipedia — skills.[28] Career assessments can also provide a window of potential opportunities by helping individuals discover the tasks, experience,
Career - Wikipedia — education and training that is needed for a career they would want to pursue.[29] Career counselors, executive coaches, educational
Career - Wikipedia — institutions, career development centers, and outplacement companies often administer career assessments to help individuals focus their
Career - Wikipedia — search on careers that closely match their unique personal proﬁle.
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Career counseling assesses people's interests, personality, values and skills, and helps them to explore career options and research graduate
Career - Wikipedia — and professional schools. Career counseling provides one-on-one or group professional assistance in exploration and decision making tasks
Career - Wikipedia — related to choosing a major/occupation, transitioning into the world of work or further professional training.
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Career education describes a process by which individuals come to learn about themselves, their careers and the world of work. There is a
Career - Wikipedia — strong tradition of career education in schools,[30] however career education can also occur in a wider range of other contexts including further
Career - Wikipedia — and higher education and the workplace. A commonly used framework for careers education is DOTS which stands for decision learning (D),
Career - Wikipedia — opportunity awareness (O), transition learning (T), and self-awareness (S).[31] Oftentimes, higher education is thought of as being too narrow or
Career - Wikipedia — too researched based and lacking of a deeper understanding of the material to develop the skills necessary for a certain career.[32]
Career - Wikipedia — Some research shows adding one year of schooling beyond high school creates an increase of wages 17.8% per worker. However, additional years of schooling, beyond 9
Career - Wikipedia — or 10 years, have lile eﬀect on worker's wages. In summary, beer educated, bigger beneﬁts. In 2010, 90% of the U.S. Workforce had a high school diploma, 64% had
Career - Wikipedia — some college, and 34% had at least a bachelor's degree.[33]
Career - Wikipedia — e common problem that people may encounter when trying to achieve an education for a career is the cost. e career that comes with the education must pay well
Career - Wikipedia — enough to be able to pay oﬀ the schooling. e beneﬁts of schooling can diﬀer greatly depending on the degree (or certiﬁcation) obtained, the programs the school may
Career - Wikipedia — oﬀer, and the ranking of the school. Sometimes, colleges provide students more with just education to prepare for careers. It is not uncommon for colleges to provide
Career - Wikipedia — pathways and support straight into the workforce the students may desire.[34]
Career - Wikipedia — Much career support is delivered face-to-face, but an increasing amount of career support is delivered online.[10]

Employment - Wikipedia — Employment
Employment - Wikipedia — Employment is a relationship between two parties regulating the provision of paid labour services. Usually based on a contract, one party, the employer, which might
Employment - Wikipedia — be a corporation, a not-for-proﬁt organization, a co-operative, or any other entity, pays the other, the employee, in return for carrying out assigned work.[1] Employees
Employment - Wikipedia — work in return for wages, which can be paid on the basis of an hourly rate, by piecework or an annual salary, depending on the type of work an employee does, the
Employment - Wikipedia — prevailing conditions of the sector and the bargaining power between the parties. Employees in some sectors may receive gratuities, bonus payments or stock options.
Employment - Wikipedia — In some types of employment, employees may receive beneﬁts in addition to payment. Beneﬁts may include health insurance, housing, and disability insurance.
Employment - Wikipedia — Employment is typically governed by employment laws, organization or legal contracts.
Employment - Wikipedia — An employee contributes labour and expertise to an endeavor of an employer or of a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCB)[2] and is usually hired to
Employment - Wikipedia — perform speciﬁc duties which are packaged into a job. In a corporate context, an employee is a person who is hired to provide services to a company on a regular basis
Employment - Wikipedia — in exchange for compensation and who does not provide these services as part of an independent business.[3]
Employment - Wikipedia — An issue that arises in most companies, especially the ones that are in the gig economy, is the classiﬁcation of workers. A lot of workers that fulﬁll gigs are oen hired
Employment - Wikipedia — as independent contractors.
Employment - Wikipedia — To categorize a worker as an independent contractor rather than an employee, an independent contractor must agree with the client on what the ﬁnished work product
Employment - Wikipedia — will be and then the contractor controls the means and manner of achieving the desired outcome. Secondly, an independent contractor oﬀers services to the public at
Employment - Wikipedia — large, not just to one business, and is responsible for disbursing payments from the client, paying unreimbursed expenses, and providing his or her own tools to
Employment - Wikipedia — complete the job. ird, the relationship of the parties is oen evidenced by a wrien agreement that speciﬁes that the worker is an independent contractor and is not
Employment - Wikipedia — entitled to employee beneﬁts; the services provided by the worker are not key to the business; and the relationship is not permanent.[4]
Employment - Wikipedia — As a general principle of employment law, in the United States, there is a diﬀerence between an agent and an independent contractor. e default status of a worker is
Employment - Wikipedia — an employee unless speciﬁc guidelines are met, which can be determined by the ABC test.[5][6] us, clarifying whether someone who performs work is an independent
Employment - Wikipedia — contractor or an employee from the beginning, and treating them accordingly, can save a company from trouble later on.
Employment - Wikipedia — Provided key circumstances, including ones such as that the worker is paid regularly, follows set hours of work, is supplied with tools from the employer, is closely
Employment - Wikipedia — monitored by the employer, acting on behalf of the employer, only works for one employer at a time, they are considered an employee,[7] and the employer will
Employment - Wikipedia — generally be liable for their actions and be obliged to give them beneﬁts.[8] Similarly, the employer is the owner of any invention created by an employee "hired to

Employment - Wikipedia — perform at the job, and to help the employee grow within the organization. An appropriate level of training and development
Employment - Wikipedia — helps to improve employee's job satisfaction.[10]
Employment - Wikipedia — ere are many ways that employees are paid, including by hourly wages, by piecework, by yearly salary, or by gratuities
Employment - Wikipedia — (with the laer oen being combined with another form of payment). In sales jobs and real estate positions, the employee

Employment - Wikipedia — Employee beneﬁts are various non-wage compensation provided to employees in addition to their wages or salaries. e beneﬁts can include: housing (employer-
Employment - Wikipedia — provided or employer-paid), group insurance (health, dental, life etc.), disability income protection, retirement beneﬁts, daycare, tuition reimbursement, sick leave,
Employment - Wikipedia — vacation (paid and non-paid), social security, proﬁt sharing, funding of education, and other specialized beneﬁts. In some cases, such as with workers employed in
Employment - Wikipedia — remote or isolated regions, the beneﬁts may include meals. Employee beneﬁts can improve the relationship between employee and employer and lowers staﬀ turnover.

Employment - Wikipedia — Organizational justice is an employee's perception and judgement of employer's treatment in the context of fairness or justice. e resulting actions to inﬂuence the
Employment - Wikipedia — employee-employer relationship is also a part of organizational justice.[16]
Employment - Wikipedia — Employees can organize into trade or labor unions, which represent the workforce to collectively bargain with the management of organizations about working, and
Employment - Wikipedia — contractual conditions and services.[17]
Employment - Wikipedia — Usually, either an employee or employer may end the relationship at any time, oen subject to a certain notice period. is is referred to as at-will employment. e
Employment - Wikipedia — contract between the two parties speciﬁes the responsibilities of each when ending the relationship and may include requirements such as notice periods, severance pay,
Employment - Wikipedia — and security measures.[17] A contract forbidding an employee from leaving their employment, under penalty of a surety bond, is referred to as an employment bond. In
Employment - Wikipedia — some professions, notably teaching, civil servants, university professors, and some orchestra jobs, some employees may have tenure, which means that they cannot be
Employment - Wikipedia — dismissed at will. Another type of termination is a layoﬀ.
Employment - Wikipedia — Wage labor is the socioeconomic relationship between a worker and an employer, where the worker sells their labor under a formal or informal employment contract.
Employment - Wikipedia — ese transactions usually occur in a labor market where wages are market-determined.[10][16] In exchange for the wages paid, the work product generally becomes the
Employment - Wikipedia — undiﬀerentiated property of the employer, except for special cases such as the vesting of intellectual property patents in the United States where patent rights are
Employment - Wikipedia — usually vested in the original personal inventor. A wage laborer is a person whose primary means of income is from the selling of his or her labor in this way.[17]
Employment - Wikipedia — In modern mixed economies such as that of the OECD countries, it is currently the dominant form of work arrangement. Although most work occurs following this
Employment - Wikipedia — structure, the wage work arrangements of CEOs, professional employees, and professional contract workers are sometimes conﬂated with class assignments, so that
Employment - Wikipedia — "wage labor" is considered to apply only to unskilled, semi-skilled or manual labor.[18]

Employment - Wikipedia — According to Swedish law,[43] there are three types of employment.
Employment - Wikipedia — ▪ Test employment (Swedish: Provanställning), where the employer hires a person for a test period of 6 months maximum. The employment can
Employment - Wikipedia — be ended at any time without giving any reason. This type of employment can be oﬀered only once per employer and in employee
Employment - Wikipedia — combination. Usually, a time limited or normal employment is oﬀered after a test employment.[44]
Employment - Wikipedia — ▪ Time limited employment (Swedish: Tidsbegränsad anställning). The employer hires a person for a speciﬁed time. Usually, they are extended for
Employment - Wikipedia — a new period. Total maximum two years per employer and employee combination, then it automatically counts as a normal employment.
Employment - Wikipedia — ▪ Normal employment (Swedish: Tillsvidareanställning / Fast anställning), which has no time limit (except for retirement etc.). It can still be ended
Employment - Wikipedia — for two reasons: personal reason, immediate end of employment only for strong reasons such as crime, or lack of work tasks (Swedish:
Employment - Wikipedia — Arbetsbrist), cancellation of employment, usually because of bad income for the company. There is a cancellation period of 1–6 months, and
Employment - Wikipedia — rules for how to select employees, basically those with shortest employment time shall be cancelled ﬁrst.[44]
Employment - Wikipedia — ere are no laws about minimum salary in Sweden. Instead, there are agreements between employer organizations and trade unions about minimum salaries, and other
Employment - Wikipedia — employment conditions.

Employment - Wikipedia — employment (unlimited), but the work time is unregulated and decided per immediate need basis. e employee is expected to be answering the phone and come to

Employment - Wikipedia — Scholars conceptualize the employment relationship in various ways.[60] A key assumption is the extent to which the employment relationship necessarily includes
Employment - Wikipedia — conﬂicts of interests between employers and employees, and the form of such conﬂicts.[61] In economic theorizing, the labor market mediates all such conﬂicts such that
Employment - Wikipedia — employers and employees who enter into an employment relationship are assumed to ﬁnd this arrangement in their own self-interest. In human resource management
Employment - Wikipedia — theorizing, employers and employees are assumed to have shared interests (or a unity of interests, hence the label "unitarism"). Any conﬂicts that exist are seen as a
Employment - Wikipedia — manifestation of poor human resource management policies or interpersonal clashes such as personality conﬂicts, both of which can and should be managed away.
Employment - Wikipedia — From the perspective of pluralist industrial relations, the employment relationship is characterized by a plurality of stakeholders with legitimate interests (hence the
Employment - Wikipedia — label “pluralism), and some conﬂicts of interests are seen as inherent in the employment relationship (e.g., wages v. proﬁts). Lastly, the critical paradigm emphasizes
Employment - Wikipedia — Models of the employment relationship
Employment - Wikipedia — antagonistic conﬂicts of interests between various groups (e.g., the competing capitalist and working classes in a Marxist framework) that are part of a deeper social
Employment - Wikipedia — conﬂict of unequal power relations. As a result, there are four common models of employment:[62]
Employment - Wikipedia — 1. Mainstream economics: employment is seen as a mutually advantageous transaction in a free market between self-interested legal and
Employment - Wikipedia — economic equals
Employment - Wikipedia — 2. Human resource management (unitarism): employment is a long-term partnership of employees and employers with common interests
Employment - Wikipedia — 3. Pluralist industrial relations: employment is a bargained exchange between stakeholders with some common and some competing economic
Employment - Wikipedia — interests and unequal bargaining power due to imperfect labor markets[44]
Employment - Wikipedia — 4. Critical industrial relations: employment is an unequal power relation between competing groups that is embedded in and inseparable from
Employment - Wikipedia — systemic inequalities throughout the socio-politico-economic system.
Employment - Wikipedia — ese models are important because they help reveal why individuals hold diﬀering perspectives on human resource management policies, labor unions, and
Employment - Wikipedia — employment regulation.[63] For example, human resource management policies are seen as dictated by the market in the ﬁrst view, as essential mechanisms for aligning
Employment - Wikipedia — the interests of employees and employers and thereby creating proﬁtable companies in the second view, as insuﬃcient for looking out for workers’ interests in the third
Employment - Wikipedia — view, and as manipulative managerial tools for shaping the ideology and structure of the workplace in the fourth view.[64]
Employment - Wikipedia — Literature on the employment impact of economic growth and on how growth is associated with employment at a macro, sector and industry level was aggregated in
Employment - Wikipedia — 2013.[65]
Employment - Wikipedia — Researchers found evidence to suggest growth in manufacturing and services have good impact on employment. ey found GDP growth on employment in agriculture
Employment - Wikipedia — to be limited, but that value-added growth had a relatively larger impact.[44] e impact on job creation by industries/economic activities as well as the extent of the
Employment - Wikipedia — body of evidence and the key studies. For extractives, they again found extensive evidence suggesting growth in the sector has limited impact on employment. In
Employment - Wikipedia — textiles, however, although evidence was low, studies suggest growth there positively contributed to job creation. In agri-business and food processing, they found
Employment - Wikipedia — impact growth to be positive.[65]
Employment - Wikipedia — ey found that most available literature focuses on OECD and middle-income countries somewhat, where economic growth impact has been shown to be positive on
Employment - Wikipedia — employment. e researchers didn't ﬁnd suﬃcient evidence to conclude any impact of growth on employment in LDCs despite some pointing to the positive impact,
Employment - Wikipedia — others point to limitations. ey recommended that complementary policies are necessary to ensure economic growth's positive impact on LDC employment. With
Employment - Wikipedia — trade, industry and investment, they only found limited evidence of positive impact on employment from industrial and investment policies and for others, while large
Employment - Wikipedia — bodies of evidence does exist, the exact impact remains contested.[65]
Employment - Wikipedia — Researchers have also explored the relationship between employment and illicit activities. Using evidence from Africa, a research team found that a program for
Employment - Wikipedia — Liberian ex-ﬁghters reduced work hours on illicit activities. e employment program also reduced interest in mercenary work in nearby wars. e study concludes that
Employment - Wikipedia — while the use of capital inputs or cash payments for peaceful work created a reduction in illicit activities, the impact of training alone is rather low.[66]
Employment - Wikipedia — Academic literature
Employment - Wikipedia — e balance of economic eﬃciency and social equity is the ultimate debate in the ﬁeld of employment relations.[67] By meeting the needs of the employer; generating
Employment - Wikipedia — proﬁts to establish and maintain economic eﬃciency; whilst maintaining a balance with the employee and creating social equity that beneﬁts the worker so that he/she
Employment - Wikipedia — can fund and enjoy healthy living; proves to be a continuous revolving issue in westernized societies.[67]
Employment - Wikipedia — Globalization has aﬀected these issues by creating certain economic factors that disallow or allow various employment issues. Economist Edward Lee (1996) studies the
Employment - Wikipedia — eﬀects of globalization and summarizes the four major points of concern that aﬀect employment relations:
Employment - Wikipedia — 1. International competition, from the newly industrialized countries, will cause unemployment growth and increased wage disparity for unskilled
Employment - Wikipedia — workers in industrialized countries. Imports from low-wage countries exert pressure on the manufacturing sector in industrialized countries
Employment - Wikipedia — and foreign direct investment (FDI) is attracted away from the industrialized nations, towards low-waged countries.[67]
Employment - Wikipedia — 2. Economic liberalization will result in unemployment and wage inequality in developing countries. This happens as job losses in uncompetitive
Employment - Wikipedia — industries outstrip job opportunities in new industries.
Employment - Wikipedia — 3. Workers will be forced to accept worsening wages and conditions, as a global labor market results in a “race to the bottom”. Increased
Employment - Wikipedia — international competition creates a pressure to reduce the wages and conditions of workers.[67]
Employment - Wikipedia — 4. Globalization reduces the autonomy of the nation state. Capital is increasingly mobile and the ability of the state to regulate economic activity
Employment - Wikipedia — is reduced.
Employment - Wikipedia — What also results from Lee's (1996) ﬁndings is that in industrialized countries an average of almost 70 per cent of workers are employed in the service sector, most of
Employment - Wikipedia — which consists of non-tradable activities. As a result, workers are forced to become more skilled and develop sought aer trades, or ﬁnd other means of survival.
Employment - Wikipedia — Ultimately this is a result of changes and trends of employment, an evolving workforce, and globalization that is represented by a more skilled and increasing highly
Employment - Wikipedia — diverse labor force, that are growing in non standard forms of employment (Markey, R. et al. 2006).[67]
Employment - Wikipedia — Various youth subcultures have been associated with not working, such as the hippie subculture in the 1960s and 1970s (which endorsed the idea of "dropping out" of
Employment - Wikipedia — society) and the punk subculture.
Employment - Wikipedia — One of the alternatives to work is engaging in post-secondary education at a college, university or professional school. One of the major costs of obtaining a post-
Employment - Wikipedia — Globalization and employment relations

Employment - Wikipedia — Post-secondary education
Employment - Wikipedia — secondary education is the opportunity cost of forgone wages due to not working. At times when jobs are hard to ﬁnd, such as during recessions, unemployed
Employment - Wikipedia — individuals may decide to get post-secondary education, because there is less of an opportunity cost.
Employment - Wikipedia — In some countries, individuals who are not working can receive social assistance support (e.g., welfare or food stamps) to enable them to rent housing, buy food, repair
Employment - Wikipedia — or replace household goods, maintenance of children and observe social customs that require ﬁnancial expenditure.
Employment - Wikipedia — Workers who are not paid wages, such as volunteers who perform tasks for charities, hospitals or not-for-proﬁt organizations, are generally not considered employed.
Employment - Wikipedia — One exception to this is an internship, an employment situation in which the worker receives training or experience (and possibly college credit) as the chief form of
Employment - Wikipedia — compensation.[68]
Employment - Wikipedia — ose who work under obligation for the purpose of fulﬁlling a debt, such as indentured servants, or as property of the person or entity they work for, such as slaves, do
Employment - Wikipedia — not receive pay for their services and are not considered employed. Some historians suggest that slavery is older than employment, but both arrangements have existed
Employment - Wikipedia — for all recorded history. Indentured servitude and slavery are not considered compatible with human rights or with democracy.[68]
Employment - Wikipedia — Self-employment is the state of working for oneself rather than an employer. Tax authorities will generally view a person as self-employed if the person chooses to be
Employment - Wikipedia — recognised as such or if the person is generating income for which a tax return needs to be ﬁled. In the real world, the critical issue for tax authorities is not whether a
Employment - Wikipedia — person is engaged in business activity (called trading even when referring to the provision of a service) but whether the activity is proﬁtable and therefore potentially
Employment - Wikipedia — taxable. In other words, the trading is likely to be ignored if there is no proﬁt, so occasional and hobby- or enthusiast-based economic activity is generally ignored by
Employment - Wikipedia — tax authorities. Self-employed people are usually classiﬁed as a sole proprietor (or sole trader), independent contractor, or as a member of a partnership.
Employment - Wikipedia — Self-employed people generally ﬁnd their own work rather than being provided with work by an employer and instead earn income from a profession, a trade, or a
Employment - Wikipedia — business that they operate. In some countries, such as the United States and the United Kingdom, the authorities are placing more emphasis on clarifying whether an
Employment - Wikipedia — individual is self-employed or engaged in disguised employment, in other words pretending to be in a contractual intra-business relationship to hide what is in fact an
Employment - Wikipedia — employer-employee relationship.

Work (physics) - Wikipedia — In science, work is the energy transferred to or from an object via the application of force along a displacement. In its
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — simplest form, for a constant force aligned with the direction of motion, the work equals the product of the force
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — strength and the distance traveled. A force is said to do positive work if it has a component in the direction of the
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — displacement of the point of application. A force does negative work if it has a component opposite to the direction of
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — the displacement at the point of application of the force.[1]
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — For example, when a ball is held above the ground and then dropped, the work done by the gravitational force on the
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — ball as it falls is positive, and is equal to the weight of the ball (a force) multiplied by the distance to the ground (a
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — displacement). If the ball is thrown upwards, the work done by the gravitational force is negative, and is equal to the
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — weight multiplied by the displacement in the upwards direction.

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — (Redirected from Human life span)
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Human life expectancy is a statistical measure of the estimate of the average remaining years of life at a given age.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e most commonly used measure is life expectancy at birth (LEB, or in demographic notation e0, where ex denotes
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — the average life remaining at age x). is can be deﬁned in two ways. Cohort LEB is the mean length of life of a birth
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — cohort (in this case, all individuals born in a given year) and can be computed only for cohorts born so long ago that
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — all their members have died. Period LEB is the mean length of life of a hypothetical cohort[3][4] assumed to be
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — exposed, from birth through death, to the mortality rates observed at a given year.[5] National LEB ﬁgures reported by
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — national agencies and international organizations for human populations are estimates of period LEB.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Human remains from the early Bronze Age indicate an LEB of 24.[6] In 2019, world LEB was 73.3.[7] A combination of
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — high infant mortality and deaths in young adulthood from accidents, epidemics, plagues, wars, and childbirth, before
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — modern medicine was widely available, signiﬁcantly lowers LEB. For example, a society with a LEB of 40 would have
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — relatively few people dying at exactly 40: most will die before 30 or aer 55. In populations with high infant mortality
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — rates, LEB is highly sensitive to the rate of death in the ﬁrst few years of life. Because of this sensitivity, LEB can be
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — grossly misinterpreted, leading to the belief that a population with a low LEB would have a small proportion of older
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — people.[8] A diﬀerent measure, such as life expectancy at age 5 (e5), can be used to exclude the eﬀect of infant
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — mortality to provide a simple measure of overall mortality rates other than in early childhood. For instance, in a
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — society with a life expectancy of 30, it may nevertheless be common to have a 40-year remaining timespan at age 5
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — (but not a 60-year one).
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Aggregate population measures—such as the proportion of the population in various age groups—are also used
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — alongside individual-based measures—such as formal life expectancy—when analyzing population structure and
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — dynamics. Pre-modern societies had universally higher mortality rates and lower life expectancies at every age for
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — both males and females.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Life expectancy, longevity, and maximum lifespan are not synonymous. Longevity refers to the relatively long
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — lifespan of some members of a population. Maximum lifespan is the age at death for the longest-lived individual of a
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — species. Mathematically, life expectancy is denoted
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — [a] and is the mean number of years of life remaining at a given age , with a particular mortality.[9] Because life
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — expectancy is an average, a particular person may die many years before or aer the expected survival.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Life expectancy is also used in plant or animal ecology,[10] and in life tables (also known as actuarial tables). e concept of life expectancy may also be used in the
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — context of manufactured objects,[11] though the related term shelf life is commonly used for consumer products, and the terms "mean time to breakdown" and "mean

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — before reaching adulthood.[53] During the Industrial Revolution, the life expectancy of children increased dramatically.[54] Recorded deaths among children under the

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — immigration (hence more dying in the metropolis than were born there) and incomplete registration (particularly of births, and especially in the earlier period). English

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Various species of plants and animals, including humans, have diﬀerent lifespans. Evolutionary theory states that organisms which—by virtue of their defenses or
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — lifestyle—live for long periods and avoid accidents, disease, predation, etc. are likely to have genes that code for slow aging, which oen translates to good cellular
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — repair. One theory is that if predation or accidental deaths prevent most individuals from living to an old age, there will be less natural selection to increase the intrinsic
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — life span.[139] at ﬁnding was supported in a classic study of opossums by Austad;[140] however, the opposite relationship was found in an equally prominent study of
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — guppies by Reznick.[141][142]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — One prominent and very popular theory states that lifespan can be lengthened by a tight budget for food energy called caloric restriction.[143] Caloric restriction
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — observed in many animals (most notably mice and rats) shows a near doubling of life span from a very limited caloriﬁc intake. Support for the theory has been bolstered
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — by several new studies linking lower basal metabolic rate to increased life expectancy.[144][145][146] at is the key to why animals like giant tortoises can live so long.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — [147] Studies of humans with life spans of at least 100 have shown a link to decreased thyroid activity, resulting in their lowered metabolic rate.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e ability of skin ﬁbroblasts to perform DNA repair aer UV irradiation was measured in shrew, mouse, rat, hamster, cow, elephant and human.[148] It was found that
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — DNA repair capability increased systematically with species life span. Since this original study in 1974, at least 14 additional studies were performed on mammals to test
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — this correlation.[149] In all, but two of these studies, lifespan correlated with DNA repair levels, suggesting that DNA repair capability contributes to life expectancy.[149]

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — By deﬁnition, life expectancy is an arithmetic mean. It can also be calculated by integrating the survival curve from 0 to
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — positive inﬁnity (or equivalently to the maximum lifespan, sometimes called 'omega'). For an extinct or completed cohort (all
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — people born in the year 1850, for example), it can of course simply be calculated by averaging the ages at death. For cohorts with some survivors, it is estimated by using
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — mortality experience in recent years. e estimates are called period cohort life expectancies.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e starting point for calculating life expectancy is the age-speciﬁc death rates of the population members. If a large amount of data is available, a statistical population
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — can be created that allow the age-speciﬁc death rates to be simply taken as the mortality rates actually experienced at each age (the number of deaths divided by the
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — number of years "exposed to risk" in each data cell). However, it is customary to apply smoothing to remove (as much as possible) the random statistical ﬂuctuations
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — from one year of age to the next. In the past, a very simple model used for this purpose was the Gompertz function, but more sophisticated methods are now used.[153]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e most common modern methods include:
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — ▪ ﬁtting a mathematical formula (such as the Gompertz function, or an extension of it) to the data.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — ▪ looking at an established mortality table derived from a larger population and making a simple adjustment to it (such as multiplying by a
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — constant factor) to ﬁt the data. (In cases of relatively small amounts of data.)

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e age-speciﬁc death rates are calculated separately for separate groups of data that are believed to have diﬀerent mortality
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — rates (such as males and females, or smokers and non-smokers) and are then used to calculate a life table from which one can

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e life expectancy statistic is usually based on past mortality experience and assumes that the same age-speciﬁc mortality

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Forecasting life expectancy and mortality form an important subdivision of demography. Future trends in life expectancy have huge implications for old-age support
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — programs (like U.S. Social Security and pension) since the cash ﬂow in these systems depends on the number of recipients who are still living (along with the rate of
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — return on the investments or the tax rate in pay-as-you-go systems). With longer life expectancies, the systems see increased cash outﬂow; if the systems underestimate
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — increases in life-expectancies, they will be unprepared for the large payments that will occur, as humans live longer and longer.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Life expectancy forecasting is usually based on one of two diﬀerent approaches:
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — 1. Forecasting the life expectancy directly, generally using ARIMA or other time-series extrapolation procedures. This has the advantage of
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — simplicity, but it cannot account for changes in mortality at speciﬁc ages, and the forecast number cannot be used to derive other life table
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — results. Analyses and forecasts using this approach can be done with any common statistical/mathematical software package, like EViews, R,
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — SAS, Stata, Matlab, or SPSS.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — 2. Forecasting age-speciﬁc death rates and computing the life expectancy from the results with life table methods. This is usually more complex
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — than simply forecasting life expectancy because the analyst must deal with correlated age-speciﬁc mortality rates, but it seems to be more
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — robust than simple one-dimensional time series approaches. It also yields a set of age-speciﬁc rates that may be used to derive other
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — measures, such as survival curves or life expectancies at diﬀerent ages. The most important approach in this group is the Lee-Carter model,[161]

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Maximum life span is an individual-speciﬁc concept, and therefore is an upper bound rather than an average.[166] Science author Christopher Wanjek writes, "[H]as the

Everyday life - Wikipedia — Everyday life
Everyday life - Wikipedia — Everyday life, daily life or routine life comprises the ways in which people typically act, think, and
Everyday life - Wikipedia — feel on a daily basis. Everyday life may be described as mundane, routine, natural, habitual, or normal.
Everyday life - Wikipedia — Human diurnality means most people sleep at least part of the night and are active in daytime. Most eat
Everyday life - Wikipedia — two or three meals in a day. Working time (apart from shi work) mostly involves a daily schedule,
Everyday life - Wikipedia — beginning in the morning. is produces the daily rush hours experienced by many millions, and the
Everyday life - Wikipedia — drive time focused on by radio broadcasters. Evening is oen leisure time. Bathing every day is a custom
Everyday life - Wikipedia — for many.
Everyday life - Wikipedia — Beyond these broad similarities, lifestyles vary and diﬀerent people spend their days diﬀerently. For
Everyday life - Wikipedia — example, nomadic life diﬀers from sedentism, and among the sedentary, urban people live diﬀerently
Everyday life - Wikipedia — from rural folk. Diﬀerences in the lives of the rich and the poor, or between laborers and intellectuals,
Everyday life - Wikipedia — may go beyond their working hours. Children and adults also vary in what they do each day.
Everyday life - Wikipedia — Everyday life is a key concept in cultural studies and is a specialized subject in the ﬁeld of sociology. Some argue that, motivated by capitalism and industrialism's
Everyday life - Wikipedia — degrading eﬀects on human existence and perception, writers and artists of the 19th century turned more towards self-reﬂection and the portrayal of everyday life
Everyday life - Wikipedia — represented in their writings and art to a noticeably greater degree than in past works, for example Renaissance literature's interest in hagiography and politics.[1] Other
Everyday life - Wikipedia — theorists dispute this argument based on a long history of writings about daily life which can be seen in works from Ancient Greece, medieval Christianity and the Age
Everyday life - Wikipedia — of Enlightenment.[2][3]
Everyday life - Wikipedia — In the study of everyday life, gender has been an important factor in its conceptions. Some theorists regard women as the quintessential representatives and victims of
Everyday life - Wikipedia — everyday life.[2]
Everyday life - Wikipedia — e connotation of everyday life is oen negative, and is distinctively separated from exceptional moments by its lack of distinction and diﬀerentiation. Ultimately this
Everyday life - Wikipedia — is deﬁned as the essential, taken-for-granted continuum of mundane activity that outlines forays into more esoteric experiences. It is the non-negotiable reality that
Everyday life - Wikipedia — exists amongst all social groupings without discrimination and is an unavoidable basis for which all human endeavor exists.[1]
Everyday life - Wikipedia — Much of everyday life is automatic in that it is driven by current environmental features as mediated by automatic cognitive processing of those features, and without
Everyday life - Wikipedia — any mediation by conscious choice, according to social psychologist John A. Bargh.[4] Daily life is also studied by sociologists to investigate how it is organised and
Everyday life - Wikipedia — given meaning. A sociological journal called the Journal of Mundane Behavior,[5] published from 2000 to 2004, studied these everyday actions.

Everyday life - Wikipedia — Daily entertainment once consisted mainly of telling stories in the evening. is custom developed into the theatre of ancient
Everyday life - Wikipedia — Greece and other professional entertainments. Reading later became less a mysterious specialty of scholars, and more a
Everyday life - Wikipedia — common pleasure for people who could aﬀord books. During the 20th century mass media became prevalent in rich
Everyday life - Wikipedia — countries, creating among other things a daily prime time to consume ﬁction and other professionally produced works.
Everyday life - Wikipedia — Diﬀerent media forms serve diﬀerent purposes in diﬀerent individuals' everyday lives—which gives people the opportunities
Everyday life - Wikipedia — to make choices about what media form(s)—watching television, using the Internet, listening to the radio, or reading
Everyday life - Wikipedia — newspapers or magazines—most eﬀectively help them to accomplish their tasks.[6] Many people have steadily increased their
Everyday life - Wikipedia — daily use of the Internet, over all other media forms.
Everyday life - Wikipedia — People's everyday lives are shaped through language and communication. ey choose what to do with their time based on
Everyday life - Wikipedia — opinions and ideals formed through the discourse they are exposed to.[7] Much of the dialogue people are subject to comes
Everyday life - Wikipedia — from the mass media, which is an important factor in what shapes human experience.[8] e media uses language to make an
Everyday life - Wikipedia — impact on one's everyday life, whether that be as small as helping to decide where to eat or as big as choosing a
Everyday life - Wikipedia — representative in government.
Everyday life - Wikipedia — To improve people's everyday life, Phaedra Pezzullo, professor in the Department of Communication and Culture at Indiana University Bloomington, says people should
Everyday life - Wikipedia — seek to understand the rhetoric that so oen and unnoticeably changes their lives. She writes that "…rhetoric enables us to make connections… It's about understanding
Everyday life - Wikipedia — how we engage with the world".[9]
Everyday life - Wikipedia — Activities of daily living (ADL) is a term used in healthcare to refer to daily self care activities within an individual's place of residence, in outdoor environments, or both.
Everyday life - Wikipedia — Health professionals routinely refer to the ability or inability to perform ADLs as a measurement of the functional status of a person, particularly in regard to people
Everyday life - Wikipedia — with disabilities and the elderly.[10] ADLs are deﬁned as "the things we normally do…such as feeding ourselves, bathing, dressing, grooming, work, homemaking, and
Everyday life - Wikipedia — leisure".[11] e ability and the extent to which the elderly can perform these activities is at the focus of gerontology and understandings of later life.[12]

Personal life - Wikipedia — Personal life
Personal life - Wikipedia — Personal life is the course or state of an individual's life, especially when viewed as the sum of personal choices
Personal life - Wikipedia — contributing to one's personal identity.[1]
Personal life - Wikipedia — Apart from hunter-gatherers, most pre-modern peoples' time was limited by the need to meet necessities such as food and
Personal life - Wikipedia — shelter through subsistence farming; leisure time was scarce.[2] People identiﬁed with their social role in their community
Personal life - Wikipedia — and engaged in activities based on necessity rather than on personal choice. Privacy in such communities was rare.
Personal life - Wikipedia — e modern conception of "personal life" is an oﬀshoot of modern Western society. Modern people tend to distinguish their
Personal life - Wikipedia — work activities from their personal life and may seek work–life balance.[3] It is a person's choices and preferences outside of
Personal life - Wikipedia — work that deﬁne personal life, including one's choice of hobbies, cultural interests, manner of dress, mate, friends, and so on.
Personal life - Wikipedia — In particular, what activities one engages in during leisure-time deﬁnes a person's personal life. Religious authorities,
Personal life - Wikipedia — moralists, managers and personal-development gurus have seized on the concept of an individual life as a fulcrum for
Personal life - Wikipedia — potential control and manipulation.[4][5][6]
Personal life - Wikipedia — People in Western countries, such as the United States and Canada, tend to value privacy. Privacy includes both information
Personal life - Wikipedia — privacy and decisional privacy; people expect to be le alone with respect to intimate details of their life and they expect to
Personal life - Wikipedia — be free from undue control by others.[7]
Personal life - Wikipedia — In the past, before modern technology largely alleviated issues of economic scarcity in industrialised countries, most people spent a large portion of their time
Personal life - Wikipedia — aempting to provide their basic survival needs, including water, food, and protection from the weather.[8] Humans needed survival skills for the sake of both
Personal life - Wikipedia — themselves and their community; food needed to be harvested and shelters needed to be maintained.[9] ere was lile privacy in a community, and people identiﬁed
Personal life - Wikipedia — one another according to their social role.[10] Jobs were assigned out of necessity rather than personal choice.[11]
Personal life - Wikipedia — Furthermore, individuals in many ancient cultures primarily viewed their self-existence under the aspect of a larger social whole, oen one with mythological
Personal life - Wikipedia — underpinnings which placed the individual in relation to the cosmos.[12] People in such cultures found their identity not through their individual choices—indeed, they
Personal life - Wikipedia — may not have been able to conceive a choice which was purely individual. Such individuals, if asked to describe themselves, would speak of the collective of which they
Personal life - Wikipedia — were part: the tribe, the Church, the nation.[13] Even in the 21st century, survival issues dominate in many countries and societies. For example, the continents of Africa
Personal life - Wikipedia — and Asia are still largely mired in poverty and third-world conditions, without technology, secure shelter, or reliable food sources. In such places, the concepts of a
Personal life - Wikipedia — "personal life", "self-actualization", "personal fulﬁllment", or "privacy" are oen unaﬀordable luxuries.[14]

Personal life - Wikipedia — e English philosopher John Locke (1632–1704) gures among the pioneers in discussing the concept of individual rights. In
Personal life - Wikipedia — the 17th century he promoted the natural rights of the individual to life, liberty, and property, and included the pursuit of
Personal life - Wikipedia — happiness as one of the individual's goals.
Personal life - Wikipedia — e notion of a personal life, as currently understood in the west is in part an artefact of modern Western society. People in
Personal life - Wikipedia — the United States of America, especially, place a high value on privacy. Since the colonial period, commentators have noted
Personal life - Wikipedia — Americans' individualism and their pursuit of self-deﬁnition.[15][16] Indeed, the United States Declaration of Independence
Personal life - Wikipedia — and the Constitution explicitly raise the pursuit of happiness and the expectation of privacy to the level of rights.
Personal life - Wikipedia — George Lakoﬀ sees the metaphor of life as "a journey" as a noteworthy structuring idea in "our culture".[17] Compare the
Personal life - Wikipedia — traditional Chinese concept of tao.
Personal life - Wikipedia — In modern times, many people have come to think of their personal lives as separate from their work.[18] is 9 to 5 paradigm
Personal life - Wikipedia — regards work and recreation as distinct; one is either on the job or not, and the transition is abrupt. Employees have certain
Personal life - Wikipedia — hours they are bound to work, and work during recreational time is rare. is may reﬂect the continuing specialisation of
Personal life - Wikipedia — jobs and the demand for increased eﬃciency, both at work and at home. e common phrase "Work hard, play hard"
Personal life - Wikipedia — illustrates this mindset. ere is a growing trend, however, towards living more holistically and minimising such rigid
Personal life - Wikipedia — distinctions between work and play, in order to achieve an "appropriate" work–life balance.
Personal life - Wikipedia — e concept of personal life also tends to be associated with the way individuals dress, the food they eat, their schooling and
Personal life - Wikipedia — further education as well as their hobbies, leisure activities, and cultural interests. Increasingly, in the developed world, a
Personal life - Wikipedia — person's daily life is also inﬂuenced by leisure-time use of consumer electronics such as televisions, computers and the
Personal life - Wikipedia — Internet, mobile phones and digital cameras.[19]
Personal life - Wikipedia — Other factors aﬀecting personal life include individuals' health, personal relationships, pets as well as home and personal possessions.
Personal life - Wikipedia — e way in which individuals make use of their spare time also plays an important role in deﬁning their personal lives. In general, leisure activities can be categorised as
Personal life - Wikipedia — either passive, in cases when no real eﬀort is required, or active, when substantial physical or mental energy is needed.[20]
Personal life - Wikipedia — Passive activities include watching television, listening to music, watching sports activities or going to the cinema. e individual simply relaxes without any special
Personal life - Wikipedia — eﬀort.

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Meaning of life
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e meaning of life is the concept of an individual's life, or existence in general, having an inherent signiﬁcance or a philosophical point. ere is no consensus on the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — speciﬁcs of such a concept or whether the concept itself even exists in any objective sense. inking and discourse on the topic is sought in the English language
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — through questions such as—but not limited to—"What is the meaning of life?", "What is the purpose of existence?", and "Why are we here?". ere have been many
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — proposed answers to these questions from many diﬀerent cultural and ideological backgrounds. e search for life's meaning has produced much philosophical,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — scientiﬁc, theological, and metaphysical speculation throughout history. Diﬀerent people and cultures believe diﬀerent things for the answer to this question. Opinions
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — vary on the usefulness of using time and resources in the pursuit of an answer. Excessive pondering can be indicative of, or lead to, an existential crisis.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e meaning of life can be derived from philosophical and religious contemplation of, and scientiﬁc inquiries about, existence, social ties, consciousness, and happiness.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Many other issues are also involved, such as symbolic meaning, ontology, value, purpose, ethics, good and evil, free will, the existence of one or multiple gods,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — conceptions of God, the soul, and the aerlife. Scientiﬁc contributions focus primarily on describing related empirical facts about the universe, exploring the context and
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — parameters concerning the "how" of life. Science also studies and can provide recommendations for the pursuit of well-being and a related conception of morality. An
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — alternative, humanistic approach poses the question, "What is the meaning of my life?"
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e ﬁrst English use of the expression "meaning of life" appears in omas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus (1833–1834), book II chapter IX, "e Everlasting Yea".[1]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Our Life is compassed round with Necessity; yet is the meaning of Life itself no other than Freedom, than Voluntary Force: thus have we a warfare; in the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — beginning, especially, a hard-fought bale.[2]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Carlyle may have been inspired by earlier usage of the equivalent German expression der Sinn des Lebens by German Romantic writers Novalis and Friedrich Schlegel.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Schlegel was the ﬁrst to use it in print by way of his novel Lucinde (1799), though Novalis had done so in a 1797–1798 manuscript, in which he wrote: "Only an artist can
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — divine the meaning of life." Additionally, the word lebenssinn, translated as life's meaning, had been used by Goethe in a 1796 leer to Schiller.[3] ese authors grappled
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — with the rationalism and materialism of modernity. Carlyle called this the "Torch of Science", which burned "more ﬁercely than ever" and made religion "all parched
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — away, under the Droughts of practical and spiritual Unbelief", resulting in the "Wilderness" of "the wide World in an Atheistic Century".[4]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Arthur Schopenhauer was the ﬁrst to explicitly ask the question,[1] in an essay entitled "Character".
