Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Origin of the question
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Socrates
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Since a man does not alter, and his moral character remains absolutely the same all through his life; since he must play out
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — the part which he has received, without the least deviation from the character; since neither experience, nor philosophy,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — nor religion can eﬀect any improvement in him, the question arises, What is the meaning of life at all? To what
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — purpose is it played, this farce in which everything that is essential is irrevocably ﬁxed and determined?[5]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — estions about the meaning of life, and similar, have been expressed in a broad variety of other ways, including:
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is the meaning of life? What's it all about? Who are we?[6][7][8]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ Why are we here? What are we here for?[9][10][11]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is the origin of life?[12]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is the nature of life? What is the nature of reality?[12][13][14]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is the purpose of life? What is the purpose of one's life?[13][15][16]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is the signiﬁcance of life?[16] (See also #Psychological signiﬁcance and value in life)
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is meaningful and valuable in life?[17]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is the value of life?[18]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is the reason to live? What are we living for?[11][19]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ese questions have resulted in a wide range of competing answers and explications, from scientiﬁc theories, to philosophical, theological, and spiritual explanations.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Many members of the scientiﬁc community and philosophy of science communities think that science can provide the relevant context, and set of parameters necessary
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — for dealing with topics related to the meaning of life. In their view, science can oﬀer a wide range of insights on topics ranging from the science of happiness to death
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — anxiety. Scientiﬁc inquiry facilitates this through nomological investigation into various aspects of life and reality, such as the Big Bang, the origin of life, and evolution,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — and by studying the objective factors which correlate with the subjective experience of meaning and happiness.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Researchers in positive psychology study empirical factors that lead to life satisfaction,[20] full engagement in activities,[21] making a fuller contribution by using one's
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — personal strengths,[22] and meaning based on investing in something larger than the self.[23] Large-data studies of ﬂow experiences have consistently suggested that
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — humans experience meaning and fulﬁllment when mastering challenging tasks and that the experience comes from the way tasks are approached and performed rather
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — than the particular choice of task. For example, ﬂow experiences can be obtained by prisoners in concentration camps with minimal facilities, and occur only slightly
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — more oen in billionaires. A classic example[21] is of two workers on an apparently boring production line in a factory. One treats the work as a tedious chore while the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — other turns it into a game to see how fast they can make each unit and achieves ﬂow in the process.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Scientiﬁc inquiry and perspectives
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Psychological signiﬁcance and value in life
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Neuroscience describes reward, pleasure, and motivation in terms of neurotransmier activity, especially in the limbic system and the ventral tegmental area in
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — particular. If one believes that the meaning of life is to maximize pleasure and to ease general life, then this allows normative predictions about how to act to achieve
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — this. Likewise, some ethical naturalists advocate a science of morality—the empirical pursuit of ﬂourishing for all conscious creatures.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Experimental philosophy and neuroethics research collects data about human ethical decisions in controlled scenarios such as trolley problems. It has shown that many
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — types of ethical judgment are universal across cultures, suggesting that they may be innate, whilst others are culture-speciﬁc. e ﬁndings show actual human ethical
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — reasoning to be at odds with most philosophical theories, for example consistently showing distinctions between action by cause and action by omission which would
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — be absent from utility-based theories. Cognitive science has theorized about diﬀerences between conservative and liberal ethics and how they may be based on diﬀerent
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — metaphors from family life such as strong fathers vs nurturing mother models.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Neurotheology is a controversial ﬁeld which tries to ﬁnd neural correlates and mechanisms of religious experience. Some researchers have suggested that the human
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — brain has innate mechanisms for such experiences and that living without using them for their evolved purposes may be a cause of imbalance. Studies have reported
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — conﬂicting results on correlating happiness with religious belief and it is diﬃcult to ﬁnd unbiased meta-analyses.[24][25]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Sociology examines value at a social level using theoretical constructs such as value theory, norms, anomie, etc. One value system suggested by social psychologists,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — broadly called Terror Management eory, states that human meaning is derived from a fundamental fear of death, and values are selected when they allow us to escape
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — the mental reminder of death.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Alongside this, there are a number of theories about the way in which humans evaluate the positive and negative aspects of their existence and thus the value and
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — meaning they place on their lives. For example, depressive realism posits an exaggerated positivity in all except those experiencing depressive disorders who see life as
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — it truly is, and David Benatar theorises that more weight is generally given to positive experiences, providing bias towards an over-optimistic view of life.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Emerging research shows that meaning in life predicts beer physical health outcomes. Greater meaning has been associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's disease,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — [26][27] reduced risk of heart aack among individuals with coronary heart disease,[28] reduced risk of stroke,[29] and increased longevity in both American and Japanese
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — samples.[30] ere is also growing evidence for a small decline in purpose in life in the early stages of cognitive impairment.[31]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — In 2014, the British National Health Service began recommending a ﬁve-step plan for mental well-being based on meaningful lives, whose steps are:[32]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 1. Connect with community and family
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 2. Physical exercise
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 3. Lifelong learning
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 4. Giving to others
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 5. Mindfulness of the world around you
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e exact mechanisms of abiogenesis are unknown: notable hypotheses include the RNA world hypothesis (RNA-based replicators) and the iron-sulfur world hypothesis
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Origin and nature of biological life
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — DNA contains the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — genetic instructions
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — for the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — development and
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — functioning of all
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — known organisms.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — (metabolism without genetics). e process by which diﬀerent lifeforms have developed throughout history via genetic mutation and natural
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — selection is explained by evolution.[33] At the end of the 20th century, based upon insight gleaned from the gene-centered view of evolution,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — biologists George C. Williams, Richard Dawkins, and David Haig, among others, concluded that if there is a primary function to life, it is the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — replication of DNA and the survival of one's genes.[34][35] Responding to an interview question from Richard Dawkins about "what it is all for",
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — James Watson stated "I don't think we're for anything. We're just the products of evolution."[36]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ough scientists have intensively studied life on Earth, deﬁning life in unequivocal terms is still a challenge.[37][38] Physically, one may say
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — that life "feeds on negative entropy"[39][40][41] which refers to the process by which living entities decrease their internal entropy at the expense
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — of some form of energy taken in from the environment.[42][43][44] Biologists generally agree that lifeforms are self-organizing systems which
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — regulate their internal environments as to maintain this organized state, metabolism serves to provide energy, and reproduction causes life to
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — continue over a span of multiple generations. Typically, organisms are responsive to stimuli and genetic information changes from generation
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — to generation, resulting in adaptation through evolution; this optimizes the chances of survival for the individual organism and its descendants
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — respectively.[45]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Non-cellular replicating agents, notably viruses, are generally not considered to be organisms because they are incapable of independent
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — reproduction or metabolism. is classiﬁcation is problematic, though, since some parasites and endosymbionts are also incapable of
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — independent life. Astrobiology studies the possibility of diﬀerent forms of life on other worlds, including replicating structures made from
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — materials other than DNA.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — All forms of life that are in existence today possess a self-replicating informational molecule (genome), and such an informational molecule is
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — presumably intrinsic to life. us the earliest forms of life also likely possessed a self-replicating informational molecule, possibly RNA[46][47] or
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — perhaps an informational molecule more primitive than RNA. e speciﬁc genomic sequences in all currently extant organisms contain order
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — generating information that promotes survival, reproduction, and the ability to acquire resources necessary for reproduction. Sequences with
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — such basic functions probably emerged early in the evolution of life.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — It has been proposed[48] that both the evolution of macroscopic order in life (including its basic functions) and the evolution of order in particular physical systems obey
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — a common fundamental principle that was termed the Darwinian dynamic. is principal was formulated by considering, ﬁrst, how macroscopic order is generated in a
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — simple physical, non-biological system far from thermodynamic equilibrium, and then extending consideration to short RNA replicating molecules and then further to
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — more complex forms of life. It was concluded that the fundamental order-generating process was basically similar for both types of process.[48][49] us the idea that life
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — likely emerged as a natural extension of simpler non- or pre-biological physical processes should logically be included in the concept "meaning of life".
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ough the Big Bang theory was met with much skepticism when ﬁrst introduced, it has become well-supported by several independent observations.[50] However,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — current physics can only describe the early universe from around 10−43 seconds aer the Big Bang (where zero time corresponds to inﬁnite temperature); a theory of
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — quantum gravity would be required to understand events before that time. Nevertheless, many physicists have speculated about what would have preceded this limit,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — and how the universe came into being.[51] For example, one interpretation is that the Big Bang occurred coincidentally, and when considering the anthropic principle, it
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — is sometimes interpreted as implying the existence of a multiverse.[52]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Origins and ultimate fate of the universe
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Modern view of the expansion of space. The inﬂationary epoch
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — is a period of rapidly accelerating expansion at left.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e ultimate fate of the universe, and implicitly of humanity, is hypothesized as one in which
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — biological life will eventually become unsustainable, such as through a Big Freeze, Big Rip, or Big
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Crunch.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — eoretical cosmology studies many alternative speculative models for the origin and fate of the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — universe beyond the Big Bang theory. A recent trend has been models of the creation of 'baby
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — universes' inside black holes, with our own Big Bang being a white hole on the inside of a black hole
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — in another parent universe.[53] Many-worlds theories claim that every possibility of quantum
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — mechanics is played out in parallel universes.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e nature and origin of consciousness and the mind are also widely debated in science. e
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — explanatory gap is generally equated with the hard problem of consciousness, and the question of free
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — will is also considered to be of fundamental importance. ese subjects are mostly addressed in the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ﬁelds of cognitive science, neuroscience (e.g. the neuroscience of free will) and philosophy of mind,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — though some evolutionary biologists and theoretical physicists have also made several allusions to the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — subject.[54][55]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Reductionistic and eliminative materialistic approaches, for example the Multiple Dras Model, hold that consciousness can be wholly explained by neuroscience
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — through the workings of the brain and its neurons, thus adhering to biological naturalism.[55][56][57]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — On the other hand, some scientists, like Andrei Linde, have considered that consciousness, like spacetime, might have its own intrinsic degrees of freedom, and that
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — one's perceptions may be as real as (or even more real than) material objects.[58] Hypotheses of consciousness and spacetime explain consciousness in describing a
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — "space of conscious elements",[58] oen encompassing a number of extra dimensions.[59] Electromagnetic theories of consciousness solve the binding problem of
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — consciousness in saying that the electromagnetic ﬁeld generated by the brain is the actual carrier of conscious experience; there is however disagreement about the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — implementations of such a theory relating to other workings of the mind.[60][61] antum mind theories use quantum theory in explaining certain properties of the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — mind. Explaining the process of free will through quantum phenomena is an alternative to determinism.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Based on the premises of non-materialistic explanations of the mind, some have suggested the existence of a cosmic consciousness, asserting that consciousness is
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — actually the "ground of all being".[14][62][63] Proponents of this view cite accounts of paranormal phenomena, primarily extrasensory perceptions and psychic powers, as
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — evidence for an incorporeal higher consciousness. In hopes of proving the existence of these phenomena, parapsychologists have orchestrated various experiments, but
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — successful results might be due to poor experimental controls and might have alternative explanations.[64][65][66][67]

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Nature of meaning in life
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Reker and Wong deﬁne personal meaning as the "cognizance of order, coherence and purpose in one's existence, the pursuit and aainment of worthwhile goals, and an
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — accompanying sense of fulﬁllment" (p. 221).[68] In 2016, Martela and Steger deﬁned meaning as coherence, purpose, and signiﬁcance.[69] In contrast, Wong has proposed
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — a four-component solution to the question of meaning in life,[70][71] with the four components purpose, understanding, responsibility, and enjoyment (PURE):
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 1. You need to choose a worthy purpose or a signiﬁcant life goal.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 2. You need to have suﬃcient understanding of who you are, what life demands of you, and how you can play a signiﬁcant role in life.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 3. You and you alone are responsible for deciding what kind of life you want to live, and what constitutes a signiﬁcant and worthwhile life goal.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 4. You will enjoy a deep sense of signiﬁcance and satisfaction only when you have exercised your responsibility for self-determination and actively
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — pursue a worthy life-goal.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — us, a sense of signiﬁcance permeates every dimension of meaning, rather than standing as a separate factor.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Although most psychology researchers consider meaning in life as a subjective feeling or judgment, most philosophers (e.g., addeus Metz, Daniel Haybron) propose
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — that there are also objective, concrete criteria for what constitutes meaning in life.[72][73] Wong has proposed that whether life is meaningful depends not only on
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — subjective feelings but, more importantly, on whether a person's goal-striving and life as a whole is meaningful according to some objective normative standard.[71]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e philosophical perspectives on the meaning of life are those ideologies that explain life in terms of ideals or abstractions deﬁned by humans.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Plato, a pupil of Socrates, was one of the earliest, most inﬂuential philosophers. His reputation comes from his idealism of believing in the existence of universals. His
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — theory of forms proposes that universals do not physically exist, like objects, but as heavenly forms. In the dialogue of the Republic, the character of Socrates describes
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — the Form of the Good. His theory on justice in the soul relates to the idea of happiness relevant to the question of the meaning of life.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — In Platonism, the meaning of life is in aaining the highest form of knowledge, which is the Idea (Form) of the Good, from which all good and just things derive utility
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — and value.

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — epistemology), but is general knowledge. Because it is not a theoretical discipline, a person had to study and practice in order to become "good"; thus if the person were

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Kantianism is a philosophy based on the ethical, epistemological, and metaphysical works of Immanuel Kant. Kant is known for his
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — deontological theory where there is a single moral obligation, the "Categorical Imperative", derived from the concept of duty. Kantians
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — believe all actions are performed in accordance with some underlying maxim or principle, and for actions to be ethical, they must
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — adhere to the categorical imperative.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Simply put, the test is that one must universalize the maxim (imagine that all people acted in this way) and then see if it would still be
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — possible to perform the maxim in the world without contradiction. In Groundwork, Kant gives the example of a person who seeks to
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — borrow money without intending to pay it back. is is a contradiction because if it were a universal action, no person would lend
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — money anymore as he knows that he will never be paid back. e maxim of this action, says Kant, results in a contradiction in
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — conceivability (and thus contradicts perfect duty).
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Kant also denied that the consequences of an act in any way contribute to the moral worth of that act, his reasoning being that the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — physical world is outside one's full control and thus one cannot be held accountable for the events that occur in it.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e ﬁrst English use of the expression "meaning of life" appeared in omas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus (1833–August 1834): "Our Life is compassed round with Necessity;
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — yet is the meaning of Life itself no other than Freedom, than Voluntary Force: thus have we a warfare; in the beginning, especially, a hard-fought bale."[80]

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — insight, he derived the Rule of Utility: "that the good is whatever brings the greatest happiness to the greatest number of people". He
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — deﬁned the meaning of life as the "greatest happiness principle".

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Mill was educated per Bentham's principles, including transcribing and summarizing much of his father's work.[82]

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Pragmatism originated in the late-19th-century US, concerning itself (mostly) with truth, and positing that "only in struggling
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — with the environment" do data, and derived theories, have meaning, and that consequences, like utility and practicality, are
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — also components of truth. Moreover, pragmatism posits that anything useful and practical is not always true, arguing that
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — what most contributes to the most human good in the long course is true. In practice, theoretical claims must be practically
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — veriﬁable, i.e. one should be able to predict and test claims, and, that, ultimately, the needs of humankind should guide human intellectual inquiry.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Pragmatic philosophers suggest that the practical, useful understanding of life is more important than searching for an impractical abstract truth about life. William
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — James argued that truth could be made, but not sought.[89][90] To a pragmatist, the meaning of life is discoverable only via experience.

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Kierkegaard and Camus dismiss the viability of this option.

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Per secular humanism, the human species came to be by reproducing successive generations in a progression of unguided evolution as
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — an integral expression of nature, which is self-existing.[97][98] Human knowledge comes from human observation, experimentation,

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — be.[97] Likewise, "values and realities" are determined "by means of intelligent inquiry"[97] and "are derived from human need and
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — interest as tested by experience", that is, by critical intelligence.[99][100] "As far as we know, the total personality is [a function] of the

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — lives of personal fulﬁllment that aspire to the greater good of humanity".[99] Humanism aims to promote enlightened self-interest and
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — the common good for all people. It is based on the premises that the happiness of the individual person is inextricably linked to the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — well-being of all humanity, in part because humans are social animals who ﬁnd meaning in personal relations and because cultural
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — progress beneﬁts everybody living in the culture.[98][99]

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Postmodernist thought—broadly speaking—sees human nature as constructed by language, or by structures and institutions of human society. Unlike other forms of
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — philosophy, postmodernism rarely seeks out a priori or innate meanings in human existence, but instead focuses on analyzing or critiquing given meanings in order to
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — rationalize or reconstruct them. Anything resembling a "meaning of life", in postmodernist terms, can only be understood within a social and linguistic framework and
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — must be pursued as an escape from the power structures that are already embedded in all forms of speech and interaction. As a rule, postmodernists see awareness of
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — the constraints of language as necessary to escaping those constraints, but diﬀerent theorists take diﬀerent views on the nature of this process: from a radical
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — reconstruction of meaning by individuals (as in deconstructionism) to theories in which individuals are primarily extensions of language and society, without real
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — autonomy (as in poststructuralism).

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — being in Mohist thought. is advocacy of impartiality was a target of aack by the other Chinese philosophical schools, most notably the Confucians who believed that

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — In all schools of Hinduism, the meaning of life is tied up in the concepts of karma (causal action), sansara (the cycle of birth and
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — rebirth), and moksha (liberation). Existence is conceived as the progression of the ātman (similar to the western concept of a soul)
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — across numerous lifetimes, and its ultimate progression towards liberation from karma. Particular goals for life are generally subsumed
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — under broader yogas (practices) or dharma (correct living) which are intended to create more favorable reincarnations, though they are
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — generally positive acts in this life as well. Traditional schools of Hinduism oen worship Devas which are manifestations of Ishvara (a
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — personal or chosen God); these Devas are taken as ideal forms to be identiﬁed with, as a form of spiritual improvement.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — In short, the goal is to realize the fundamental truth about oneself. is thought is conveyed in the Mahāvākyas ("Tat Tvam Asi" (thou art that), "Aham Brahmāsmi",
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — "Prajñānam Brahma" and "Ayam Ātmā Brahma" (is Ātman is Brahman)).
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Later schools reinterpreted the vedas to focus on Brahman, "e One Without a Second",[150] as a central God-like ﬁgure.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — In monist Advaita Vedanta, ātman is ultimately indistinguishable from Brahman, and the goal of life is to know or realize that one's Ātman (soul) is identical to
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Brahman.[151] To the Upanishads, whoever becomes fully aware of the Ātman, as one's core of self, realizes identity with Brahman, and, thereby, achieves Moksha
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — (liberation, freedom).[146][152][153]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Dvaita Vedanta and other bhakti schools have a dualist interpretation. Brahman is seen as a supreme being with a personality and manifest qualities. e Ātman
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — depends upon Brahman for its existence; the meaning of life is achieving Moksha through the love of God and upon His grace.[152]

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — while refusing to do so. e suﬀerings of life are the suﬀerings of the divine spirit in search of progress in the objective world.[166]

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Existential crises are crises of meaning. ey are triggered by the impression that life lacks meaning.[248][249][250] is
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — impression can lead to an inner conﬂict because there is a strong desire to ﬁnd some form of meaning in life. In the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — existentialist literature, the discrepancy between the individual's desire for meaning and the world's apparent lack thereof is
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — termed the absurd.[251][252][253] It may be summarized by the question "How does a being who needs meaning ﬁnd meaning
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — in a universe that has no meaning?".[254] While this conﬂict may aﬀect diﬀerent people at least to some extent, it reaches a
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — more severe level in the case of existential crises. is level leads to various negative experiences, such as stress, anxiety,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — despair, and depression.[254][249][250] In the more serious cases, these symptoms disturb the individual's normal functioning in
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — everyday life. A positive side eﬀect of these negative experiences is that they push the aﬀected individual to address the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — underlying issue. is opens the opportunity of developing as a person and improving one's way of life.[254][255]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — erapists oen try to treat existential crises by helping their patients discover meaning in life. An important distinction in
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — this regard is the diﬀerence between personal meaning and cosmic meaning.[254][256] In the cosmic sense, the term "meaning
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — of life" refers to the purpose of the world as a whole or why we are here. One way to solve an existential crisis is to discover a
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — satisfying answer to this question. is oen takes the form of a religious explanation involving a divine entity that created
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — the world for a certain purpose.[254][257][258] Another approach to solving existential crises is to seek meaning not on the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — cosmic but on the personal level. is usually takes a more secular form: the therapist helps the individual realize what
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — maers to them or why their life is worth living.[254][256][259] In this regard, they may discover how their personal life can be
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — meaningful, for example, by dedicating themselves to their family or their career. is approach may mitigate or solve an
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — existential crisis even if the individual still lacks an answer to the bigger question of the deeper meaning behind everything.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — [254][250][257]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e question of the meaning of life is closely related to the question of what has importance or what maers. is is reﬂected
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — in the fact that ﬁnding meaning in life is oen associated with dedicating oneself to some kind of higher purpose, which is
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — seen as having special importance.[260][261] Nonetheless, some theorists have argued that the two concepts are not identical.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — [260][262] is distinction is oen motivated by the observation that seeking the meaning of life is usually regarded as an
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — admirable goal associated with self-transcendence. Craving importance, on the other hand, seems to be a more egoistic or

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Various theorists have argued that to be important means to have an impact on the world or to make a diﬀerence. Some only require that this causal impact is big
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — enough. Others include as an additional element that the diﬀerence in question has to aﬀect the value of the world.[263][262][264] is is oen interpreted with reference
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — to well-being: the degree of importance of a thing is given by the extent to which it aﬀects the well-being of sentient entities.[265][262][266] However, the relation to a
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — purpose is usually not required for importance. In this regard, some things may be important accidentally or unintentionally without being guided by a higher goal. For
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — example, a person may by chance bump into something and thereby unwiingly trigger a buerﬂy eﬀect of extreme proportions. In such a case, the person's life has
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — acquired high importance due to the consequences it caused. Nonetheless, this does not imply that it has also acquired some form of deeper meaning or higher purpose.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — [260]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Another diﬀerence is that seeking and realizing the meaning of life is usually seen by most theorists as a positive and worthwhile undertaking. Importance, however,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — can be either positive or negative depending on the type of value diﬀerence involved.[260][262] For example, Alexander Fleming was important in a positive sense since
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — his discovery of penicillin helped many people cure their bacterial infections.[267] Adolf Hitler, on the other hand, was important in a negative sense since his policies
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — caused widespread suﬀering to innumerous people.[263]

Human condition - Wikipedia — e human condition can be deﬁned as the characteristics and key events of human life, including birth, learning, emotion,
Human condition - Wikipedia — aspiration, reason, morality, conﬂict, and death. is is a very broad topic that has been and continues to be pondered and
Human condition - Wikipedia — analyzed from many perspectives, including those of art, biology, literature, philosophy, psychology, and religion.
Human condition - Wikipedia — As a literary term, "human condition" is typically used in the context of ambiguous subjects, such as the meaning of life or
Human condition - Wikipedia — moral concerns.[2]
Human condition - Wikipedia — Each major religion has deﬁnitive beliefs regarding the human condition. For example, Buddhism teaches that existence is a
Human condition - Wikipedia — perpetual cycle of suﬀering, death, and rebirth from which humans can be liberated via the Noble Eightfold Path. Meanwhile,
Human condition - Wikipedia — many Christians believe that humans are born in a sinful condition and are doomed in the aerlife unless they receive
Human condition - Wikipedia — salvation through Jesus Christ.
Human condition - Wikipedia — Philosophers have provided many perspectives. An inﬂuential ancient view was that of the Republic in which Plato explored the question "what is justice?" and
Human condition - Wikipedia — postulated that it is not primarily a maer among individuals but of society as a whole, prompting him to devise a utopia. Two thousand years later René Descartes
Human condition - Wikipedia — declared "I think, therefore I am" because he believed the human mind, particularly its faculty of reason, to be the primary determiner of truth; for this he is oen
Human condition - Wikipedia — credited as the father of modern philosophy.[3] One such modern school, existentialism, aempts to reconcile an individual's sense of disorientation and confusion in a
Human condition - Wikipedia — universe believed to be absurd.
Human condition - Wikipedia — Many works of literature provide a perspective on the human condition.[2] One famous example is Shakespeare's monologue "All the world's a stage" which pensively
Human condition - Wikipedia — summarizes seven phases of human life.[4]
Human condition - Wikipedia — Psychology has many theories, including Maslow's hierarchy of needs and the notions of identity crisis and terror management. It also has various methods, e.g. the
Human condition - Wikipedia — logotherapy developed by Holocaust survivor Viktor Frankl to discover and aﬃrm a sense of meaning. Another method, cognitive behavioral therapy, has become a
Human condition - Wikipedia — widespread treatment for clinical depression.[5]
Human condition - Wikipedia — Charles Darwin established the biological theory of evolution, which posits that the human species is related to all others, living and extinct, and that natural selection
Human condition - Wikipedia — is the primary survival factor. is led to subsequent beliefs, such as social Darwinism, which eventually lost its connection to natural selection,[6] and theistic evolution
Human condition - Wikipedia — of a creator deity acting through laws of nature, including evolution.[7]

Human rights - Wikipedia — Human rights
Human rights - Wikipedia — Human rights are universally recognized moral principles or norms that establish standards of human behavior and
Human rights - Wikipedia — are oen protected by both national and international laws. ese rights are considered inherent and inalienable,
Human rights - Wikipedia — meaning they belong to every individual simply by virtue of being human, regardless of characteristics like nationality,
Human rights - Wikipedia — ethnicity, religion, or socio-economic status. ey encompass a broad range of civil, political, economic, social, and
Human rights - Wikipedia — cultural rights, such as the right to life, freedom of expression, protection against enslavement, and right to education.
Human rights - Wikipedia — e modern concept of human rights gained signiﬁcant prominence aer World War II, particularly in response to the
Human rights - Wikipedia — atrocities of the Holocaust, leading to the adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) by the
Human rights - Wikipedia — United Nations General Assembly in 1948. is document outlined a comprehensive framework of rights that countries
Human rights - Wikipedia — are encouraged to protect, seing a global standard for human dignity, freedom, and justice. e UDHR has since
Human rights - Wikipedia — inspired numerous international treaties and national laws designed to promote and safeguard these rights globally.
Human rights - Wikipedia — While the principle of universal human rights is widely accepted, debates persist regarding which rights should take
Human rights - Wikipedia — precedence, how they should be implemented, and their applicability in diﬀerent cultural contexts. Criticisms oen
Human rights - Wikipedia — arise from perspectives like cultural relativism, which argue that individual human rights are inappropriate for
Human rights - Wikipedia — societies that prioritise a communal or collectivist identity, and may conﬂict with certain cultural or traditional
Human rights - Wikipedia — practices.
Human rights - Wikipedia — Nonetheless, human rights remain a central focus in international relations and legal frameworks, supported by institutions such as the United Nations, various non-
Human rights - Wikipedia — governmental organizations, and national bodies dedicated to monitoring and enforcing human rights standards worldwide.
Human rights - Wikipedia — Many of the basic ideas that animated the human rights movement developed in the aermath of the Second World War and the events of the Holocaust,[1] culminating

Human rights - Wikipedia — e UDHR was framed by members of the Human Rights Commission, with Eleanor Roosevelt as chair, who began to discuss
Human rights - Wikipedia — an International Bill of Rights in 1947. e members of the Commission did not immediately agree on the form of such a bill
Human rights - Wikipedia — of rights, and whether, or how, it should be enforced. e Commission proceeded to frame the UDHR and accompanying
Human rights - Wikipedia — treaties, but the UDHR quickly became the priority.[19] Canadian law professor John Humphrey and French lawyer René
Human rights - Wikipedia — Cassin were responsible for much of the cross-national research and the structure of the document respectively, where the
Human rights - Wikipedia — articles of the declaration were interpretative of the general principle of the preamble. e document was structured by Cassin to include the basic principles of dignity,
Human rights - Wikipedia — liberty, equality and brotherhood in the ﬁrst two articles, followed successively by rights pertaining to individuals; rights of individuals in relation to each other and to
Human rights - Wikipedia — groups; spiritual, public and political rights; and economic, social and cultural rights. e ﬁnal three articles place, according to Cassin, rights in the context of limits,
Human rights - Wikipedia — duties and the social and political order in which they are to be realized.[19] Humphrey and Cassin intended the rights in the UDHR to be legally enforceable through
Human rights - Wikipedia — some means, as is reﬂected in the third clause of the preamble:[19]
Human rights - Wikipedia — Whereas it is essential, if man is not to be compelled to have recourse, as a last resort, to rebellion against tyranny and oppression, that human rights should
Human rights - Wikipedia — be protected by the rule of law.

Human rights - Wikipedia — All major governments at the time of drafting the U.N. charter and the Universal declaration did their best to ensure, by all means known to
Human rights - Wikipedia — domestic and international law, that these principles had only international application and carried no legal obligation on those governments
Human rights - Wikipedia — to be implemented domestically. All tacitly realized that for their own discriminated-against minorities to acquire leverage on the basis of
Human rights - Wikipedia — legally being able to claim enforcement of these wide-reaching rights would create pressures that would be political dynamite.
Human rights - Wikipedia — e onset of the Cold War soon aer the UDHR was conceived brought to the fore divisions over the inclusion of both economic and social rights and civil and political
Human rights - Wikipedia — rights in the declaration. Capitalist states tended to place strong emphasis on civil and political rights (such as freedom of association and expression), and were
Human rights - Wikipedia — reluctant to include economic and social rights (such as the right to work and the right to join a union). Socialist states placed much greater importance on economic
Human rights - Wikipedia — and social rights and argued strongly for their inclusion.[24] Because of the divisions over which rights to include and because some states declined to ratify any treaties
Human rights - Wikipedia — including certain speciﬁc interpretations of human rights, and despite the Soviet bloc and a number of developing countries arguing strongly for the inclusion of all
Human rights - Wikipedia — rights in a Unity Resolution, the rights enshrined in the UDHR were split into two separate covenants, allowing states to adopt some rights and derogate others.
Human rights - Wikipedia — Although this allowed the covenants to be created, it denied the proposed principle that all rights are linked, which was central to some interpretations of the UDHR.[24]
Human rights - Wikipedia — [25] Although the UDHR is a non-binding resolution, it is now considered to be a central component of international customary law which may be invoked under
Human rights - Wikipedia — appropriate circumstances by state judiciaries and other judiciaries.[26]

Human rights - Wikipedia — In 2021 the United Nations Human Rights Council oﬃcially recognized "having a clean, healthy and sustainable environment" as a human right.[29] In April 2024, the

Human rights - Wikipedia — Charles Beitz proposes a typology of six paradigms of action that agents, such as human rights agencies, international organizations, individual states, and NGOs, could
Human rights - Wikipedia — use to enforce human rights: (1) accountability, (2) inducement, (3) assistance, (4) domestic contestation and engagement, (5) compulsion, and (6) external adaptation.[31]
Human rights - Wikipedia — Accountability refers to the process of examining and evaluating reports to ensure that states adhering to treaties are meeting their obligations. Inducement consists of
Human rights - Wikipedia — the use of incentive systems, including the threat of sanctions, to deter violations and promote adherence to human rights standards. Assistance means providing
Human rights - Wikipedia — support to societies that lack the resources or capabilities to meet human rights commitments. Domestic contestation and engagement refers to the notion that external
Human rights - Wikipedia — actors can impact a state's behavior by participating in its internal political and social processes. Compulsion is the most extreme method of enforcing human rights
Human rights - Wikipedia — through external action involves the use of coercive measures. External adaptation as a paradigm of implementation recognizes that human rights compliance may
Human rights - Wikipedia — require not only domestic eﬀorts but also reforming external factors like trade policies or international laws that hinder a government's ability to uphold rights.[32]
Human rights - Wikipedia — Responsibility to protect refers to a doctrine for United Nations member states to intervene to protect populations from atrocities. It has been cited as justiﬁcation in the
Human rights - Wikipedia — use of recent military interventions. An example of an intervention that is oen criticized is the 2011 military intervention in the First Libyan Civil War by NATO and
Human rights - Wikipedia — Qatar where the goal of preventing atrocities is alleged to have taken upon itself the broader mandate of removing the target government.[33][34]
Human rights - Wikipedia — Economic sanctions are oen levied upon individuals or states who commit human rights violations. Sanctions are oen criticized for its feature of collective
Human rights - Wikipedia — punishment in hurting a country's population economically in order dampen that population's view of its government.[35][36] It is also argued that, counterproductively,
Human rights - Wikipedia — sanctions on oﬀending authoritarian governments strengthen that government's position domestically as governments would still have more mechanisms to ﬁnd
Human rights - Wikipedia — funding than their critics and opposition, who become further weakened.[37][38]
Human rights - Wikipedia — e risk of human rights violations increases with the increase in ﬁnancially vulnerable populations. Girls from poor families in non-industrialized economies are oen
Human rights - Wikipedia — viewed as a ﬁnancial burden on the family and marriage of young girls is oen driven in the hope that daughters will be fed and protected by wealthier families.[39]

Human rights - Wikipedia — experts who monitor compliance with human rights standards and norms ﬂowing from the core international human rights treaties. ey are supported by and are

Human rights - Wikipedia — ▪ The Human Rights Committee promotes participation with the standards of the ICCPR. The members of the committee express opinions on
Human rights - Wikipedia — member countries and make judgments on individual complaints against countries which have ratiﬁed an Optional Protocol to the treaty. The
Human rights - Wikipedia — judgments, termed "views", are not legally binding. The member of the committee meets around three times a year to hold sessions.[48]
Human rights - Wikipedia — ▪ The Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights monitors the ICESCR and makes general comments on ratifying countries performance.
Human rights - Wikipedia — It will have the power to receive complaints against the countries that opted into the Optional Protocol once it has come into force. Unlike the
Human rights - Wikipedia — other treaty bodies, the economic committee is not an autonomous body responsible to the treaty parties, but directly responsible to the
Human rights - Wikipedia — Economic and Social Council and ultimately to the General Assembly. This means that the Economic Committee faces particular diﬃculties at its
Human rights - Wikipedia — disposal only relatively "weak" means of implementation in comparison to other treaty bodies.[49] Particular diﬃculties noted by commentators
Human rights - Wikipedia — include: perceived vagueness of the principles of the treaty, relative lack of legal texts and decisions, ambivalence of many states in addressing
Human rights - Wikipedia — economic, social and cultural rights, comparatively few non-governmental organisations focused on the area and problems with obtaining
Human rights - Wikipedia — relevant and precise information.[49][50]
Human rights - Wikipedia — ▪ The Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination monitors the CERD and conducts regular reviews of countries' performance. It can
Human rights - Wikipedia — make judgments on complaints against member states allowing it, but these are not legally binding. It issues warnings to attempt to prevent
Human rights - Wikipedia — serious contraventions of the convention.
Human rights - Wikipedia — ▪ The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women monitors the CEDAW. It receives states' reports on their performance and
Human rights - Wikipedia — comments on them, and can make judgments on complaints against countries which have opted into the 1999 Optional Protocol.
Human rights - Wikipedia — ▪ The Committee Against Torture monitors the CAT and receives states' reports on their performance every four years and comments on them.
Human rights - Wikipedia — Its subcommittee may visit and inspect countries which have opted into the Optional Protocol.
Human rights - Wikipedia — ▪ The Committee on the Rights of the Child monitors the CRC and makes comments on reports submitted by states every ﬁve years. It does not
Human rights - Wikipedia — have the power to receive complaints.

Human rights - Wikipedia — every ﬁve years. It will have the power to receive complaints of speciﬁc violations only once ten member states allow it.

Human rights - Wikipedia — not have jurisdiction over individuals.
Human rights - Wikipedia — ▪ The International Criminal Court (ICC) is the body responsible for investigating and punishing war crimes,
Human rights - Wikipedia — and crimes against humanity when such occur within its jurisdiction, with a mandate to bring to justice
Human rights - Wikipedia — perpetrators of such crimes that occurred after its creation in 2002. A number of UN members have not
Human rights - Wikipedia — joined the court and the ICC does not have jurisdiction over their citizens, and others have signed but not
Human rights - Wikipedia — yet ratiﬁed the Rome Statute, which established the court.[52]
Human rights - Wikipedia — e ICC and other international courts (see Regional human rights below) exist to take action where the national legal
Human rights - Wikipedia — system of a state is unable to try the case itself. If national law is able to safeguard human rights and punish those who breach human rights legislation, it has primary
Human rights - Wikipedia — jurisdiction by complementarity. Only when all local remedies have been exhausted does international law take eﬀect.[53]

Human rights - Wikipedia — Several theoretical approaches have been advanced to explain how and why human rights become part of social expectations. One of the oldest Western philosophies on
Human rights - Wikipedia — human rights is that they are a product of a natural law, stemming from diﬀerent philosophical or religious grounds. Other theories hold that human rights codify moral
Human rights - Wikipedia — behavior which is a human social product developed by a process of biological and social evolution (associated with David Hume). Human rights are also described as a
Human rights - Wikipedia — sociological paern of rule seing (as in the sociological theory of law and the work of Max Weber). ese approaches include the notion that individuals in a society
Human rights - Wikipedia — accept rules from legitimate authority in exchange for security and economic advantage (as in John Rawls) – a social contract.
Human rights - Wikipedia — Natural law theories base human rights on a "natural" moral, religious or even biological order which is independent of transitory human laws or traditions. Socrates
Human rights - Wikipedia — and his philosophic heirs, Plato and Aristotle, posited the existence of natural justice or natural right (dikaion physikon, δικαιον φυσικον, Latin ius naturale). Of these,
Human rights - Wikipedia — Aristotle is oen said to be the father of natural law,[84] although evidence for this is due largely to the interpretations of his work by omas Aquinas.[85] e
Human rights - Wikipedia — development of this tradition of natural justice into one of natural law is usually aributed to the Stoics.[86]
Human rights - Wikipedia — Some of the early Church Fathers sought to incorporate the until then pagan concept of natural law into Christianity. Natural law theories have featured greatly in the
Human rights - Wikipedia — philosophies of omas Aquinas, Francisco Suárez, Richard Hooker, omas Hobbes, Hugo Grotius, Samuel von Pufendorf, and John Locke. In the 17th century, omas
Human rights - Wikipedia — Hobbes founded a contractualist theory of legal positivism on what all men could agree upon: what they sought (happiness) was subject to contention, but a broad
Human rights - Wikipedia — consensus could form around what they feared (violent death at the hands of another). e natural law was how a rational human being, seeking to survive and prosper,
Human rights - Wikipedia — would act. It was discovered by considering humankind's natural rights, whereas previously it could be said that natural rights were discovered by considering the
Human rights - Wikipedia — natural law. In Hobbes' opinion, the only way natural law could prevail was for men to submit to the commands of the sovereign. In this lay the foundations of the
Human rights - Wikipedia — theory of a social contract between the governed and the governor.
Human rights - Wikipedia — Hugo Grotius based his philosophy of international law on natural law. He wrote that "even the will of an omnipotent being cannot change or abrogate" natural law,
Human rights - Wikipedia — which "would maintain its objective validity even if we should assume the impossible, that there is no God or that he does not care for human aﬀairs." (De iure belli ac

Human rights - Wikipedia — [94][95] e philosopher Zhao Tingyang argues that the traditional human rights framework fails to be universal, because it arose from contingent aspects of Western
Human rights - Wikipedia — culture, and that the concept of inalienable and unconditional human rights is in tension with the principle of justice. He proposes an alternative framework called
Human rights - Wikipedia — "credit human rights", in which rights are tied to responsibilities.[96][97]
Human rights - Wikipedia — e most common categorization of human rights is to split them into civil and political rights, and economic, social and cultural rights. Civil and political rights are
Human rights - Wikipedia — enshrined in articles 3 to 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and in the ICCPR. Economic, social and cultural rights are enshrined in articles 22 to 28 of the
Human rights - Wikipedia — Universal Declaration of Human Rights and in the ICESCR. e UDHR included both economic, social and cultural rights and civil and political rights because it was
Human rights - Wikipedia — based on the principle that the diﬀerent rights could only successfully exist in combination:
Human rights - Wikipedia — e ideal of free human beings enjoying civil and political freedom and freedom from fear and want can only be achieved if conditions are created whereby
Human rights - Wikipedia — everyone may enjoy his civil and political rights, as well as his social, economic and cultural rights

Human rights - Wikipedia — is is held to be true because without civil and political rights the public cannot assert their economic, social and cultural rights. e freedom from fear and the

Human rights - Wikipedia — Although accepted by the signatories to the UDHR, most of them do not in practice give equal weight to the diﬀerent types of rights. Western cultures have oen given
Human rights - Wikipedia — priority to civil and political rights, sometimes at the expense of economic and social rights such as the right to work, to education, health and housing. For example, in
Human rights - Wikipedia — the United States there is no universal access to healthcare free at the point of use.[98] at is not to say that Western cultures have overlooked these rights entirely (the
Human rights - Wikipedia — welfare states that exist in Western Europe are evidence of this). Similarly, the ex Soviet bloc countries and Asian countries have tended to give priority to economic,
Human rights - Wikipedia — social and cultural rights, but have oen failed to provide civil and political rights.
Human rights - Wikipedia — Another categorization, oﬀered by Karel Vasak, is that there are three generations of human rights: ﬁrst-generation civil and political rights (right to life and political
Human rights - Wikipedia — participation), second-generation economic, social and cultural rights (right to subsistence) and third-generation solidarity rights (right to peace, right to clean
Human rights - Wikipedia — environment). Out of these generations, the third generation is the most debated and lacks both legal and political recognition. is categorization is at odds with the
Human rights - Wikipedia — indivisibility of rights, as it implicitly states that some rights can exist without others. Prioritization of rights for pragmatic reasons is however a widely accepted
Human rights - Wikipedia — necessity. Human rights expert Philip Alston argues:
Human rights - Wikipedia — If every possible human rights element is deemed to be essential or necessary, then nothing will be treated as though it is truly important.[99]

Human rights - Wikipedia — not all universal, and indeed conﬂict with some cultures and threaten their survival. Rights which are most oen contested
Human rights - Wikipedia — with relativistic arguments are the rights of women. For example, female genital mutilation occurs in diﬀerent cultures in
Human rights - Wikipedia — Africa, Asia and South America. It is not mandated by any religion, but has become a tradition in many cultures. It is
Human rights - Wikipedia — considered a violation of women's and girl's rights by much of the international community, and is outlawed in some
Human rights - Wikipedia — countries.

Human rights - Wikipedia — Universal jurisdiction is a controversial principle in international law whereby states claim criminal jurisdiction over persons whose alleged crimes were commied
Human rights - Wikipedia — outside the boundaries of the prosecuting state, regardless of nationality, country of residence, or any other relation with the prosecuting country. e state backs its
Human rights - Wikipedia — claim on the grounds that the crime commied is considered a crime against all, which any state is authorized to punish. e concept of universal jurisdiction is
Human rights - Wikipedia — therefore closely linked to the idea that certain international norms are erga omnes, or owed to the entire world community, as well as the concept of jus cogens. In
Human rights - Wikipedia — 1993, Belgium passed a law of universal jurisdiction to give its court's jurisdiction over crimes against humanity in other countries, and in 1998 Augusto Pinochet was
Human rights - Wikipedia — arrested in London following an indictment by Spanish judge Baltasar Garzón under the universal jurisdiction principle.[109] e principle is supported by Amnesty
Human rights - Wikipedia — International and other human rights organisations as they believe certain crimes pose a threat to the international community as a whole and the community has a
Human rights - Wikipedia — moral duty to act, but others, including Henry Kissinger, argue that state sovereignty is paramount, because breaches of rights commied in other countries are outside
Human rights - Wikipedia — states' sovereign interest and because states could use the principle for political reasons.[110]
Human rights - Wikipedia — Companies, NGOs, political parties, informal groups, and individuals are known as non-State actors. Non-State actors can also commit human rights abuses, but are not
Human rights - Wikipedia — subject to human rights law other than International Humanitarian Law, which applies to individuals. Multinational companies play an increasingly large role in the
Human rights - Wikipedia — world, and are responsible for a large number of human rights abuses.[111] Although the legal and moral environment surrounding the actions of governments is
Human rights - Wikipedia — reasonably well developed, that surrounding multinational companies is both controversial and ill-deﬁned. Multinational companies oen view their primary
Human rights - Wikipedia — responsibility as being to their shareholders, not to those aﬀected by their actions. Such companies are oen larger than the economies of the states in which they
Human rights - Wikipedia — operate, and can wield signiﬁcant economic and political power. No international treaties exist to speciﬁcally cover the behavior of companies with regard to human
Human rights - Wikipedia — rights, and national legislation is very variable. Jean Ziegler, Special Rapporteur of the UN Commission on Human Rights on the right to food stated in a report in 2003:
Human rights - Wikipedia — the growing power of transnational corporations and their extension of power through privatization, deregulation and the rolling back of the State also mean
Human rights - Wikipedia — that it is now time to develop binding legal norms that hold corporations to human rights standards and circumscribe potential abuses of their position of
Human rights - Wikipedia — power.[112]

Biography - Wikipedia — education, work, relationships, and death; it portrays a person's experience of these life events. Unlike a proﬁle or
Biography - Wikipedia — curriculum vitae (résumé), a biography presents a subject's life story, highlighting various aspects of their life,
Biography - Wikipedia — including intimate details of experience, and may include an analysis of the subject's personality.
Biography - Wikipedia — Biographical works are usually non-ﬁction, but ﬁction can also be used to portray a person's life. One in-depth form
Biography - Wikipedia — of biographical coverage is called legacy writing. Works in diverse media, from literature to ﬁlm, form the genre
Biography - Wikipedia — known as biography.
Biography - Wikipedia — An authorized biography is wrien with the permission, cooperation, and at times, participation of a subject or a
Biography - Wikipedia — subject's heirs. An unauthorized biography is one wrien without such permission or participation. An
Biography - Wikipedia — autobiography is wrien by the person themselves, sometimes with the assistance of a collaborator or ghostwriter.
Biography - Wikipedia — At ﬁrst, biographical writings were regarded merely as a subsection of history with a focus on a particular individual
Biography - Wikipedia — of historical importance. e independent genre of biography as distinct from general history writing, began to emerge in the 18th century and reached its
Biography - Wikipedia — contemporary form at the turn of the 20th century.[1]
Biography - Wikipedia — Biography is the earliest literary genre in history. According to Egyptologist Miriam Lichtheim, writing took its ﬁrst steps toward literature in the context of the private
Biography - Wikipedia — tomb funerary inscriptions. ese were commemorative biographical texts recounting the careers of deceased high royal oﬃcials.[2] e earliest biographical texts are
Biography - Wikipedia — from the 26th century BC.
Biography - Wikipedia — In the 21st century BC, another famous biography was composed in Mesopotamia about Gilgamesh. One of the ﬁve versions could be historical.
Biography - Wikipedia — From the same region a couple of centuries later, according to another famous biography, departed Abraham. He and his 3 descendants became subjects of ancient
Biography - Wikipedia — Hebrew biographies whether ﬁctional or historical.
Biography - Wikipedia — One of the earliest Roman biographers was Cornelius Nepos, who published his work Excellentium Imperatorum Vitae ("Lives of outstanding generals") in 44 BC. Longer

Biography - Wikipedia — and more extensive biographies were wrien in Greek by Plutarch, in his Parallel Lives, published about 80 A.D. In this work
Biography - Wikipedia — famous Greeks are paired with famous Romans, for example, the orators Demosthenes and Cicero, or the generals Alexander
Biography - Wikipedia — the Great and Julius Caesar; some ﬁy biographies from the work survive. Another well-known collection of ancient
Biography - Wikipedia — biographies is De vita Caesarum ("On the Lives of the Caesars") by Suetonius, wrien about AD 121 in the time of the
Biography - Wikipedia — emperor Hadrian. Meanwhile, in the eastern imperial periphery, Gospel described the life of Jesus.
Biography - Wikipedia — In the early Middle Ages (AD 400 to 1450), there was a decline in awareness of the classical culture in Europe. During this
Biography - Wikipedia — time, the only repositories of knowledge and records of the early history in Europe were those of the Roman Catholic
Biography - Wikipedia — Church. Hermits, monks, and priests used this historic period to write biographies. eir subjects were usually restricted to
Biography - Wikipedia — the church fathers, martyrs, popes, and saints. eir works were meant to be inspirational to the people and vehicles for
Biography - Wikipedia — conversion to Christianity (see Hagiography). One signiﬁcant secular example of a biography from this period is the life of
Biography - Wikipedia — Charlemagne by his courtier Einhard.
Biography - Wikipedia — In Medieval Western India, there was a Sanskrit Jain literary genre of writing semi-historical biographical narratives about
Biography - Wikipedia — the lives of famous persons called Prabandhas. Prabandhas were wrien primarily by Jain scholars from the 13th century
Biography - Wikipedia — onwards and were wrien in colloquial Sanskrit (as opposed to Classical Sanskrit).[3] e earliest collection explicitly titled
Biography - Wikipedia — Prabandha- is Jinabhadra's Prabandhavali (1234 CE).
Biography - Wikipedia — In Medieval Islamic Civilization (c. AD 750 to 1258), similar traditional Muslim biographies of Muhammad and other important ﬁgures in the early history of Islam
Biography - Wikipedia — began to be wrien, beginning the Prophetic biography tradition. Early biographical dictionaries were published as compendia of famous Islamic personalities from the
Biography - Wikipedia — 9th century onwards. ey contained more social data for a large segment of the population than other works of that period. e earliest biographical dictionaries
Biography - Wikipedia — initially focused on the lives of the prophets of Islam and their companions, with one of these early examples being e Book of e Major Classes by Ibn Sa'd al-
Biography - Wikipedia — Baghdadi. And then began the documentation of the lives of many other historical ﬁgures (from rulers to scholars) who lived in the medieval Islamic world.[4]
Biography - Wikipedia — By the late Middle Ages, biographies became less church-oriented in Europe as biographies of kings, knights, and tyrants began to appear. e most famous of such
Biography - Wikipedia — biographies was Le Morte d'Arthur by Sir omas Malory. e book was an account of the life of the fabled King Arthur and his Knights of the Round Table. Following
Biography - Wikipedia — Malory, the new emphasis on humanism during the Renaissance promoted a focus on secular subjects, such as artists and poets, and encouraged writing in the
Biography - Wikipedia — vernacular.
Biography - Wikipedia — Giorgio Vasari's Lives of the Artists (1550) was the landmark biography focusing on secular lives. Vasari made celebrities of his subjects, as the Lives became an early
Biography - Wikipedia — "bestseller". Two other developments are noteworthy: the development of the printing press in the 15th century and the gradual increase in literacy.
Biography - Wikipedia — Biographies in the English language began appearing during the reign of Henry VIII. John Foxe's Actes and Monuments (1563), beer known as Foxe's Book of Martyrs,
Biography - Wikipedia — was essentially the ﬁrst dictionary of the biography in Europe, followed by omas Fuller's e History of the Worthies of England (1662), with a distinct focus on public
Biography - Wikipedia — life.
Biography - Wikipedia — Inﬂuential in shaping popular conceptions of pirates, A General History of the Pyrates (1724), by Charles Johnson, is the prime source for the biographies of many well-
Biography - Wikipedia — known pirates.[5]

Biography - Wikipedia — e American biography followed the English model, incorporating omas Carlyle's view that biography was a part of history.
Biography - Wikipedia — Carlyle asserted that the lives of great human beings were essential to understanding society and its institutions. While the historical
Biography - Wikipedia — impulse would remain a strong element in early American biography, American writers carved out a distinct approach. What emerged
Biography - Wikipedia — was a rather didactic form of biography, which sought to shape the individual character of a reader in the process of deﬁning national
Biography - Wikipedia — character.[6][7]
Biography - Wikipedia — e ﬁrst modern biography, and a work that exerted considerable inﬂuence on the evolution of the genre, was James Boswell's e Life of Samuel Johnson, a biography
Biography - Wikipedia — of lexicographer and man-of-leers Samuel Johnson published in 1791.[8][9][10]
Biography - Wikipedia — While Boswell's personal acquaintance with his subject only began in 1763, when Johnson was 54 years old, Boswell covered the entirety of Johnson's life by means of
Biography - Wikipedia — additional research. Itself an important stage in the development of the modern genre of biography, it has been claimed to be the greatest biography wrien in the
Biography - Wikipedia — English language. Boswell's work was unique in its level of research, which involved archival study, eye-witness accounts and interviews, its robust and aractive
Biography - Wikipedia — narrative, and its honest depiction of all aspects of Johnson's life and character – a formula which serves as the basis of biographical literature to this day.[11]
Biography - Wikipedia — Biographical writing generally stagnated during the 19th century – in many cases there was a reversal to the more familiar hagiographical method of eulogizing the
Biography - Wikipedia — dead, similar to the biographies of saints produced in Medieval times. A distinction between mass biography and literary biography began to form by the middle of the
Biography - Wikipedia — century, reﬂecting a breach between high culture and middle-class culture. However, the number of biographies in print experienced a rapid growth, thanks to an
Biography - Wikipedia — expanding reading public. is revolution in publishing made books available to a larger audience of readers. In addition, aﬀordable paperback editions of popular
Biography - Wikipedia — biographies were published for the ﬁrst time. Periodicals began publishing a sequence of biographical sketches.[12]
Biography - Wikipedia — Autobiographies became more popular, as with the rise of education and cheap printing, modern concepts of fame and celebrity began to develop. Autobiographies were
