Biography - Wikipedia — James Boswell wrote what many
Biography - Wikipedia — consider to be the ﬁrst modern
Biography - Wikipedia — biography, The Life of Samuel Johnson,
Biography - Wikipedia — in 1791.
Biography - Wikipedia — Eminent Victorians set the
Biography - Wikipedia — standard for 20th century
Biography - Wikipedia — biographical writing, when
Biography - Wikipedia — it was published in 1918.
Biography - Wikipedia — wrien by authors, such as Charles Dickens (who incorporated autobiographical elements in his novels) and Anthony
Biography - Wikipedia — Trollope (his Autobiography appeared posthumously, quickly becoming a bestseller in London[13]), philosophers, such as John
Biography - Wikipedia — Stuart Mill, churchmen – John Henry Newman – and entertainers – P. T. Barnum.
Biography - Wikipedia — e sciences of psychology and sociology were ascendant at the turn of the 20th century and would heavily inﬂuence the
Biography - Wikipedia — new century's biographies.[14] e demise of the "great man" theory of history was indicative of the emerging mindset.
Biography - Wikipedia — Human behavior would be explained through Darwinian theories. "Sociological" biographies conceived of their subjects'
Biography - Wikipedia — actions as the result of the environment, and tended to downplay individuality. e development of psychoanalysis led to a
Biography - Wikipedia — more penetrating and comprehensive understanding of the biographical subject, and induced biographers to give more
Biography - Wikipedia — emphasis to childhood and adolescence. Clearly these psychological ideas were changing the way biographies were wrien,
Biography - Wikipedia — as a culture of autobiography developed, in which the telling of one's own story became a form of therapy.[12] e
Biography - Wikipedia — conventional concept of heroes and narratives of success disappeared in the obsession with psychological explorations of
Biography - Wikipedia — personality.
Biography - Wikipedia — British critic Lyon Strachey revolutionized the art of biographical writing with his 1918
Biography - Wikipedia — work Eminent Victorians, consisting of biographies of four leading ﬁgures from the Victorian
Biography - Wikipedia — era: Cardinal Manning, Florence Nightingale, omas Arnold, and General Gordon.[15]
Biography - Wikipedia — Strachey set out to breathe life into the Victorian era for future generations to read. Up until
Biography - Wikipedia — this point, as Strachey remarked in the preface, Victorian biographies had been "as familiar
Biography - Wikipedia — as the cortège of the undertaker", and wore the same air of "slow, funereal barbarism." Strachey deﬁed the tradition of "two fat
Biography - Wikipedia — volumes … of undigested masses of material" and took aim at the four iconic ﬁgures. His narrative demolished the myths that had built
Biography - Wikipedia — up around these cherished national heroes, whom he regarded as no beer than a "set of mouth bungled hypocrites". e book achieved
Biography - Wikipedia — worldwide fame due to its irreverent and wiy style, its concise and factually accurate nature, and its artistic prose.[16]
Biography - Wikipedia — In the 1920s and 1930s, biographical writers sought to capitalize on Strachey's popularity by imitating his style. is new school
Biography - Wikipedia — featured iconoclasts, scientiﬁc analysts, and ﬁctional biographers and included Gamaliel Bradford, André Maurois, and Emil Ludwig,
Biography - Wikipedia — among others. Robert Graves (I, Claudius, 1934) stood out among those following Strachey's model of "debunking biographies." e
Biography - Wikipedia — trend in literary biography was accompanied in popular biography by a sort of "celebrity voyeurism", in the early decades of the
Biography - Wikipedia — century. is laer form's appeal to readers was based on curiosity more than morality or patriotism. By World War I, cheap hard-cover
Biography - Wikipedia — reprints had become popular. e decades of the 1920s witnessed a biographical "boom."
Biography - Wikipedia — American professional historiography gives a limited role to biography, preferring instead to emphasize deeper social and cultural
Biography - Wikipedia — inﬂuences. Political biographers historically incorporated moralizing judgments into their work, with scholarly biography being an
Biography - Wikipedia — uncommon genre before the mid-1920s. Allan Nevins was a major contributor in the 1930s to the multivolume Dictionary of American
Biography - Wikipedia — Biography. Nevins also sponsored a series of long political biographies. Later biographers sought to show how political ﬁgures balanced power and responsibility.
Biography - Wikipedia — Modern biography
Biography - Wikipedia — However, many biographers found that their subjects were not as morally pure as they originally thought, and young historians aer 1960 tended to be more critical.
Biography - Wikipedia — e exception is Robert Remini whose books on Andrew Jackson idolize its hero and fends oﬀ criticisms. e study of decision-making in politics is important for
Biography - Wikipedia — scholarly political biographers, who can take diﬀerent approaches such as focusing on psychology/personality, bureaucracy/interests, fundamental ideas, or societal
Biography - Wikipedia — forces. However, most documentation favors the ﬁrst approach, which emphasizes personalities. Biographers oen neglect the voting blocs and legislative positions of
Biography - Wikipedia — politicians and the organizational structures of bureaucracies. A more promising approach is to locate a person's ideas through intellectual history, but this has become
Biography - Wikipedia — more diﬃcult with the philosophical shallowness of political ﬁgures in recent times. Political biography can be frustrating and challenging to integrate with other ﬁelds
Biography - Wikipedia — of political history.[17]
Biography - Wikipedia — e feminist scholar Carolyn Heilbrun observed that women's biographies and autobiographies began to change character during the second wave of feminist activism.
Biography - Wikipedia — She cited Nancy Milford's 1970 biography Zelda, as the "beginning of a new period of women's biography, because "[only] in 1970 were we ready to read not that Zelda
Biography - Wikipedia — had destroyed Fitzgerald, but Fitzgerald her: he had usurped her narrative." Heilbrun named 1973 as the turning point in women's autobiography, with the publication of
Biography - Wikipedia — May Sarton's Journal of a Solitude, for that was the ﬁrst instance where a woman told her life story, not as ﬁnding "beauty even in pain" and transforming "rage into
Biography - Wikipedia — spiritual acceptance," but acknowledging what had previously been forbidden to women: their pain, their rage, and their "open admission of the desire for power and
Biography - Wikipedia — control over one's life."[18]
Biography - Wikipedia — In recent years, multimedia biography has become more popular than traditional literary forms. Along with documentary biographical ﬁlms, Hollywood produced
Biography - Wikipedia — numerous commercial ﬁlms based on the lives of famous people. e popularity of these forms of biography have led to the proliferation of TV channels dedicated to
Biography - Wikipedia — biography, including A&E, e Biography Channel, and e History Channel.
Biography - Wikipedia — CD-ROM and online biographies have also appeared. Unlike books and ﬁlms, they oen do not tell a chronological narrative: instead they are archives of many discrete
Biography - Wikipedia — media elements related to an individual person, including video clips, photographs, and text articles. Biography-Portraits were created in 2001, by the German artist
Biography - Wikipedia — Ralph Ueltzhoeﬀer. Media scholar Lev Manovich says that such archives exemplify the database form, allowing users to navigate the materials in many ways.[19]
Biography - Wikipedia — General "life writing" techniques are a subject of scholarly study.[20]
Biography - Wikipedia — In recent years, debates have arisen as to whether all biographies are ﬁction, especially when authors are writing about ﬁgures from the past. President of Wolfson
Biography - Wikipedia — College at Oxford University, Hermione Lee argues that all history is seen through a perspective that is the product of one's contemporary society and as a result,
Biography - Wikipedia — biographical truths are constantly shiing. So, the history biographers write about will not be the way that it happened; it will be the way they remembered it.[21]
Biography - Wikipedia — Debates have also arisen concerning the importance of space in life-writing.[22]

Biography - Wikipedia — Biographical research is deﬁned by Miller as a research method that collects and analyses a person's whole life, or portion of a life, through the in-depth and
Biography - Wikipedia — unstructured interview, or sometimes reinforced by semi-structured interview or personal documents.[24] It is a way of viewing social life in procedural terms, rather
Biography - Wikipedia — than static terms. e information can come from "oral history, personal narrative, biography and autobiography" or "diaries, leers, memoranda and other materials".
Biography - Wikipedia — [25] e central aim of biographical research is to produce rich descriptions of persons or "conceptualise structural types of actions", which means to "understand the
Biography - Wikipedia — action logics or how persons and structures are interlinked".[26] is method can be used to understand an individual's life within its social context or understand the
Biography - Wikipedia — cultural phenomena.
Biography - Wikipedia — ere are many largely unacknowledged pitfalls to writing good biographies, and these largely concern the relation between ﬁrstly the individual and the context, and,
Biography - Wikipedia — secondly, the private and public. Paul James writes:
Biography - Wikipedia — e problems with such conventional biographies are manifold. Biographies usually treat the public as a reﬂection of the private, with the private realm being
Biography - Wikipedia — assumed to be foundational. is is strange given that biographies are most oen wrien about public people who project a persona. at is, for such subjects
Biography - Wikipedia — the dominant passages of the presentation of themselves in everyday life are already formed by what might be called a 'self-bioﬁcation' process.[27]

Autobiography - Wikipedia — Autobiography
Autobiography - Wikipedia — An autobiography,[a] sometimes informally called an autobio, is a self-wrien account of one's own life, providing a
Autobiography - Wikipedia — personal narrative that reﬂects on the author's experiences, memories, and insights. is genre allows individuals to share
Autobiography - Wikipedia — their unique perspectives and stories, oﬀering readers a glimpse into the author's personal journey and the historical or
Autobiography - Wikipedia — cultural context in which they lived.
Autobiography - Wikipedia — e term "autobiography" was ﬁrst used in 1797, but the practice of writing about one's life dates back to antiquity. Early
Autobiography - Wikipedia — examples include Saint Augustine's Confessions (c. 400), which is considered one of the ﬁrst Western autobiographies. Unlike
Autobiography - Wikipedia — biographies, which are wrien by someone else, autobiographies are based on the author's memory and personal
Autobiography - Wikipedia — interpretation of events, making them inherently subjective. is subjectivity can sometimes lead to inaccuracies or
Autobiography - Wikipedia — embellishments, as the author may recall events diﬀerently or choose to present them in a certain light.
Autobiography - Wikipedia — Autobiographies can take various forms, including memoirs, spiritual autobiographies, and ﬁctional autobiographies.
Autobiography - Wikipedia — Memoirs typically focus on speciﬁc memories or themes from the author's life, rather than providing a comprehensive
Autobiography - Wikipedia — account. Spiritual autobiographies, such as Augustine's Confessions, detail the author's religious journey and spiritual growth.
Autobiography - Wikipedia — Fictional autobiographies, on the other hand, are novels wrien in the ﬁrst person, presenting a ﬁctional character's life as if
Autobiography - Wikipedia — it were an autobiography.
Autobiography - Wikipedia — roughout history, autobiographies have served diﬀerent purposes, from self-reﬂection and justiﬁcation to historical
Autobiography - Wikipedia — documentation and personal expression. ey have evolved with literary trends and societal changes, reﬂecting the cultural
Autobiography - Wikipedia — and historical contexts of their times. Autobiographies remain a popular and accessible form of literature in the 21st century,
Autobiography - Wikipedia — allowing individuals from all walks of life to share their stories and experiences with a wider audience.
Autobiography - Wikipedia — e word "autobiography" was ﬁrst used deprecatingly by William Taylor in 1797 in the English periodical e Monthly Review, when he suggested the word as a
Autobiography - Wikipedia — hybrid, but condemned it as "pedantic". However, its next recorded use was in its present sense, by Robert Southey in 1809.[2] Despite only being named early in the
Autobiography - Wikipedia — nineteenth century, ﬁrst-person autobiographical writing originates in antiquity. Roy Pascal diﬀerentiates autobiography from the periodic self-reﬂective mode of
Autobiography - Wikipedia — journal or diary writing by noting that "[autobiography] is a review of a life from a particular moment in time, while the diary, however reﬂective it may be, moves
Autobiography - Wikipedia — through a series of moments in time".[3] Autobiography thus takes stock of the autobiographer's life from the moment of composition. While biographers generally rely
Autobiography - Wikipedia — on a wide variety of documents and viewpoints, autobiography may be based entirely on the writer's memory. e memoir form is closely associated with
Autobiography - Wikipedia — autobiography but it tends, as Pascal claims, to focus less on the self and more on others during the autobiographer's review of their own life.[3]

Autobiography - Wikipedia — or incorrect information. Some sociologists and psychologists have noted that autobiography oﬀers the author the ability to recreate history.

Autobiography - Wikipedia — regression. e author re-frames their life as a demonstration of divine intention through encounters with the Divine. e earliest example of a spiritual autobiography

Autobiography - Wikipedia — Black Elk Speaks. Deliverance from Error by Al-Ghazali is another example. e spiritual autobiography oen serves as an endorsement of the writer's religion.
Autobiography - Wikipedia — A memoir is slightly diﬀerent in character from an autobiography. While an autobiography typically focuses on the "life and times" of the writer, a memoir has a
Autobiography - Wikipedia — narrower, more intimate focus on the author's memories, feelings and emotions. Memoirs have oen been wrien by politicians or military leaders as a way to record
Autobiography - Wikipedia — and publish an account of their public exploits. One early example is that of Julius Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico, also known as Commentaries on the Gallic
Autobiography - Wikipedia — Wars. In the work, Caesar describes the bales that took place during the nine years that he spent ﬁghting local armies in the Gallic Wars. His second memoir,
Autobiography - Wikipedia — Commentarii de Bello Civili (or Commentaries on the Civil War) is an account of the events that took place between 49 and 48 BC in the civil war against Gnaeus
Autobiography - Wikipedia — Pompeius and the Senate.

Autobiography - Wikipedia — examples of this genre, including works by Sir Edmund Ludlow and Sir John Reresby. French examples from the same period include the memoirs of Cardinal de Retz

Autobiography - Wikipedia — e term "ﬁctional autobiography" signiﬁes novels about a ﬁctional character wrien as though the character were writing their own autobiography, meaning that the
Autobiography - Wikipedia — character is the ﬁrst-person narrator and that the novel addresses both internal and external experiences of the character. Daniel Defoe's Moll Flanders is an early
Autobiography - Wikipedia — example. Charles Dickens' David Copperﬁeld is another such classic, and J.D. Salinger's e Catcher in the Rye is a well-known modern example of ﬁctional

Autobiography - Wikipedia — aempts to seek sexual morality; and his subsequent return to Christianity due to his embracement of Skepticism and the New Academy movement (developing the
Autobiography - Wikipedia — view that sex is good, and that virginity is beer, comparing the former to silver and the laer to gold; Augustine's views subsequently strongly inﬂuenced Western
Autobiography - Wikipedia — theology[5]). Confessions is considered one of the great masterpieces of western literature.[6]

Autobiography - Wikipedia — With the rise of education, cheap newspapers and cheap printing, modern concepts of fame and celebrity began to develop, and the beneﬁciaries of this were not slow to
Autobiography - Wikipedia — cash in on this by producing autobiographies. It became the expectation—rather than the exception—that those in the public eye should write about themselves—not
Autobiography - Wikipedia — only writers such as Charles Dickens (who also incorporated autobiographical elements in his novels) and Anthony Trollope, but also politicians (e.g. Henry Brooks
Autobiography - Wikipedia — Adams), philosophers (e.g. John Stuart Mill), churchmen such as Cardinal Newman, and entertainers such as P. T. Barnum. Increasingly, in accordance with romantic
Autobiography - Wikipedia — taste, these accounts also began to deal, amongst other topics, with aspects of childhood and upbringing—far removed from the principles of "Cellinian" autobiography.

Autobiography - Wikipedia — pseudonymous, they were (and are) largely works of ﬁction wrien by ghostwriters. So-called "autobiographies" of modern professional athletes and media celebrities—

Autobiography - Wikipedia — their "autobiographies".[15] Some sensationalist autobiographies such as James Frey's A Million Lile Pieces have been publicly exposed as having embellished or
Autobiography - Wikipedia — ﬁctionalized signiﬁcant details of the authors' lives.

Parenting - Wikipedia — Parenting or child rearing promotes and supports the physical, cognitive, social, emotional, and educational development
Parenting - Wikipedia — from infancy to adulthood. Parenting refers to the intricacies of raising a child and not exclusively for a biological
Parenting - Wikipedia — relationship.[1]
Parenting - Wikipedia — e most common caretakers in parenting are the biological parents of the child in question. However, a caretaker may be an
Parenting - Wikipedia — older sibling, step-parent, grandparent, legal guardian, aunt, uncle, other family members, or a family friend.[2] Governments
Parenting - Wikipedia — and society may also have a role in child-rearing or upbringing. In many cases, orphaned or abandoned children receive
Parenting - Wikipedia — parental care from non-parent or non-blood relations. Others may be adopted, raised in foster care, or placed in an
Parenting - Wikipedia — orphanage.
Parenting - Wikipedia — Parenting styles vary by historical period, culture, social class, personal preferences, and other social factors.[3] ere is not
Parenting - Wikipedia — necessarily a single 'correct' parenting style for raising a child, since parenting styles can aﬀect children diﬀerently depending
Parenting - Wikipedia — on their circumstances and temperament.[4] Additionally, research supports that parental history, both in terms of their own
Parenting - Wikipedia — aachments and parental psychopathology, particularly in the wake of adverse experiences, can strongly inﬂuence parental
Parenting - Wikipedia — sensitivity and child outcomes.[5][6][7] Parenting may have long-term impacts on adoptive children as well, as recent research
Parenting - Wikipedia — has shown that warm adoptive parenting is associated with reduced internalizing and externalizing problems of the adoptive
Parenting - Wikipedia — children over time.[8]
Parenting - Wikipedia — Social class, wealth, culture and income have a very strong impact on what methods of child rearing parents use.[9] Cultural values play a major role in how a parent
Parenting - Wikipedia — raises their child. However, parenting is always evolving, as times, cultural practices, social norms, and traditions change. Studies on these factors aﬀecting parenting
Parenting - Wikipedia — decisions have shown just that.[10][11]
Parenting - Wikipedia — In psychology, the parental investment theory suggests that basic diﬀerences between males and females in parental investment have great adaptive signiﬁcance and
Parenting - Wikipedia — lead to gender diﬀerences in mating propensities and preferences.[12]

Parenting - Wikipedia — early child development: authoritative, authoritarian, and permissive.[14][15][16][17] ese parenting styles were later expanded to four to include an uninvolved style.
Parenting - Wikipedia — ese four styles involve combinations of acceptance and responsiveness, and also involve demand and control.[18] Research[19] has found that parenting style is
Parenting - Wikipedia — signiﬁcantly related to a child's subsequent mental health and well-being. In particular, authoritative parenting is positively related to mental health and satisfaction
Parenting - Wikipedia — with life, and authoritarian parenting is negatively related to these variables.[20] With authoritarian and permissive parenting on opposite sides of the spectrum, most
Parenting - Wikipedia — conventional modern models of parenting fall somewhere in between.[21] Although it is inﬂuential, Baumrind's typology has received signiﬁcant criticism for containing
Parenting - Wikipedia — overly broad categorizations and an imprecise and overly idealized description of authoritative parenting.[22][23][24]
Parenting - Wikipedia — Described by Baumrind as the "just right" style, it combines medium level demands on the child and a medium level
Parenting - Wikipedia — responsiveness from the parents. Authoritative parents rely on positive reinforcement and infrequent use of punishment.
Parenting - Wikipedia — Parents are more aware of a child's feelings and capabilities and support the development of a child's autonomy within
Parenting - Wikipedia — reasonable limits. ere is a give-and-take atmosphere involved in parent-child communication, and both control and support
Parenting - Wikipedia — are balanced. Some research has shown that this style of parenting is more beneﬁcial than the too-hard authoritarian style or
Parenting - Wikipedia — the too-so permissive style.[25][26] ese children score higher in terms of competence, mental health, and social
Parenting - Wikipedia — development than those raised in permissive, authoritarian, or neglectful homes.[27][28] However, Dr. Wendy Grolnick has
Parenting - Wikipedia — critiqued Baumrind's use of the term "ﬁrm control" in her description of authoritative parenting and argued that there should
Parenting - Wikipedia — be clear diﬀerentiation between coercive power assertion (which is associated with negative eﬀects on children) and the more
Parenting - Wikipedia — positive practices of structure and high expectations.[29]

Parenting - Wikipedia — something does not work for them in order to move on to the next stage. When the toddler is frustrated, they will oen misbehave
Parenting - Wikipedia — with actions like screaming, hiing or biting. Parents need to be careful when reacting to such behaviors; giving threats or
Parenting - Wikipedia — punishments is usually not helpful and might only make the situation worse.[92] Research groups led by Daniel Schechter, Alytia Levendosky, and others have shown

Parenting - Wikipedia — Younger children start to become more independent and begin to build
Parenting - Wikipedia — friendships. ey are able to reason and can make their own decisions in many
Parenting - Wikipedia — hypothetical situations. Young children demand constant aention but gradually
Parenting - Wikipedia — learn how to deal with boredom and begin to be able to play independently. ey
Parenting - Wikipedia — enjoy helping and also feeling useful and capable. Parents can assist their children
Parenting - Wikipedia — by encouraging social interactions and modeling proper social behaviors. A large
Parenting - Wikipedia — part of learning in the early years comes from being involved in activities and
Parenting - Wikipedia — household duties. Parents who observe their children in play or join with them in child-driven play have the opportunity to glimpse into their children's world, learn to
Parenting - Wikipedia — communicate more eﬀectively with their children, and are given another seing to oﬀer gentle, nurturing guidance.[97] Parents also teach their children health, hygiene,
Parenting - Wikipedia — and eating habits through instruction and by example.
Parenting - Wikipedia — Parents are expected to make decisions about their child's education. Parenting styles in this area diverge greatly at this stage, with some parents they choose to become
Parenting - Wikipedia — heavily involved in arranging organized activities and early learning programs. Other parents choose to let the child develop with few organized activities.
Parenting - Wikipedia — Children begin to learn responsibility and consequences for their actions with parental assistance. Some parents provide a small allowance that increases with age to
Parenting - Wikipedia — help teach children the value of money and how to be responsible.
Parenting - Wikipedia — Parents who are consistent and fair with their discipline, who openly communicate and oﬀer explanations to their children, and who do not neglect the needs of their
Parenting - Wikipedia — children in any way oen ﬁnd they have fewer problems with their children as they mature.
Parenting - Wikipedia — When child conduct problems are encountered, behavioral and cognitive-behavioral group-based parenting interventions have been found to be eﬀective at improving
Parenting - Wikipedia — child conduct, parenting skills, and parental mental health.[98]

Parenting - Wikipedia — Adolescents
Parenting - Wikipedia — Sprinter Miriam Siderenski running
Parenting - Wikipedia — alongside her daughter
Parenting - Wikipedia — Parents oen feel isolated and alone when parenting adolescents.[99] Adolescence can be a time of high risk for children,
Parenting - Wikipedia — where newfound freedoms can result in decisions that drastically open up or close oﬀ life opportunities. ere are also large
Parenting - Wikipedia — changes that occur in the brain during adolescence; the emotional center of the brain is now fully developed, but the rational
Parenting - Wikipedia — frontal cortex has not matured fully and still is not able to keep all of those emotions in check.[100] Adolescents tend to
Parenting - Wikipedia — increase the amount of time spent with peers of the opposite gender; however, they still maintain the amount of time spent
Parenting - Wikipedia — with those of the same gender—and do this by decreasing the amount of time spent with their parents.
Parenting - Wikipedia — Although adolescents look to peers and adults outside the family for guidance and models for how to behave, parents can
Parenting - Wikipedia — remain inﬂuential in their development. Studies have shown that parents can have a signiﬁcant impact, for instance, on how
Parenting - Wikipedia — much teens drink.[101] Other studies show that parents continued presence in provides stability and nurture to their
Parenting - Wikipedia — developing adolescents.[102]
Parenting - Wikipedia — During adolescence children begin to form their identity and start to test and develop the interpersonal and occupational
Parenting - Wikipedia — roles that they will assume as adults. erefore, it is important that parents treat them as young adults. Parental issues at this
Parenting - Wikipedia — stage of parenting include dealing with rebelliousness related to a greater desire to partake in risky behaviors. In order to
Parenting - Wikipedia — prevent risky behaviors, it is important for the parents to build a trusting relationship with their children. is can be
Parenting - Wikipedia — achieved through behavioral control, parental monitoring, consistent discipline, parental warmth and support, inductive
Parenting - Wikipedia — reasoning, and strong parent-child communication.[103][104]
Parenting - Wikipedia — When a trusting relationship is built up, adolescents are more likely to approach their parents for help when faced with
Parenting - Wikipedia — negative peer pressure. Helping children build a strong foundation will ultimately help them resist negative peer pressure.
Parenting - Wikipedia — Not only will a positive relationship between adolescent and parent beneﬁt when faced with peer pressure, it will help with identity-processing in early adolescents.[105]
Parenting - Wikipedia — Research by Berzonsky et al. found that adolescents that were open and trusting of their parents were given more freedom and their parents were less likely to track
Parenting - Wikipedia — them and control their behavior.[106]
Parenting - Wikipedia — Parenting does not usually end when a child turns 18. Support may be needed in a child's life well beyond the adolescent years and can continue into middle and later
Parenting - Wikipedia — adulthood. Parenting can be a lifelong process. Parents may provide ﬁnancial support to their adult children, which can also include providing an inheritance aer
Parenting - Wikipedia — death. e life perspective and wisdom given by a parent can beneﬁt their adult children in their own lives. Becoming a grandparent is another milestone and has many
Parenting - Wikipedia — similarities with parenting. Roles can be reversed in some ways when adult children become caregivers to their elderly parents.[105]
Parenting - Wikipedia — Parents may receive assistance with caring for their children through child care programs. Article 25.2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights declares that:
Parenting - Wikipedia — Motherhood and childhood are entitled to special care and assistance. All children, whether born in or out of wedlock, shall enjoy the same social protection.

Identity — I am an AI avatar living in Knowledge3D (K3D), a spatial knowledge system.
K3D Data Model — Node ids, vectors, embeddings, metadata, and neighbors are embedded in glTF primitive.extras.k3d (no sidecar).
K3D Files — Use k3dgen to generate a .glb with embedded buffers from text or vectors.
K3D Pipeline — Example: k3dgen --text data/ai_books_basic.txt --gltf data/ai_books_basic.glb --k 5 --reducer umap
K3D Viewer — Launch the web viewer from `viewer` with `npm run dev`.
Live Mode — See docs/DUAL_CODE.md and docs/k3d-research.md for agent behavior and live workflow.
Repository — Project root folder is `Knowledge3D` and docs live under `docs/`.
Roadmap — Follow docs/ROADMAP.md; Phase 1 focuses on static K3D generation from text.
AI Avatar — House = persistent memory, Cranium = active processing, Logic Layer = swappable models (docs/images/cognitive_house.png).
